Furthermore, they may be penalized within the Saṃgha by being ordered to prostrate, rebuked, censured, or deprived of their share of the community's benefits.

Alternatively, they may be made to cast themselves prostrate on the ground before the Saṃgha to confess their transgressions, or at times they may be expelled so as not to dwell together with the community.
I know the various natures of sentient beings and the directions in which their minds tend, and I am able to inspire in them faith and understanding.

For their benefit, I eliminate their darkness, dry up the swift currents [of suffering], and enable them to attain the bliss of nirvana. Desiring to discipline those who violate the precepts, I extensively expound upon the various sutras concerning the sufferings of the hells and other realms.

If there are sentient beings who can give rise to faith, reverence, and the skillful means of a pure mind, I shall explain various roots of goodness according to their individual capacities and characteristics, so that they may become endowed with virtue and even reach the city of fearlessness.
"Good son! This is called the third wheel.

By means of this wheel, according to the various inclinations attained by those sentient beings, they cultivate all manner of karmas and fully possess the roots of goodness; they are brought to peace and security, reaching the place of fearlessness. Just as that Worthy and Holy One turns the Buddha’s Wheel of Dharma, external paths and hostile enemies are naturally subdued, and he is able to roar the lion's roar."

“Good son! For example, suppose there is a consecrated Kṣatriya great king whose subjects have various kinds of wrong refuge, wrong views, wrong understanding, and wrong renunciation; or who, being devoted solely to such auspicious signs, cause immeasurable suffering and harm to sentient beings.

The consecrated Great King, by means of the ancient laws of his predecessors, caused those sentient beings to single-mindedly practice and study so as to eliminate their inverted views, and also caused them to practice the virtuous methods of statecraft established by his predecessors.

The consecrated Kṣatriya Great King establishes a law that causes all sentient beings to become of one mind, together disciplined, sharing the same aspirations and the same desires, and uniting them so that they all turn toward the same goal in harmony.
In accordance with the ancient laws of the former kings, they receive and obey imperial edicts; all together they submit and collectively uphold the national law.

At that time, the consecrated Kṣatriya Great King constantly shares his food and drink with the people of the land and enjoys their company in play and pleasure. They do not harbor mutual suspicion or doubt, but trust one another in heart as they jointly carry out the royal law. This is called the fourth wheel of the consecrated Great King.
"By means of such a wheel, one can cause one's own kingdom to flourish in every way, subdue all enemies, and ensure the preservation of the realm and the protection of one's life."
"Good son! The Tathāgata, the World-Honored One, perceives that sentient beings possess various kinds of false refuges, false views, and delight in false karma.

Observing all sentient beings through these causes and conditions, he has, in the presence of the great assemblies before the Buddhas and Tathāgatas of the past, repeatedly revealed the causes and effects of the Buddha-dharma, preached the practice of the Six Pāramitās as the right path, and expounded upon the holy seeds of the Triple Gem—Buddha, Dharma, and Saṅgha. He has repeatedly manifested all karmic retributions, instructing, benefiting, and gladdening them to lead them forward, so that all those with false views may attain liberation, and likewise bring the fourfold assembly to complete liberation."

Fully cultivating wholesome conduct, gentle and compliant, they sport within the four foundations of mindfulness; regarding the path of knowledge and vision for liberation, they attain complete happiness and cause the Dharma to abide for a long time.

They cause the lineage of the Triple Gem to never be severed, and even regarding the four right efforts, the four bases of power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, and the eightfold noble path, as well as all meditative concentrations, liberations, and knowledge-and-vision, they attain complete mastery and unimpeded play.
Thus it is, good son! This is called the fourth wheel of the Tathāgata.

Because the Tathāgata has accomplished such a wheel, he causes all sentient beings to take refuge in him, to cultivate all wholesome deeds, and to share in his knowledge and vision; he brings them peace, security, and happiness, causing them all to dwell in the ground of fearlessness.
In the place realized by the Exalted Great Seer, he turns the Wheel of the Dharma, which no śramaṇa, brāhmaṇa, Brahmā, Māra, or deva can turn.
He subdues the celestial Māras, all external paths, and can roar the lion’s roar amidst the fourfold assembly. "Good son!
It is like a consecrated great king who, regarding his own country and the people of other lands, as well as the beauty of his own wife, never feels satiated in his heart."

They develop greedy attachment toward the property and wives of others; they guard city walls and prohibit various goods, strictly restricting access to the kingdom, villages, towns, and royal palaces, even down to the frontier outposts, making these defenses extremely dense and secure.
"Good son! This is called the fifth wheel of restraint of the consecrated great king.

When the consecrated king has thus accomplished this wheel, he is able to cause all external enemies and adversaries to be completely subdued, and he also ensures that his own kingdom constantly prospers and that the lives of its inhabitants are protected."

“Good son! The Tathāgata, the Arhat, is able to cause Māra Pāpīyān, the ninety-five kinds of heterodox outsiders, and all immeasurable sentient beings to have no sense of satiety regarding their own possessions; even to the point that they wish to harm me by using fire pits and poisoned rice, pushing down mountains to crush me, releasing intoxicated elephants, or drawing sharp swords—with such means as these they pursue me. Some scatter filth and dirt upon the Buddha, some slander the Tathāgata with lustful desires, or say he is neither a human nor a great man. Through various forms of calumny and disparagement, they utter evil curses against the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha; and for the sake of various gains and conditions, they give rise to jealousy and slander the Śrāvakas.”

The Tathāgata, the World-Honored One, who well guards the six sense faculties and dwells in the four Brahma-abodes, instructs the śrāvakas—sometimes by means of the four foundations of mindfulness and sometimes by means of the four analytical knowledges—and for them he expounds the three gates of liberation of the śrāvakas.
In this way, the Tathāgata possesses various modes; whether by means of mundane dharmas or supramundane dharmas, he is able to cause all things to be known as they truly are.
"Good son! This is called the fifth wheel of the Tathāgata.

The Tathāgata cultivates this wheel by means of supramundane wisdom, causing other sentient beings to take refuge in various ways; they all share in his same livelihood and common knowledge and vision, dwelling in peace, happiness, and fearlessness."

In these abodes of the most exalted great seers, the wheel of the Buddha’s Dharma is turned—a wheel that śramaṇas, brahmins, Brahmās, Māras, and devas cannot turn—and which completely subdues all celestial Māras and non-Buddhist paths, enabling one to roar the lion’s roar amidst the fourfold assembly.
The Vaipulya Daśacakra Sūtra, Volume Two;
The Vaipulya Daśacakra Sūtra, Volume Three.
Translator unknown; now appended to the Northern Liang Record.
Chapter Four: The Parable of the Consecration “Good son!

It is like a consecrated Kṣatriya great king who has fully prepared all the secret essential dharmas for his protection. Thereafter, surrounded by his palace ladies and court beauties, he indulges in the five desires, living in negligence and self-indulgence; he does not restrain the six sense faculties but gives rein to his passions for pleasure. This is called the sixth wheel of the consecrated Kṣatriya great king.”
All external enemies and adversaries are completely subdued, and one’s own kingdom is augmented with long life.
Son of good family!
The Tathāgatas, World-Honored Ones, as well as the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas and the assembly of Śrāvakas, deeply protect themselves so as to attain fearlessness.

"At that time, the Tathāgata entered the first dhyāna, the second, the third, and even the fourth dhyāna; he entered the sphere of infinite space, the sphere of infinite consciousness, the sphere of nothingness, and the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, fully entering the samādhis that are the spheres of practice of all Buddhas."

"At that time, when the Tathāgata had entered into samādhi, there were immeasurable billions of nayutas of devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, humans, and non-humans; as well as pretas, piśācas, pūtanas, and kaṭapūtanas—beings of coarse and evil minds, stubborn and perverse in their intentions, devoid of compassion, who did not give rise to thoughts of loving-kindness toward sentient beings and claimed that there is no future world."

Because they behold me entering the Samādhi of Entering the Sphere of Action of All Buddhas, they attain supreme joy; they achieve the most excellent prosperity regarding the Triple Gem, and they experience unprecedented love, delight, reverence, and respect. They abandon all evil intentions and frequently repent their transgressions. In a single kṣaṇa, they are able to completely extinguish all kinds of immeasurable and innumerable karmic obstructions, afflictive obstructions, and dharma obstructions. They become fully endowed with merit and wisdom, turn their backs on saṃsāra and head toward nirvāṇa, and all of them come to protect and uphold the Buddha-dharma. This is called the sixth wheel of the Tathāgata.

"Because the Tathāgata has accomplished such wheels as these, he severs the fetters of sentient beings through dhyāna, vimokṣa, and samāpatti; by means of this wisdom, he extinguishes all afflictions, reaches the state of peace and security, and attains fearlessness."
The Great, Exalted, and Victorious Sage turns the Brahma-wheel, which no śramaṇa, brāhmaṇa, Māra, or Brahmā can turn.
Having utterly subdued all external paths, afflictions, and adversaries, he roars the lion’s roar amidst the fourfold assembly.

“Good son! It is like a consecrated Kṣatriya great king who, together with his fourfold army, surveys his entire kingdom—including its cities, towns, villages, gardens, trees, fields, marshes, springs, ponds, ravines, valleys, hills, streams, and all wildernesses—and observes all the resources therein. If there are places where he fears many threats from enemy nations or hostile bandits, the Kṣatriya great king will station loyal guards in those locations to ward off the enemies and bandits, thereby well-protecting his own kingdom and ensuring its peace and happiness. This is called the seventh wheel of the consecrated Kṣatriya great king.”
All external enemies are completely subdued; one’s own country is strengthened, and one’s lifespan is extended. In this way, son of good family!

The Tathāgata, the World-Honored One, reveals the Buddha-eye for the sake of all sentient beings: if there is a mind of desire, he knows the mind of desire as it truly is; if there is a mind of hatred, he knows the mind of hatred as it truly is; if there is a mind of delusion, he knows the mind of delusion as it truly is. Furthermore, he knows that sentient beings have various ailments caused by their afflictions, and he knows them as they truly are according to their respective conduct.

In all such places as these, the Tathāgata, through the power of skillful means and diligence, causes all sentient beings to eliminate their afflictions by means of the medicine of meditative concentration, according to their respective categories and faculties.

If there are sentient beings who have much greed and attachment, he teaches them the meditation on impurity; if there are sentient beings who can be cured by the four Brahma-vihāras, he teaches them to cultivate the four Brahma-vihāras; if there are sentient beings who have much ignorance, he teaches them to contemplate dependent origination; if there are sentient beings who should cultivate counting the breath, he teaches them counting the breath; if there are sentient beings who should cultivate the three gates of liberation, he teaches them the three gates of liberation; if there are sentient beings who should cultivate meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), he teaches them meditative concentration; if there are sentient beings who should cultivate the formless attainments (*ārūpya-samāpatti*), he teaches them the formless attainments; and even for those sentient beings whose afflictions and illnesses should be severed by the Śūraṅgama Samādhi, he likewise teaches them to cultivate the Śūraṅgama Samādhi.
Why is this? It is so that sentient beings do not fall into the four māras, thereby enabling them to attain mastery and sever the paths of humans and devas;
nor does it allow sentient beings to enter the evil destinies and sever the seeds of the Three Jewels.
"O son of good family!
The Tathāgata is able to know all destinations; this is called the seventh wheel of the Tathāgata.

Because the Tathāgata has accomplished such a wheel, he has reached the place of peace and attained fearlessness. As a great and supreme sage, he is able to turn the Wheel of Dharma, which no śramaṇas, brahmins, māras, or Brahmās can turn."
Having completely subdued all other non-Buddhists and adversaries, he lets out a lion’s roar amidst the fourfold assembly:
“Good son! It is like a consecrated Kṣatriya great king who, for the sake of all sentient beings, keeps in mind his ancestral lineage.”

From the place where he was born during his childhood play, through his various baths, reclining, and nursing; from the clipping and grooming of all his nails on hands and feet, to the massaging of his limbs and joints; even including his playful handling of dust and earth, his service and offerings, his training in immeasurable varieties of arts and crafts, his travels to other lands and his dwellings by day and night; his respectful service to kings and great ministers, and his progression from being a crown prince until ascending the throne—having thus become a Great King, he now enjoys all manner of pleasures with sovereign ease and without hindrance.

At that time, from all directions, the four intermediate points, above, and below, there arose great sounds proclaiming verses of praise, wishing that he might always rule the kingdom with the True Dharma and not afflict sentient beings, for the sake of protecting the land; this is called the eighth wheel of the consecrated Great King of the Kṣatriya caste.

"Once such a wheel has been accomplished, at that time the consecrated Kṣatriya Great King will be able to cause all externalists and enemies to be completely subdued, and he shall preserve his own life-span so that it may increase."
In this way, noble son!

The Tathāgata, the World-Honored One, contemplates past lives among the great assembly—recalling one life, two lives, three lives, and even immeasurable hundreds of thousands of billions of births; he recalls the formation of kalpas and the destruction of kalpas, even all the formations and destructions throughout immeasurable billions of kalpas.

"I was born in such a place, of such a lineage, with such a name, in such a birthplace; I ate such food, experienced such suffering and pleasure, had such a long life, remained for such a duration, and reached such a limit of lifespan. Having passed away from there, I was reborn here; and having again passed away from here, I was reborn there. He is able to know all those characteristics and locations, as well as the various distinct details of his past lives. This is called the eighth wheel of the Tathāgata.

“Having accomplished such a wheel as this, the Tathāgata reaches the state of peace and attains fearlessness; as the most supreme Great Sage, he turns the Wheel of Dharma, which cannot be turned by any śramaṇas, brahmins, Māras, or Brahmās; he completely subdues all externalists and adversaries, and utters the lion’s roar amidst the fourfold assembly.”
“Good son! It is like a consecrated Kṣatriya great king who, regarding all the people within his realm, fully knows their origins, their lineages, and their kinsmen;
he knows them all to be brave and strong, and their various skills and arts; he knows their poverty, and—
Whether wealthy, handsome, or ugly, even unto the time of death, they may die at the end of their natural lifespan due to their own karma;
or they may die executed for violating the king’s law; or they may die an untimely death through mutual slaughter;
or they may die from being whipped, flogged, imprisoned, or bound; or they may die through arts, warfare, or strife.
Whether it be due to wealth and possessions, or desire, or anger, or hunger and thirst, or one’s own faults and afflictions,
or old age and death, or middle age, or youth, or the performance of wholesome deeds,
or the performance of unwholesome deeds— he thoroughly discerns the causes and conditions for all who die.
The Fundamental Text: "He reflects thus:

'If there are sentient beings who cultivate the causes and conditions of goodness with the desire to be born in the heavens, or there are sentient beings who cultivate the causes and conditions of evil and head toward the evil realms.'"

Thus he reflects: "I shall cultivate wholesome conduct of body, wholesome conduct of speech, and wholesome conduct of mind; I will constantly employ skillful means to teach and encourage the cultivation of generosity, so that all may be tamed and brought into accord with this practice."
"When one's life comes to an end, one shall be reborn in the heavens, dwelling forever in the auspicious realms and remaining far removed from the evil paths.
Thus it is, O consecrated Kṣatriya Great King!

Diligently cultivate all wholesome deeds of body and speech, and take pleasure in practicing generosity by giving food, drink, clothing, elephants, horses, vehicles, bedding, medicine, and all manner of necessities—even bestowing servants, male and female slaves, and attendants—and furthermore, relinquishing your head, eyes, hands, and feet, not begrudging even your own body or life.
They completely abandon killing, stealing, sexual misconduct, false speech, harsh speech, divisive speech, frivolous speech, greed, anger, and wrong views.

"Thus, an anointed Kṣatriya great king possesses ten kinds of benefits: he protects his good reputation and acquires wealth and enterprise; his physical marks are subtle and excellent, and he gains many followers; he has little illness and little affliction, and he obtains a retinue of wise and virtuous people; he proceeds toward auspicious realms, where all provide him with offerings and serve him closely; his fame reaches the ten directions, and everyone recites verses in praise of him; all the great celestial deities come to protect him; and when his body perishes and his life ends, he is reborn in the heavens. This is called the ninth wheel of the anointed Kṣatriya great king."
"Having accomplished such a wheel, the realm is augmented and life is extended.
In this way, son of good family!

The Tathāgata, the World-Honored One, for the sake of all sentient beings, knows truly and as it is how others die here and are reborn there: if there are sentient beings who have accomplished unwholesome bodily karma, unwholesome verbal karma, and unwholesome mental karma; who revile the noble ones; and who hold perverted wrong views;"

Due to these causes and conditions of wrong views and karma, at the dissolution of the body after death, they fall into the evil destinies, being born in the hells, or among animals, or as various hungry ghosts.

If there are sentient beings who accomplish wholesome deeds of body, speech, and mind; who do not revile the noble ones; and who possess right view—due to the causes and conditions of accomplishing such karma of right view, at the breaking up of the body after death, they enter a good destination and are reborn in the heavens. Having been born in the heavens, or being born among humans, they exhaust all fetters and outflows.
"In this way, the Tathāgata thoroughly understands the causes and conditions of the various karmas of sentient beings.

Toward all sentient beings, the Tathāgata is able to give rise to great loving-kindness and great compassion; he is always diligently energetic, manifesting three kinds of supernormal powers, and is able to cause them to dwell securely in mundane and supramundane faith."
What are the three? First, supernormal powers; second, preaching the Dharma; and third, knowing the minds of others.

By means of these three types of supernormal powers, they establish all sentient beings in mundane and supramundane faith, enabling them to know all realms of existence, all conditioned phenomena, and all modes of rebirth, thereby attaining liberation.
"Good son! This is called the ninth wheel of the Tathāgata.

Because the Tathāgata has accomplished such a wheel, he has reached the place of peace and attained fearlessness; as the most supreme Great Sage, he turns the Wheel of Dharma, which no śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, Māras, or Brahmās can turn. He completely subdues all non-Buddhists and other adversaries, and utters the lion’s roar amidst the fourfold assembly."

“Good son! It is like a consecrated Kṣatriya great king over the four continents who, seeing all sentient beings afflicted by illness, renounces his royal throne, bathes himself with various kinds of fragrant water, washes his hair, puts on fresh and clean garments, and sits upright in contemplation to eliminate the suffering and pain of all sentient beings so that they may all attain liberation.”

In this way, the consecrated Kṣatriya Great King, having offered flowers, incense, necklaces, and various musical performances, made offerings to all the devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, and mahoragas.
They said to one another:

"This consecrated Kṣatriya great king possesses many merits; he ought to become a Wheel-Turning Sage King (Cakravartin) who governs the four continents. We should establish this king in the administration of state affairs."
At that time, all the celestial emperors, down to the mahoragas and others, likewise spoke these words:
"One should establish this king as the sovereign over the four continents."

At that time, the Kṣatriya Great King, endowed with the seven treasures and ruling over the four quarters of the world as a Cakravartin, possessed a full thousand sons—all of them exceedingly brave and robust, handsome in appearance, capable of subduing external enemies, and traveling across the four seas. He traversed the entire earth under heaven, yet never employed punishment, nor did he inflict harm with sword or staff; all followed his righteous instructions and accepted his governance.
"Good son! This is called the tenth great wheel of the Wheel-Turning Sage King.

By the power of this, the Wheel-Turning Sage King rules over the four continents and the eighty-four thousand islands of the sea; he causes all to cultivate and accumulate every wholesome dharma so that nothing remains unestablished, and he protects their bodies and lives so that their longevity increases."
“In this way, son of good family!

From the time the Tathāgata first resolved upon enlightenment, regarding all the various afflictions and manifold diseases of his own body and life, as well as those of others, he has bathed them all with the pure water of meditative concentration (*dhyāna-samādhi*). He has sprinkled the crown of his head with the great kindness and great compassion (*mahāmaitrī-mahākaruṇā*) of the Dharma of reality, and donned the robe of shame and remorse (*hrī-apatrāpya*). The Tathāgatas of the ten directions, through the power of the knowledge of meditative concentration, the power of great diligence, and immeasurable skillful means (*upāya*), observe with a concentrated mind, desiring to extinguish the various faults and afflictions of all sentient beings. As the Buddha, the World-Honored One, has spoken thus:”

"The one of supreme wisdom, adorned with merit, is a fit vessel for the Dharma; he possesses the three gates of liberation, the four fearlessnesses, the ten powers of a Tathāgata, and the eighteen unique qualities. As a vessel of omniscience, he benefits others through great compassion, rescuing and delivering all sentient beings from suffering."

The Buddha, the Great Caravan Leader, delivers immeasurable sentient beings from suffering and affliction, bestowing upon them the bliss of nirvana; through the power of his vows, he desires to bring them to fulfillment so that they may achieve equal and perfect enlightenment as unsurpassed Dharma Kings.

"Endowed with such merit, possessing wisdom, valor, and diligence, one correctly contemplates and realizes the Four Noble Truths as they truly are, thereby attaining Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi; this is called the Tathāgata’s tenth wheel of Dharma, which is able to exhaust the root of all outflows."
“Good son! For example, just as a Wheel-Turning Sage King exercises sovereign mastery in playing throughout the four continents, so too is the Tathāgata:

he has attained sovereign mastery of mind over the four dhyānas; he cultivates the four bases of Brahma-faring through the four formless attainments; he possesses the four analytical knowledges and correctly contemplates the four noble truths; and regarding the four fearlessnesses, the ten powers, and the eighteen unique qualities, he has attained the power of mastery over all-knowledge.”

“Good son! Just as a wheel-turning sage king is fully endowed with the seven treasures, so too is the Tathāgata, the World-Honored One, fully endowed with the seven factors of enlightenment. Good son!”
Just as a Wheel-Turning Sage King possesses a thousand sons, so too does the Tathāgata have all his great śrāvaka disciples, with Kauṇḍinya as the first and Subhadra as the last.

Truly, you are my sons, born from the Buddha's mouth and transformed by the Dharma; having severed all outflows, you practice the four Brahma-abodes with courageous diligence, just as the fourfold army subdues the enemies of Māra.
“Good son! For example, when a Wheel-Turning Sage King rules over the four continents, his eighty-four thousand islands all follow his commands.

Likewise, the Tathāgata, the World-Honored One, has ten billion Jambudvīpas, ten billion Aparagoyanīs, ten billion Pūrvavidehas, ten billion Uttarakurus, ten billion oceans, ten billion Sumeru Kings of Mountains, ten billion Four Heavenly Kings, and so on up to ten billion heavens of Neither-Perception-Nor-Non-Perception, as well as ten billion Cakravāḍa and Mahācakravāḍa mountains. This Buddha-field is vast and immeasurable; everything therein follows the Tathāgata’s transformation and teaching.”
"Good son! This is called the tenth wheel of the Tathāgata.

Because the Tathāgata has accomplished such a wheel, even in the evil world of the five turbidities—where all the merits and virtues of the Buddha-dharma have declined and vanished; where beings are separated from the seven noble riches and all wise ones; where, for the sake of severing and eliminating all afflictions and extinguishing the three evil destinies—even in future generations, throughout the dark ignorance of all worlds that are entirely harmonized with the ten unwholesome paths, where beings commit the five heinous crimes, slander the true Dharma, distance themselves from all goodness, and are completely defiled by the roots of all that is unwholesome."

Thus, having accomplished these ten kinds of Buddha-wheels, he reaches the place of peace and attains fearlessness. As a sublime and great Sage, he is able to turn the Wheel of Dharma, which cannot be turned by any śramaṇas, brahmins, Māras, or Brahmās. He subdues all externalists and adversaries; with his vajra-like wisdom, he shatters all the afflictions of sentient beings, causing those of the three vehicles to attain non-retrogression, and he utters the lion’s roar amidst the fourfold assembly.

At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas, along with all the great Śrāvakas, devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, pretas, piśācas, humans, non-humans, and others, all exclaimed, "Excellent! They rained down showers of various flowers, showers of diverse jewels, showers of garments, and showers of exquisite perfumes; the entire great earth shook in every direction.

When the Buddha had spoken this *Daśacakra Sūtra*, among the great assembly gathered there, eighty-four thousand *koṭi-nayuta* hundreds of thousands of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas attained the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
Furthermore, immeasurable bodhisattva-mahāsattvas attained profound meditative concentrations (*dhyāna*) and the dhāraṇī of forbearance (*kṣānti*).

Moreover, immeasurable sentient beings who had not yet resolved their minds toward enlightenment now all generated the aspiration for awakening and established themselves on the stage of non-retrogression (*avaivartika-bhūmi*).

At that time, there were also immeasurable great assemblies who attained the fruits of the *srotāpanna*, *sakṛdāgāmin*, *anāgāmin*, and *arhat*; they cultivated and studied in succession, realizing the fruits of the śramaṇa.

Chapter Five: The Chapter on the Crest-Orb (Cakra). In the *Mahāvaipulya Daśacakra Sūtra*, this is the fifth chapter, titled "The Chapter on the Crest-Orb" (in the Danben edition, it is called "The Chapter on Realizing the Marks"). At that time, there was a Great Brahmā named Devagarbha, who had long cultivated roots of goodness and dwelt in the tenth stage; he was a great Bodhisattva Mahāsattva.

At that time, within the assembly, there was the Great Brahmā named Devasaṃbhava, who rose from his seat, adjusted his robes, knelt with his right knee on the ground, and addressed the Buddha in verse:
“I now bow my head in inquiry to you, O Ocean of Boundless Merit.
I pray that you will grant me leave at this time, to sever all doubts and regrets.”
"Thirsting for and upholding its merit, it is the most supreme among the flavors of the Dharma;
all sentient beings delight in hearing such a primary truth.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the Great Brahmā Tianzang:

"According to whatever you ask, the Tathāgata, the World-Honored One, shall likewise answer in accordance with your questions, so that you may be filled with joy and attain what you have never experienced before.
At that time, the Great Brahmā Devagarbha said:
"So be it, World-Honored One!"
He asked in verse:
“With wisdom and cultivated meditative concentration, Abiding securely in heedfulness;
For the sake of dwelling in the ultimate truth, One remains within the cycle of birth and death.”
Diligently practicing recitation and study, one can cross the ocean of afflictions;
will this lead to the realization of non-retrogression, or will one fall into the evil realms?
Constantly diligent in exhorting and transforming others, will one surely proceed toward Nirvana?
Are you dwelling in birth and death, or have you fallen into the evil realms?
You, a wise kṣatriya, rely upon the ten wheels;
do you remain within saṃsāra, or will you attain the path of Buddhahood?
"The mind is turbid and difficult to subdue; afflictions are many and scattered.
By what means can one purify the mind, and through meditation, recitation, and exhortation?
At that time, the Buddha addressed the Great Brahmā Tiṣya:
“Excellent, excellent!

That which the Great Brahmā has asked is purely wholesome and supreme. You have already fulfilled all practices; for as many Buddhas as there are grains of sand in the Ganges in the past, you have cultivated the three karmas, concentrated your mind in dhyāna, constantly and diligently recited the sūtras, managed monastic affairs, and caused the Buddha-dharma to flourish. You have established the Three Jewels like great pillars, and furthermore, you are able to ask the Tathāgata about such a meaning for the sake of many people and immeasurable sentient beings.”

"O noble son! Relying upon the Great Prophecy Treatise on Dignified Conduct (*airyāpatha*), which was expounded by the Buddhas of the past and sustained through supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), this is called the Tathāgata’s maturing of sentient beings so that they may all become weary of and detached from [suffering]. It is for the purpose of extinguishing the disease of all afflictions (*kleśa*) and for the desire to fulfill the paths of the three vehicles (*triyāna*)."

The present Buddhas of the ten directions, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, also proclaim this Great Discourse on the Prophecy Based upon Dignified Conduct (*Āśraya-īryāpatha-mahāvyākaraṇa-śāstra*), for the sake of bringing all sentient beings to maturity, to cause them to attain weary detachment from the world, to desire the destruction of all fetters and afflictions, and to enable them to fulfill the fruits of the paths of the Three Vehicles and maintain the True Dharma.

What you have heard from the Buddhas of the past, I likewise teach, relying upon the Great Prophecy Treatise on Dignified Conduct (*īryāpatha-mahāvyākaraṇa-śāstra*), for the sake of maturing all sentient beings, causing them to attain weary detachment, extinguishing all fetters and afflictions, and for the sake of fulfilling the teachings of the Three Vehicles.
"Therefore, Mahābrahmā, you should listen attentively and reflect upon this well.
The Great Brahmā Devagarbha replied,
"So be it, World-Honored One!"
The Buddha said:

"If one relies upon the wheel of the ten unwholesome actions, one will not be endowed with the meditative concentrations (*dhyāna*) of the desire realm, nor will one be able to fulfill the wholesome roots (*kuśalamūla*) of the desire realm; how much less could one achieve any of the meditative concentrations of the form or formless realms, or even accomplish the three vehicles and other various virtues?"

“What are these ten? There are those who wish to practice dhyāna but lack the necessary conditions; those who wish to break the precepts and accomplish evil dharmas; those who give rise to inverted views and are attached to auspicious signs; those whose evil minds are difficult to tame and who do not accord with the noble ones; those whose faculties are restless and unsettled, lacking even a small measure of roots of goodness; those who engage only in divisive speech and take pleasure in inciting strife and discord; those who speak coarse and wicked words and constantly revile others; those who delight in frivolous talk and various falsehoods; those who give rise to greed and envy, always feeling jealousy when they see others gain benefit; and those who harbor harmful intentions toward all sentient beings, holding great wrong views and asserting that there is no cause or effect.”
Devendra Mahābrahmā!

If one fails to fulfill ten matters, even if they wish to practice dhyāna, they cannot achieve even the minor virtues of the desire realm, much less achieve the roots of goodness of the form and formless realms, or the wholesome dharmas of the Three Vehicles.
"Furthermore, Great Brahmā!
There are ten things by which one cannot achieve the accomplishment of meditative concentration (*dhyāna-samādhi*). What are these ten?

They delight in performing arts and crafts; they delight in verbal discourse; they are excessively fond of sleep; they seek after various things; they are greedily attached to beautiful forms; they delight in fragrances; they delight in flavors; they delight in sounds; they delight in tangibles; and they delight in discursive thought and examination.
"Mahābrahmā! These are called the ten kinds [of practitioners], yet they are unable to achieve success in dhyāna. Even if they should achieve it, they immediately fall away and can never complete it;

they do so merely to obtain the faithful offerings of donors, and because of those gains and honors, evil states of mind arise within them. If they are among the assembly of Kṣatriya kings, they commit many transgressions and are reviled by others, or are subjected to whips and staves and have their limbs severed. Or, having committed great crimes, they undergo various sufferings for a long time; if they die suddenly, they will surely fall into the evil realms, even entering the Avīci Hell—just like Aḷāra Kālāma, Udraka Rāmaputra, Śaṇḍa, Kokālika, and Devadatta. Such as these destroy meditative concentration and consequently undergo heavy and grave punishments in the Avīci Hell."
At that time, the Buddha addressed Ājñātakauṇḍinya:
“I now permit you, pure bhikṣu, to receive the foremost of bedding, seats, and lying requisites, as well as food and delicacies, which can eliminate the epidemics of all sentient beings.”

Why is this? If a bhikṣu practicing dhyāna lacks the necessary requisites, all mental factors will frequently give rise to distraction; he will only contemplate various evils and be unable to achieve meditative concentration, eventually falling into the Avīci Hell to undergo the retribution of his sins.
If one cultivates various meditative concentrations when all requisite conditions are fully met, then it is easy to achieve success and attain single-mindedness of mind.

One should cause whatever has already been attained to increase; one must be able to recognize all unwholesome thoughts, discursive reflections, and distracted minds so as not to allow them to arise, and thus proceed toward Nirvana and reach the further shore.

If there are those who practice seated meditation but have not yet attained accomplishment, they should diligently cultivate it during the first, middle, and last watches of the night; they should distance themselves from clamor and bustle, maintain few desires and be content, and give rise to a mind of equanimity toward all fetters and afflictions. They shall completely distance themselves from all greed, anger, pride, arrogance, double-tongued speech, harsh speech, and false speech. Such individuals deserve the offerings and respect of hundreds of thousands of nayutas of Śakras, Brahmās, and the Four Heavenly Kings, let alone the offerings of Brahmins, Kṣatriyas, householders, Vaiśyas, and Śūdras.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
“Cultivating dhyāna extinguishes all fetters; no other practice can do so.
Therefore, dhyāna is supreme; the wise should honor it.”
At that time, the Great Brahmā Deva-garbha addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!

If there are bhikṣus who are able to cultivate dhyāna, should kṣatriya ministers inflict punishments upon them such as flogging with whips and canes, even to the point of mutilating their hands and feet?"
The Buddha said,

“Good son! If bhikṣus have left the household life for the sake of the Buddha-dharma, shaving off their hair and beards and donning the kāṣāya robes, all devas, humans, and asuras should make offerings to them.”

If one upholds and protects the precepts, they should not be punished, imprisoned, mutilated by having their hands or feet severed, nor even deprived of life; such actions are entirely contrary to the Dharma. Why is this?

With the exception of those who are widely learned and uphold the precepts, if there is a bhikṣu who has broken the precepts and gone forth within my Dharma, who has become as full of evil as putrid pus and decay, who is not a brāhmaṇa yet claims to be a brāhmaṇa, who does not practice the holy life yet claims to practice the holy life, who has fallen away and lost the fruits and realizations of the Noble Path, and who is overcome and destroyed by the fetters and latent tendencies of affliction—[such a person may be dealt with].

Furthermore, even those evil bhikṣus who have broken their precepts can show to devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, humans, non-humans, and others, the hidden treasures of immeasurable merit.

"If there are those who leave the household life in reliance upon me, sentient beings should form ten kinds of superior conceptions toward them, thereby attaining immeasurable and boundless merit. What are these ten?"

There are sentient beings who, upon seeing those who have left the household life in reliance upon me, should conceive the thought of mindfulness of the Buddha. By virtue of this pure mind and the causes and conditions of their joy, they will not believe in any other heterodox paths or the scriptures of heterodox teachers. When they encounter them, they should immediately contemplate and resolve upon the noble precepts. Through these causes and conditions, they are able to sever killing, stealing, sexual misconduct, false speech, and even the drinking of intoxicants, thereby entering the city of Nirvana.

Upon seeing those who have gone forth out of reliance upon me, one should give rise to a mind of generosity; by this cause and condition, in future lives one will possess immeasurable wealth, proceed rightly and head toward the goal, always receive abundant and excellent offerings, and ultimately enter the city of great nirvana, free from fear.

Furthermore, I see those who have gone forth in my Buddha-dharma, who are gentle and upright, constantly practicing patience and never giving way to violence; whose minds are free from derangement and who delight in the True Dharma; who always prefer secluded and quiet forest hermitages (āraṇyaka), even desiring to enter the fearless city of Nirvāṇa.

"If there are sentient beings who break the precepts, act contrary to the Dharma, and engage in misconduct and improper demeanor, upon seeing such persons, one should speak to them with gentle words and even prostrate at their feet.

By this cause and condition, these individuals will in future lives be born into noble families and possess great power; they will always be looked up to by all, and shall eventually enter the city of Nirvana."
"Devarāja Mahābrahmā!

If one who has gone forth according to my Dharma commits evil deeds, such a bhikṣu is blind and sees nothing; he is not a śramaṇa though claiming to be a śramaṇa, nor does he practice the holy life though claiming to practice the holy life. He is fallen and degraded, utterly ruined by the various afflictions."

Even if such a bhikṣu practices unwholesome dharmas, he is still able to reveal the hidden treasury of all wholesome dharmas and merits for all devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, humans, and non-humans, serving as a spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra).

Although they may not have few desires and be content, and though they shave their hair and beards and don the saffron robes, by virtue of these causes and conditions, they are able to increase the roots of goodness for sentient beings and reveal the path of excellence to gods and humans.

Therefore, whether a bhikṣu who has gone forth under me observes the precepts or violates them, I do not permit a wheel-turning sage king, his ministers, or his high officials to punish, imprison, subject him to flogging or caning, or even to cut off his hands and feet or take his life.

How much more so for other bhikṣus who have committed minor offenses or violated the rules of minor decorum; although they are dead, the residual power of their precepts is like ox-bile, which people still extract from the carcass of a cow even after it has died.
It is also like musk, which remains useful even after the animal has died, being able to bring great benefit to all sentient beings.
Although a bhikṣu of evil conduct may violate the prohibitive precepts, the power of his former discipline can still benefit immeasurable devas and humans.

"It is, for example, like a merchant who enters the great ocean, takes the lives of immeasurable sentient beings and plucks out their eyes, then takes *amala* fruits, pounds and mixes them together to create a precious medicine."

If there are sentient beings who are blind and sightless, even those born blind from within the womb, by applying this precious medicinal ointment to them, all their ailments will be removed and their eyes will become clear and bright.

"So it is, so it is! Even if certain bhikṣus have violated the prohibitions and committed evil deeds, they are called 'the dead' within the Buddha-dharma; yet if they can cause all other sentient beings to attain the pure Dharma-eye of wisdom, such is the merit even for those who merely behold them, let alone for those who reveal and expound the various teachings."
“Mahābrahmā! It is like burning incense: although the substance of the incense is consumed, it perfumes others with its fragrance.
A bhikṣu who violates the precepts is also like this; though he himself falls into the evil realms, he can cause sentient beings to increase their roots of goodness.”

A bhikṣu of evil conduct, consumed by lack of faith, will fall into the three evil realms upon the dissolution of the body and the end of life; yet he can bring great benefit to others by showing them the path to nirvāṇa.

For this reason, no layperson should violate, destroy, or treat with contempt a bhikṣu who has broken the precepts; rather, they should all protect, honor, and provide offerings to him, and must not permit his punishment, imprisonment, or even the taking of his life.

When the time for the *poṣadha* or *pravāraṇā* of the Saṃgha of the four quarters arrives, they shall be ordered to depart and excluded from the communal Dharma activities; they are not permitted to use any of the food, drink, or bedding belonging to the Saṃgha of the three periods of time.

In all places where *karmavācanā* and the recitation of the *Prātimokṣa* are performed, they shall all be expelled and not permitted to remain within the assembly; yet, neither kings nor ministers shall be allowed to inflict upon them whips, staves, imprisonment, fines, or even the taking of life.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke in verse:
“Though the campaka flower has withered, it is superior to all other flowers;
even a bhikṣu who has broken the precepts is still superior to all non-Buddhists.”
"Furthermore, Devakūṭa Mahābrahmā!
There are five kinds of heinous crimes that are the most extreme evils. What are these five?

Therefore, intentionally killing one’s father, mother, or an arhat; causing a schism in the harmonious Saṃgha of śrāvakas; and even shedding the blood of a Buddha with an evil mind—such acts as these are called the five ānantarya transgressions.
If a person commits any one of the five heinous crimes (*ānantarya*), they shall not be permitted to leave the household life or receive full ordination (*upasampadā*);
if they are allowed to leave the household life, they commit a grave offense and should be expelled.
If one already possesses the various dignified demeanors of a renunciant, one should not subject them to whips, staves, or any form of confinement.
Furthermore, there are four kinds of great offenses that are equivalent to the four pārājikas and constitute fundamental transgressions.
What are the four? Killing a pratyekabuddha is called the fundamental offense of killing.
Engaging in sexual misconduct with an arhat or a bhikṣuṇī is called the fundamental offense of sexual misconduct.
If a person takes charge of property given to the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Sangha, and uses it arbitrarily, this is called stealing and constitutes a root offense.
If a person, holding perverted views, causes schism within the community of bhikṣus, this is called breaking the Sangha and constitutes a root offense.
If a person commits any one of the four root offenses, they are in all cases forbidden from leaving the household life in accordance with the Buddha-dharma;
even if they should leave the household life, they are not permitted to receive full ordination (*upasampadā*);
if they have already received it, they should be expelled.
Because there exists the dharma of the monastic deportment, one must not whip, flog, imprison, or deprive another of life.
Such acts constitute root offenses (*mūlāpatti*) but are not transgressions against the Dharma (*ānantarya-karma*);

furthermore, there are cases where an act is both a root offense and a transgression against the Dharma, cases where it is a transgression against the Dharma but not a root offense, and cases where it is neither a root offense nor a transgression against the Dharma.
What constitutes both a transgression (ānantarya) and a fundamental offense (mūlāpatti)?

If one who has left the household life and received full ordination (upasampadā) attains the Path of Seeing (darśanamārga), and one then takes his life, this is called both a transgression and a fundamental offense.
Such sentient beings should be expelled from my precepts.
What constitutes a root offense that is not a heinous crime (*ānantarya*)?

If a person has gone forth within my Dharma, and one—being an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*)—takes the life of such a being, whether by means of poison or by causing an abortion, this is called a root offense that is not a heinous crime.
If there are provisions for food, drink, or bedding belonging to the Saṃgha of the four quarters, one must not share in such offerings and gains with them.

If there are sentient beings who harbor doubts regarding the Buddha, Dharma, and Saṃgha, claiming that there is another World-Honored One besides him, or who give rise to doubt and confusion regarding various auspicious signs;

or if there are others who harbor doubts regarding the teachings spoken by the Tathāgatas, slandering the Śrāvakas, Pratyekabuddhas, and even the Mahāyāna by exposing their faults; or who, seeing others reciting the scriptures, create obstacles—even for a single verse; [one should not associate with them].
This is neither a root offense nor a heinous crime (ānantarya), yet it is called an extremely grave transgression that closely approaches a heinous crime.
Such sentient beings shall never be permitted to leave the household life for the sake of the Buddha-dharma unless they repent and eliminate the roots of their offenses;
even if they have left the household life and received full ordination, those who do not repent must be expelled.

Why is this? Because they do not believe in the True Dharma and slander the Three Vehicles; they destroy the Eye of the True Dharma and seek to extinguish the Lamp of the Dharma; they sever the seeds of the Triple Gem and diminish the realms of humans and devas; thus, lacking any benefit, they fall into the evil paths.

These two types of people are called slanderers of the True Dharma and revilers of the worthy and holy ones; once the lifespan in hell has increased through such evil karma, this is termed a fundamental and grave offense.
"What are the fundamental dharmas that constitute a lack of dignified decorum? They are:

if a bhikṣu intentionally commits sexual misconduct, he commits a fundamental offense; if he intentionally kills an ordinary person, he commits a fundamental offense; if he takes what is not given, except for the property of the Triple Gem, he commits a fundamental offense; and if he intentionally speaks falsehoods, he commits a fundamental offense."
Among these four root offenses, if one commits even a single transgression, one is not permitted to participate in any of the ritual activities performed by the bhikṣus.
Furthermore, one may not share in the use of the property of the Saṃgha from the four directions, nor its food, drink, or bedding.

However, emperors, ministers, and all officials of the realm must not subject him to flogging, caning, imprisonment, or judicial punishment, nor even deprive him of life; this is the essential nature and characteristic of the fundamental offense.
Why are these called fundamental grave offenses?

If a person commits such actions, at the dissolution of the body after death they will fall into the evil realms; since committing such actions is the root of the evil paths, they are therefore called fundamental offenses.
"Just as an iron ball, though thrown into the air, does not remain suspended for even a moment but falls swiftly to the ground,
so it is with those who commit the five heinous crimes, violate the four grave prohibitions, or— being of two kinds of beings— corrupt the True Dharma and slander the worthy and holy."
Among these eleven kinds of offenses, if a person commits even one, at the dissolution of the body after death, they shall all fall into the Avīci Hell.
For this reason, those who have committed acts of immediate retribution (ānantarya) or fundamental grave offenses are strictly forbidden from being ordained as monastics.

Those who have committed the crimes of immediate retribution, such as these individuals, will never be able to exhaust the fetters of all afflictions or achieve meditative concentration within a single lifetime, much less transcend to the state of a determined bodhisattva; after their lives end, they will inevitably fall into hell and undergo the sufferings of the evil realms.

If there are sons or daughters of noble family who, with deep faith, take refuge in the Buddha and the Dharma—whether they incline toward the Śrāvaka vehicle, the Pratyekabuddha vehicle, or the Mahāyāna—and go forth from home within my Dharma, receiving the full precepts with supreme faith; if they guard the four root offenses and other transgressions, constantly exerting themselves with tireless vigor and diligence, daily protecting all humans and non-humans, never receiving the offerings of devas and humans in vain, and following whichever of the three vehicles they desire.
For what reason?
Because they are resolute in seeking liberation, they would never violate their precepts even at the cost of their lives.
For what reason?

These three kinds of sentient beings all seek nirvana and practice its causes; they rely upon the World-Honored One, rely upon the Sūtras and the Vinaya, and rely upon the Śrāvaka disciples who have attained the state of right determination.

If there are sentient beings who have committed the four grave prohibitions and are no longer disciples of the Buddha, they will be unable to see—like those who are blind—the profound characteristics of phenomena that I have revealed: that all things are impermanent, suffering, empty, and without self; nor will they see the Dharma of liberation and the Prātimokṣa that I have taught for the benefit and peace of all sentient beings, nor these sūtras, śāstras, and various meditative concentrations. Having broken the precepts and fallen away, they will plummet into the three evil realms.

If there are sons or daughters of noble family who do not violate the fundamental precepts within this pure Dharma of the Prātimokṣa, I am their World-Honored One, and they are my disciples; following my words, they dwell securely in the Buddha-Dharma, and all that they undertake shall be fully accomplished.
They establish the aggregate of ethical discipline and all wholesome dharmas, and are also able to provide great benefit, peace, and happiness for devas and humans.
World-Honored One!
Such persons as these are fully endowed with all the vehicles—the vehicles of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, up to the Mahāyāna—and abide well within them all.

"Why is this? Because these fundamental precepts protect all true dharmas, as well as all phenomena—both with outflows and without outflows—which are all established on this basis; therefore, they are called the 'root of the precepts.'"

"Just as all things upon the earth—the myriad plants, medicinal herbs, and grains—all grow because of it; likewise, by properly training in the four root precepts, all wholesome dharmas arise because of them."
Just as all mountains upon the great earth, including the Iron Ring Mountains, the Great Iron Ring Mountains, and Sumeru, the King of Mountains, all rest and abide upon it;
so too do the Śrāvaka and Pratyekabuddha vehicles, up to the unsurpassed Mahāyāna, all rest and abide by relying on a thorough understanding of the four fundamental precepts.

"Just as all things and their flavors depend upon the great earth for their existence, so too do the four fundamental precepts, when well-mastered, give rise to meditative concentration, liberation, and dhāraṇīs, up to and including anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi."
"Just as the great earth carries all things, both pure and impure, so too,

sons and daughters of noble family who have well trained in the four fundamental precepts fulfill all beings— whether they uphold the precepts or violate them, whether they are vessels for the Dharma or not."

One should observe with discernment, not disparaging the faults of others, neither exalting oneself nor belittling others; one can serve as an island for all wholesome dharmas, just as the great earth is the support for all sentient beings.

"In this way, sons and daughters of noble family who are well able to cultivate and study the four fundamental precepts will develop love, joy, and delight for all the sūtras and śāstras spoken by the Tathāgatas, receiving and upholding them; they will not give rise to various thoughts contrary to the Dharma, and all sentient beings shall sustain their lives by relying upon the four means of integration."
At that time, the Venerable Upāli rose from his seat, adjusted his robes, and with palms joined in reverence, addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
If the World-Honored One speaks thus, then those who are vessels of the Dharma and those who are not vessels will both be beyond reproach.

When others come in the future and commit various evil deeds—such as bhikṣus who are not śramaṇas yet act as śramaṇas, or who do not practice the holy life yet act as if they do—how then should one rebuke their minds and expel them?
The Buddha said:
“I do not permit laypeople to revile or criticize [the monastics] at all.
Furthermore, there are ten kinds of unrighteous reviling that incur great offense.”
What are the ten? If the Saṃgha is not in harmony and censures [the offender] before a king, this is called unrighteous (adharma).
If the Saṃgha is not in harmony and censures [the offender] among a multitude of Brahmins, this also is called unrighteous.
"If the Saṃgha is not in harmony, yet censures the king’s retinue and various great ministers, this is called unrighteous (adharma).
If the Saṃgha is not in harmony, yet censures among white-robed laypeople, this is called unrighteous."
"If the Saṃgha is not in harmony, yet one censures [the offender] among women and children, this is called unrighteous (adharma).
If the Saṃgha is not in harmony, yet one censures [the offender] before the saṃgha’s attendants (vaiyāvṛtyakara), this is called unrighteous."
"To criticize and revile within the assembly of bhikṣuṇīs while the Saṃgha is not in harmony is called illegal.
To criticize and revile before those with whom one has prior enmity or resentment while the Saṃgha is not in harmony is called illegal."
"If the Saṃgha is not in harmony, yet they revile and reproach one another with a mind of anger, this is called 'unlawful.
There are ten such unlawful acts; one should not revile or reproach [those who commit them]."
Even if one is accused of a minor offense, one should not accept it; likewise, if one is reproached for even a slight transgression according to the Buddha’s Dharma, one should not accept it.
Furthermore, there are ten kinds of unrighteous reproaches that should not be accepted.
What are the ten? If other non-Buddhists come to revile or censure you, you should not accept [their accusations].

Nor should you accept [accusations] from a layperson who does not observe the precepts yet has committed a heinous crime, who slanders the True Dharma, or who destroys the worthy and the holy; nor from one whose mind is deranged or distracted; nor from a *karmadāna* (steward) of the various heavens, earths, or the four quarters of the Sangha; nor from any bhikṣu who has violated the prohibitions—none of these charges should be accepted.
These are called the ten unrighteous grounds for censure that should not be accepted.

"If there is a bhikṣu who commits various evil deeds while dwelling among the Saṃgha, and a pure bhikṣu who is fully endowed with proper deportment and does nothing at all in an unrighteous manner, having accomplished five qualities, he should prostrate at the feet of the Saṃgha and say to the evil bhikṣu:
'I now wish to bring forward your offense.'"

This is true and not false; at this time, with a mind of compassion and gentle speech, whether it be timely or untimely, he acts so that the Buddha-dharma may long abide and so that all the Buddha-dharmas may blaze forth.
‘If you will listen to me, I shall reprove you in accordance with the Dharma.
If he does not listen, I shall prostrate at the feet of the elder bhikṣus who maintain the precepts and say to them:
‘Venerable sirs!’”
‘This bhikṣu has committed such an offense; his transgression shall be raised according to the five dharmas. The senior bhikṣus should examine these words:

if they accord with the Vinaya and the Sūtras, they should eliminate the dispute according to the Dharma by means of the methods for settling disputes. If he has committed a grave offense, it should be dealt with as a grave offense; if he has committed a middling offense, it should be dealt with as a middling offense; if he has committed a minor offense, it should be dealt with as a minor offense, instructing him to repent.
Upāli said to the Buddha:
“World-Honored One!

If a bhikṣu who has committed evil deeds actually possesses faults and offenses, yet relies upon all the power of laypeople, or relies upon the power of vast wealth and property, or relies upon extensive learning, or relies upon eloquence in speech, or relies upon his disciples—relying on such powers as these—the Saṃgha should act in harmony together.”

Regarding those who uphold the Sūtras, uphold the Vinaya, and possess the virtue of the precepts—should one not heed their words but instead rely on power and influence? How should such matters as these be handled?
The Buddha replied:
"One should go to the king, ministers, or high officials to have the offense punished according to the law.
Upāli then addressed the Buddha again:
“World-Honored One!

If such bhikṣus of evil conduct, by means of their wealth and power, or their power of extensive learning, or their power of eloquence, can cause kings and great ministers to take pleasure in them, or if they have unlawful factions of supporters, should they not be set aside and abandoned?”
The Buddha said, “Upāli!
If the matter has not yet manifested, one should depart; if the matter has already emerged, the Saṃgha should assemble and swiftly expel the person, so that they may no longer dwell together.”

Upāli! It is like the *go-maya*, the *śyāmāka*, and the weeds; their roots, stalks, branches, and leaves resemble those of wheat. While the ears have not yet emerged, they cannot be distinguished; but once the grain has come forth, the skilled farmer discards them all together with their roots.
Why is this? Because it destroys the pure barley. "Upāli!..."

If such a bhikṣu of broken precepts and evil conduct relies on laypeople or various powers of influence to remain within the saṃgha, no one will dare to rebuke him until his transgression has been exposed.
Once these matters have become manifest, the devas will then criticize them, saying that there is no restraint within the Saṃgha.
If there is a bhikṣu of evil conduct, the community of monks should quickly assemble in harmony and swiftly expel him together.

“Upāli! Just as the great ocean does not harbor a corpse, so too it is with my great assembly of disciples, the śrāvakas: these evil persons who have broken the precepts and are deceitful should not dwell together with me.”

If a precept-breaking bhikṣu forms an illegal faction with a kṣatriya king and various ministers, such a bhikṣu may rely on his own powers—such as extensive learning, wealth, great riches, and eloquence—and, acting with a reckless mind and without fear, forcibly remain within the Saṃgha.
"At that time, a bhikṣu who possesses shame and maintains the precepts should not engage in dispute when doubts arise in his mind, nor should he protect or form a faction with others;
such a precept-keeping bhikṣu shall then speak to the king and the various ministers and depart for another country."
The Vaipulya Daśacakra Sūtra, Volume Three.
The Vaipulya Daśacakra Sūtra, Volume Four.
Translator unknown; now appended to the Northern Liang Record.
Chapter Six: The Kṣatriya Caṇḍāla Manifesting the Signs of Wisdom.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Kṣitigarbha addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

These are the outcaste Kṣatriyas and the outcaste ministers; possessing few roots of goodness, they refuse to have faith or incline toward the Dharma. Deceitful, crooked, and foolish, they claim to possess great knowledge and give rise to arrogance. Fearing neither the consequences of evil karma in future lives nor the company of virtuous friends, they will eventually head toward the Avīci Hell.
"For the sake of wealth and profit, you have formed an unlawful faction with these bhikṣus of evil conduct.
The Buddha said, "So it is, so it is!"

"Good son! In future ages, there will be Kṣatriya-cāṇḍālas, even up to Brāhmaṇa-cāṇḍālas, who possess meager roots of goodness and lack faith; they are deceitful and crooked, and these deluded ones will manifest the appearance of wisdom."
Not following the words of virtuous friends, they are actually foolish while appearing to be wise.

Their minds are constantly filled with doubt and regret, yet they fear nothing of the future life; lacking prohibitive precepts, they commit acts of killing, even harboring wrong views to deceive others, and they constantly engage in slanderous speech throughout the world.
Kṣatriya-cāṇḍālas and Brāhmaṇa-cāṇḍālas who corrupt and disrupt the Buddha-dharma leave the household life within my teaching, yet they constantly violate the precepts and commit various evil deeds.

Yet these kṣatriyas and brahmins exhaust their hearts in making offerings while amassing great wealth; stained by greed, they seize upon empty words, acting as messengers for letters and commands, engaging in trade and commerce, delighting in the study of external scriptures, and practicing agriculture and planting. They guard their money, property, and dwellings; they protect their wives and children, reciting incantations and seeking elixirs. Greedily attached to clothing, food, and drink, they break the precepts and commit evil deeds, their voices sounding like conch shells. Though they are not truly śramaṇas, they call themselves śramaṇas;
though they do not truly practice the Brahma-faring, they claim to practice the Brahma-faring, even receiving the respect and offerings of kṣatriyas and brahmins and listening to their teachings.

Whether they be Kṣatriya-cāṇḍālas or Brāhmaṇa-cāṇḍālas who delight in breaking the precepts and distance themselves from those who uphold them, if within my Dharma there is anyone seen to uphold the precepts, cultivate goodness, and be humble, all those in training and those beyond training shall turn toward them.
In this way, such bhikṣus shall not receive respect or offerings, and whatever they say shall not be accepted or heard. Good son!

It is like a person who arrives at an island of jewels, yet abandons the blue jewel of Śakra and the great blue jewel, and having completely cast aside gold, silver, and pearls, takes up common crystal for precious gems of high value.
If within my Dharma there are those who maintain such precepts and possess great merit, yet one constantly treats them with humility and then abandons them;

instead taking up those who break the precepts and commit evil deeds—those who have perfected unwholesome dharmas, who feel no shame and lack a sense of moral dread (*hrī* and *apatrāpya*), and who are far removed from all great loving-kindness and great compassion—and conversely accepts such fields of merit for evil, listening to their words and making offerings to such evildoers, then both teacher and disciple shall fall into hell, fully possessing these ten kinds of evil wheels.
Kṣatriya-cāṇḍālas, brāhmaṇa-cāṇḍālas, śramaṇa-cāṇḍālas, and minister-cāṇḍālas—having previously cultivated roots of goodness that are now entirely extinguished—even fall into the Avīci Hell.
"What are the ten forms of breaking the precepts and committing evil conduct?

In this way, monks—even those among the Kṣatriyas and Brāhmaṇas—who tolerate and delight in evil views, who slander forest-dwelling bhikṣus, who are foolish and devious, who revile the noble ones, and who deceive the world; who, for the sake of food, drink, money, wealth, and various gains, and for the sake of seeking fame, torment their own bodies, slander others, and engage in jealousy and strife solely for the sake of profit; do not listen to, accept, or place trust in their words. Reject them, cause them to fall low, and keep them far from the true Dharma. They all claim that there are none who have attained the fruits of the path, nor any who have left desire behind to exhaust the fetters; they merely manifest themselves for the sake of gain. Be careful not to serve or make offerings to such as these, for they are people of deceit and delusion, and are truly not fields of merit for those treading the path.
At that time, those who are outcaste Kṣatriyas and outcaste Brāhmaṇas will harbor no sense of reverence or wonder toward forest-dwelling bhikṣus;

their minds being perverted, they will neither serve, revere, nor make offerings to them, nor will they be willing to listen to, accept, or place faith in their words. This is precisely what it means to be unable to protect and uphold the Eye of the Dharma and to fail to continue the lineage of the Triple Gem.

At that time, the devas, nāgas, and spirits of the land, who possessed deep and profound faith in the Triple Gem, all became filled with indignation toward such kṣatriyas and brahmins and said to one another:

"Behold now these kṣatriya-cāṇḍālas, śramaṇa-cāṇḍālas, brahmin-cāṇḍālas, and minister-cāṇḍālas! They have all given rise to arrogance; they have severed their roots of goodness regarding the Triple Gem and drawn near to evil associates. Having fallen away from wholesome dharmas, they shall enter the evil realms. From this day forward, we shall no longer protect such kṣatriyas and brahmins of this land."

Once all the devas, nāgas, and various benevolent spirits had departed, those within that kingdom who were capable vessels of the Dharma and worthy fields of merit all conceived a spirit of renunciation.

If all the celestial deities and those worthy of being vessels for the Dharma who ought to serve as fields of merit were to give rise to a spirit of indifference toward those kṣatriyas who are like caṇḍālas, then within their own kingdoms and neighboring lands, armies would arise, along with famine and pestilence; they would further slaughter one another and no longer find joy.

They will be separated from all that they previously cherished; their minds will be filled with anger and stinginess, devoid of compassion, and they will fail to give rise to loving-kindness toward any sentient being. From killing to wrong views, they will be shameless and lack remorse. They will consume everything belonging to stupas, monasteries, and the Saṃgha, using it for their own clothing.
They will harbor resentment toward their attendants and create enmity with them all. If they go to war with others, their own army will naturally retreat and scatter.
When the time of death approaches, their tongues will be bound so that they cannot speak, and they will head straight for hell.
"Furthermore, noble son!

Whether they be *kṣatriya-cāṇḍālas* or even *brāhmaṇa-cāṇḍālas*, they all remain far removed from virtuous spiritual friends; they treat the Triple Gem with contempt and lack a heart of reverence, showing no fear of the future world."

To have gained a slight degree of faith in the Śrāvaka-yāna and to consider oneself wise and learned, yet to slander and disbelieve the sūtras and teachings of the Pratyekabuddha-yāna and the Mahāyāna—neither reading nor reciting them, and even giving rise to a lack of faith in so little as a single verse—this is called slandering the Dharma.

Furthermore, if there are those who have slight faith in the Dharma of the Pratyekabuddhas and the Mahāyāna, yet do not believe in the Dharma of the Śrāvakas, disparaging and reviling it, this is also called slandering the True Dharma. This is called slandering the treasury of the True Dharma of all Buddhas of the three periods of time; it severs the Eightfold Noble Path and destroys the Dharma-eye of immeasurable sentient beings.

Furthermore, if there should be someone who creates obstacles or conceals and hides even a single verse from what the Tathāgata has taught regarding the Śrāvaka-yāna, the Pratyekabuddha-yāna, and the Bodhisattva-yāna, and fails to show reverence toward the Triple Gem, then by this cause and condition, the devas, nāgas, and benevolent spirits who protect all lands will become enraged due to their unwavering faith. Consequently, these kṣatriya ministers and others shall die with their tongues tied, unable to speak, and fall into the Avīci Hell.
"Furthermore, son of good family!

If one who upholds the precepts possesses merit, they shall dwell in that land fully endowed with the vessel of the Dharma. They will skillfully enter into equanimity and abide peacefully in a quiet chamber, without frequently visiting the houses of donors. Nor shall they reproach or scold bhikṣus of evil conduct so as to make them aware of it, nor shall they mock, disparage, or rebuke those who have broken the precepts."

Yet these bhikṣus of evil conduct, in turn, give rise to slander and suspicion toward those who are pure and uphold the precepts, claiming they commit fraud and various kinds of falsehoods; before kṣatriya ministers and all the people of the land—men and women, great and small—they utter all manner of calumnies.

Yet those Kṣatriya-cāṇḍālas and others, toward those who are pure, fully observant of the precepts, endowed with the merit of practice, and renowned—such bhikṣus who are my true disciples, complete in all meditative concentrations and liberations, and skillful in speech—will give rise to disparagement and malice, assailing them with various evil words and coarse language to cause them suffering and distress;

or they will seize their robes and bowls, as well as the requisites, bedding, and furniture belonging to the Sangha of the four quarters, driving them out, or at times imprisoning them, or even decapitating them.
Good son! Observe closely how much sin one incurs by associating with bhikṣus of evil conduct, even to the point of falling into the Avīci Hell.
If a sentient being commits the five heinous crimes (ānantarya), the four root transgressions, slanders the noble ones, or slanders the true Dharma, it exceeds all other fundamental sins.

Regarding such evil-doing bhikṣus, I likewise do not permit their punishment by flogging, binding, imprisonment, or even the taking of life; for by such causes and conditions, one incurs the retribution of great sin—how much more so for those who firmly uphold the prohibitive precepts and practice with purity?

If there is a bhikṣu who commits even one of the natural grave offenses (*āpatti*), although he has committed a grave offense, the precepts he received remain potent through the harmonious *karmavācanā* performed by the assembly of preceptors and the Saṃgha.
For example, although a wondrous incense may lack a substantial core, its pervasive fragrance should not be disregarded.

A bhikṣu who has broken the precepts is likewise; laypeople should not treat him with contempt or disdain. Although he is no longer a vessel for the Dharma, having regressed, fallen away, and abandoned the monastic life within the Vinaya of the Noble Ones, and thus being forbidden from using the property of the Saṃgha from the four quarters, the fragrance of his remaining precepts—those he did not violate while receiving them through the harmony of the Saṃgha—is still powerful. For this reason, it is not permitted for laypeople to impose punishments upon him.
“Good son! In the distant past, there was a kingdom named Kāśi, and at that time there was a king named Brahmadatta. He commanded a caṇḍāla, saying:
‘Beneath the Snowy Mountains there is a king of six-tusked white elephants named Utpalavilocana; you should extract his tusks.’”
"If you cannot capture him, all five of you must take his life.

At that time, the caṇḍāla, cherishing his own life, feigned the guise of a śramaṇa; outwardly manifesting diligence, he donned the kāṣāya robe and, following the king’s command, went to that mountain and arrived at the place where the elephant king was.
When the female elephant saw him, she drew her bow and pulled back an arrow, feeling a sense of dread, and said to the elephant king:
"This is a hunter; he has now come with his bow drawn and an arrow pulled back. Is it not that our lives are about to end?"
At that time, the Elephant King saw him immediately—his hair and beard shaven and wearing the saffron robe—and spoke this verse:
“The Dharma-robes of those Buddhas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, Are the banner-like signs of the Dharma;
having abandoned all evils, How could one harm living beings?”
At that time, the female elephant spoke again in verse:
“Though his body is clad in the saffron robe, He holds a bow and grasps a poisoned arrow;
A wicked Caṇḍāla, Devoid of any heart of compassion.”
At that time, the Elephant King spoke again in verse:
“The saffron robe is the definitive garment, With compassion as its very foundation;
This is surely one who has taken refuge in the Buddha, Out of loving-kindness for all sentient beings.”
"Have no doubt regarding this robe; you should restrain your own mind.
One who can don this garment shall cross to the further shore of birth and death.
At that time, the caṇḍāla immediately shot the elephant king with a single poisoned arrow.
At that time, the female elephant, having seen the elephant king struck by the arrow, cried out in lamentation and spoke this verse:
"Such are his robes; he ought to have taken refuge in the Buddha.
Though his deportment was tranquil, his heart harbored great evil."
"Swiftly treading upon his body, he has severed the root of his life;
having extinguished this enemy to the end, he is the one who shot your body.
At that time, the Elephant King spoke again in verse:
“‘It would be better to swiftly abandon body and life than to give rise to an evil mind;
though he harbors an evil mind, he still resembles a disciple of the Buddha.’”
"The wise do not act for their own sake, Suddenly giving rise to a mind of anger;
They always contemplate acting for the sake of sentient beings, Cultivating the practice of Bodhi.
