At that time, the Elephant King gave rise to a heart of compassion, immediately called out to that man, and asked him:
"What do you require? he asked. The other replied, "I desire your tusks."
At that time, the Elephant King immediately pulled out his own tusks and, having made a great vow, spoke these verses:
"I now offer my white tusks, seeking the state of Buddhahood;
Without anger or stinginess, may I cause all beings to extinguish their afflictions."

“Good son! In the past, I have seen such beings within the bodies of animals who sought the unsurpassed path and were able to act in this way—sparing neither body nor life to protect the Buddha-dharma, and never creating obstacles for those who wear the kāṣāya.”

In future ages, there will be outcaste Kṣatriyas, outcaste ministers, outcaste Brahmins, and outcaste householders who, with crooked and deceitful minds, will deceive the world and have no fear of the next life.

If there are those in the world who seek the unsurpassed path and enter my Dharma to leave the household life, yet give rise to thoughts of harming my disciples—whether they be those destined to become vessels of the Dharma or those who are not—reviling them with foul language, punishing them with whips and staves, or oppressing their bodies; such persons commit grave offenses against the Buddhas of the past, future, and present, heading for the Avīci Hell, severing all roots of goodness, extinguishing their faith, and being shunned by all those possessed of wisdom.

For example, just as a man who, though himself sightless, can still show the way to others, so too are my disciples: although they may violate the prohibitions and precepts, they are still able to benefit the sentient beings of the world.

If, in future ages, there should be *caṇḍāla* kings, or even *caṇḍāla* householders, who, upon seeing those who have gone forth within my Dharma—whether they have become vessels for the Dharma or not—harass and disturb any of my śrāvaka disciples, they commit a grave transgression against the immeasurable Buddhas of the three periods of time; their wholesome roots will be extinguished, and it will be difficult for them to regain a human body.
How much more so if they revile those śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas established in the stage of certainty, as well as the immeasurable merits of the Mahāyāna.

“Good son! For example, in the past there was a country named Vaṃśāra, where the king was named Jayasena. When a person’s crime merited death, they were bound and placed among the terrifying Karālaka charnel grounds, and an evil spirit was ordered to devour their body.”
At that time, the jailers bound him with the fivefold fetters and sent him to be placed among the terrifying Kālāma tombs.
Upon hearing this, the man immediately shaved his hair and beard, and draped a saffron robe around his neck.
At that time, having received the king’s command, the prison guards immediately seized and bound him, escorting him to the fearsome Karālaka cemetery.

At that moment, there was a rākṣasa in the cemetery named Evil Eye (Durdarśana), who arrived at the cemetery together with five thousand other rākṣasas. They saw this man, bound by the fivefold fetters, standing in the cemetery with his hair and beard shaven and a *kāṣāya* robe tied around his neck.
At that time, the rākṣasa circumambulated the person to the right and spoke these verses:
“Now you may comfort yourself; I shall never harm you.
Having shaved your head and donned the kāṣāya, you have caused me to recollect the Buddha.”
At that time, the rākṣasī’s son spoke again in verse:
“I tell my mother that I am extremely hungry and thirsty; We must eat this man.
Only then shall I be relieved of hunger and thirst, And my body and mind will find swift peace and happiness.”
At that time, the rākṣasī mother answered her son with a verse:
“The Buddhas, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, Are the banner and sign of the Dharma;
To conceive an evil mind toward them Is to fall into the Avīci Hell.”
At that time, the rākṣasa’s son, having circumambulated him three times to the right with his retinue, spoke these verses:
“Our parents together committed evil, Performing unwholesome deeds of body, speech, and mind;
I have now abandoned evil and shall not harm you, Clad in dyed robes, bearing the marks of liberation.”
At that time, a rākṣasa named Ox-Tooth, together with five hundred attendants, surrounded him and entered a great cemetery.
There they saw a bound man who had shaved his hair and beard, with a saffron robe tied around his neck. After circumambulating him to the right, the rākṣasa spoke this verse:
"Taking refuge in the wondrous banner-mark of the assembly of sages, This person is one whose neck is bound by the saffron robe."
"It is for this reason that I pay you such respect; I only pray that you will not be afraid and that I shall not harm you.
At that time, the rākṣasī’s son spoke again in verse:
"Mother, you should now know that human flesh is delicious; you ought to eat the flesh and drink the blood."
"May his vital strength be fully perfected, And may his body be augmented so that he has no fear.
At that time, the rākṣasī mother again spoke a verse for her son:
"All the various means of pleasure in the world, Belonging to devas, nāgas, yakṣas, and rākṣasas;
"One should always revere those who wear dyed robes; one shall thereby obtain various kinds of supreme and wondrous bliss.
At that time, the rākṣasa youth and his retinue circumambulated him to the right in reverence and spoke these verses:
"One should revere and take refuge in all those who have shaved off their hair and beards and donned the kāṣāya robes."
"In the past, throughout countless kalpas, I beheld the Buddha, the World-Honored One, the Savior of the World.
At that time, the third rākṣasa, named Yellow Hair, also surrounded by five thousand followers, entered the great cemetery.
Seeing a person bound with their hair and beard shaved off, wearing a *kāṣāya* robe tied beneath the neck, and having circumambulated them to the right, he spoke this verse:
“I take refuge in the banner-mark of the Seer; If one can make offerings, one gains great benefit.
For the sake of the *kāṣāya*, practice making offerings, And you should completely sever all bonds of existence.”
At that time, the Rākṣasī daughter Pīṅgalā spoke these verses:
"I have obtained this person whom I ought to devour; I have come here because the king sent me.
I shall eat his flesh and drink his blood; Mother, as you told your son, he should be offered as sustenance."
At that time, the rākṣasī Yellow Head again spoke a verse for her son:
"One with such marks as these is not my food; if he gives rise to an evil mind, he becomes a vessel of great suffering."
At that time, the rākṣasa’s son circumambulated him to the right with reverence and spoke again in verse:
“Such a great seer is worthy of being a field of merit; therefore, he should be honored, for he is free from the bonds of existence.”

At that time, the rākṣasa Kṣuradantaka, together with five thousand other rākṣasas, came to the cemetery. Seeing the one who was bound, with his hair and beard shaven and a saffron robe tied beneath his neck, they felt deep reverence and spoke these verses:
"There are those remaining in saṃsāra who have attained nirvāṇa; One who wears the saffron robe should not be harmed.
If one harms such a person, the Buddha will rebuke them; They should be honored and provided with offerings."
At that time, the rākṣasa son spoke again in verse:
"We have always inhaled the vital essence of humans, Devouring their flesh and drinking their blood;
Therefore, we shall eat this being, To further increase the vigor and strength of our bodies."
At that time, the rākṣasī mother again spoke a verse for her son:
"If anyone gives rise to the thought of causing harm To one who has shaved off hair and beard and wears the kāṣāya,
They will surely fall into the Avīci hell, the evil destinies, And suffer immeasurable pain for an exceedingly long duration."
At that time, the rākṣasa’s son and his retinue circumambulated the one who was bound and wearing the kāṣāya robe, keeping him to their right, and further spoke in verse:
“I now fear the suffering of hell; I shall never, with an evil mind, take your life.
With one accord, we shall release you, For we too seek liberation from the suffering of hell.”
At that time, the rākṣasas immediately released those bound persons.
Then, the bound persons waited until daybreak and went to the place where the king was.
The King immediately made a public proclamation to all the people; once they had assembled, they all questioned the King, his attendants, and the surrounding ministers and officials:
"It is unprecedented that this man has been able to come here."
The king immediately established a decree and proclaimed it throughout his inner and outer realms:

"If within my kingdom there are Buddhas or any of their disciples, whether they have become vessels of the Dharma or not, anyone who fails to show them respect or who inflicts punishment upon them shall be dealt with."
"For this reason, I shall be executed, even unto death.
O son of noble family!

The kings of Jambudvīpa and the yakṣas who consume flesh and blood possess such blazing malevolence that they lack any heart of compassion; yet, even upon seeing one who has shaved off his beard and hair and wears the saṃghāṭī robe fastened around his neck, they do not inflict harm, much less treat other beings with contempt.

In future ages, there will be Kṣatriya-cāṇḍālas and householder-cāṇḍālas who commit various evils; furthermore, there will be evil spirits who sever the roots of goodness and head toward the Avīci Hell.
"If one is able to go forth in my Dharma—whether they have become a vessel for the Dharma or not—if they shave off their hair and beard, I shall take away their life-force.
O son of good family!"
For example, in the past there was a king named Puṇya. If anyone committed a crime, they were even bound in fetters.
At that time, the king did not wish to take the person’s life. A minister and counselor said to the king, "Do not grieve; if you kill this man, it may cause the king to incur great sin.
The minister, relying on his own wisdom, delivered the man over to a mad elephant.

At that time, the mad elephant seized his two feet, intending to dash him to the ground; however, because he saw that this man was wearing dyed robes, the mad elephant immediately set him down gently and calmly. Not daring to cause him harm, it crouched opposite him, licking his feet with its trunk as a heart of loving-kindness arose within it.
"Noble son! Even an elephant, a beast fallen into one of the eight difficult conditions, will not give rise to malice or a harmful intent upon seeing a person clad in dyed robes.

How much more so in the future age, if there should be a *caṇḍāla* king who, seeing someone among my Dharma who has left the household life—whether they be a fit vessel for the Dharma or not—deliberately inflicts oppression or takes their life?"
If one acts in this way, one will be unable to speak, and after the end of life, one will certainly fall into the Avīci Hell.
Good son! This is called the third wheel.

Whether they be Kṣatriya-cāṇḍālas or even householder-cāṇḍālas, although they may have planted roots of goodness in the past, because they now commit evil, those [roots] are now entirely extinguished.
"Furthermore, son of good family!

There will be *kṣatriya-cāṇḍālas* and even *gṛhapati-cāṇḍālas* who, upon seeing offerings made for the Saṅgha of the four quarters—such as beds, mats, bedding, stūpas, temples, dwellings, gardens, houses, fields, and residences; all kinds of attendants, oxen, donkeys, mules, horses, and various livestock; as well as clothing, food, drink, medicinal decoctions, and miscellaneous necessities for life—they shall not provide these to those monks who are pure in their observance of the precepts and endowed with virtue, eloquence, intelligence, and speech suited to the occasion.

Instead, they shall provide the necessary beds, mattresses, and furnishings to those monks who have broken the precepts and engage in evil conduct, allowing them to enjoy these at will and even sharing meals with laypeople."
For these reasons, both the outcaste-like kṣatriyas and the outcaste-like householders, at the end of their lives, will all fall into the Avīci Hell.
Furthermore, son of good family!

There will be outcaste kṣatriyas and outcaste householders who, seeing those who have gone forth within my Dharma—whether they be śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, or even Dharma-preachers who expound the Mahāyāna—will slander, revile, deceive, and obstruct them, thereby causing distress and confusion to these Dharma-preachers;
by reason of these causes and conditions, they shall fall into the Avīci Hell.
"Furthermore, son of good family!

If there are *kṣatriya-cāṇḍālas* or *gṛhapati-cāṇḍālas* who, seeing that someone has given property belonging to the Saṅgha of the four quarters—such as flowering trees, fruit trees, trees with various flavors, shade trees, or incense trees—to my śrāvaka disciples who maintain the precepts, are learned, practice meditation, and recite the scriptures; and if they themselves seize it or cause others to seize it, or eat it themselves or cause others to eat it;
by reason of these causes and conditions, after the end of their lives, they will fall into the Avīci Hell."
"Furthermore, son of good family!

In future ages, there will be Kṣatriya-cāṇḍālas and householder-cāṇḍālas who will destroy my Dharma. If they see those who have gone forth from within my Dharma, they will repeatedly harbor anger toward such persons, revile them, and insult them; they will be unwilling to believe or accept the Dharma I have taught, and they will destroy stūpas, temples, monasteries, halls, and dwellings, and kill bhikṣus, whereby all the roots of goodness previously cultivated will be completely extinguished."
When his life is about to end, all his limbs ache as if being consumed by fire; his tongue-root feels as if it were bound, and for many days he is unable to speak.
After his death, he falls into the Avīci Hell.

If sentient beings who are unwholesome and have accomplished these ten kinds of evil wheels find it difficult even to obtain a human body, how much more so will they be unable to achieve the fruits of a śrāvaka or pratyekabuddha, let alone accomplish the complete Great Vehicle; such beings cannot be saved by any of the Buddhas.
“Good son! It is like pressing oil:
within every single sesame seed there are living creatures, yet by using an oil-pressing wheel to press them, one immediately obtains the oil.”
"Good sons! You should observe the oil-pressers and see how many sentient beings they must inevitably kill day and night.

Furthermore, if there were a person who used these ten wheels to press oil—where each wheel presses a thousand *hu* of oil in a single day and night—and continued in this manner for a full thousand years, what measure of sin would that oil-presser incur?"
Kṣitigarbha Bodhisattva said:
“Very many, World-Honored One!
They number in the countless, boundless, asaṃkhyeya; such is the offense incurred by these oil-pressers.”
"No one is able to know the measure of this person's offenses or the number of their instances;
only a Buddha and a Buddha can know them. The Buddha said, "Good son!"
For example, the sin of ten brothels is equal to that of one house of a courtesan, where there are ten women all seeking sexual desire.
Likewise, the sin of ten such houses of courtesans is equal to that of one tavern;
likewise, ten such taverns are equal to one butcher’s shop.
Thus, the sins of ten butcher’s houses and so forth are equal to the sin of a single wheel among the Ten Wheels for one day and night committed by a kṣatriya-cāṇḍāla or a householder-cāṇḍāla.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke in verse:
"The sins of ten *cakravartin* kings are equal to those of one brothel; the sins of ten brothels are equal to those of one tavern;
ten taverns are equal to one butcher; and the sins of ten butchers are equal to those of one king."
At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Kṣitigarbha addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

If there are true and virtuous kṣatriya ministers and great officials, true and virtuous śramaṇas, true and virtuous brāhmaṇas, or true and virtuous householders, who protect themselves and others, and in future ages protect the Buddha-dharma—protecting those who are fit vessels for the Dharma as well as those who are not, even down to those who have shaved their hair and beards and donned dyed robes, who are pure in precepts and possess merit; who offer worship and respect, listening to and receiving their instructions; who protect the teachings of the Śrāvaka and Pratyekabuddha vehicles; who attentively listen to, uphold, and protect the Mahāyāna; and who, having heard it, believe and accept it, abiding in the Mahāyāna, possessing pure precepts, extensive learning, and eloquent speech—one should delight in being in the company of such persons, finding joy in their hearts, consulting and discussing with them, and respectfully receiving their instruction.

One who stays far removed from those who break the precepts or engage in non-celibate conduct; who does not consume the property of the Sangha from the four directions for personal use, nor embezzle it in violation of the Vinaya; who avoids following the ten unwholesome paths of action and causes others to likewise renounce them rather than engaging in such deeds;

who teaches the ancient laws, rituals, and systems of statecraft established by former kings; who ensures the lineage of the Triple Gem continues and remains ever-flourishing; who draws near to all spiritual friends (kalyāṇamitra); and who adheres to and implements the administrative laws enacted by previous monarchs—such a person is called a truly virtuous Kṣatriya.
"How much merit will they obtain,
and how much demerit will they extinguish?
The Buddha said:
“Noble son! Suppose there were a man who, desiring to seek transcendence from the world, gathered all manner of precious jewels until they filled Jambudvīpa.

If he were to encounter the appearance of a Buddha along with his assembly of śrāvakas, he would practice giving in the morning, and likewise give at midday; continuing in this sequence for a thousand years, he would constantly practice giving and offer various kinds of worship.”
"Noble son! Is it not so that practicing giving in this manner brings great merit?
Kṣitigarbha Bodhisattva addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
That merit is exceedingly great, immeasurable, boundless, and incalculable; no one is able to weigh such merit, for only the Buddha, the World-Honored One, can know it.”
The Buddha said: "So it is! It is just as you have said."

If there is a truly virtuous kṣatriya who stays far removed from the wheel of the ten unwholesome evils, and is also able to restrain and eliminate the various evils of others as described above, this person’s merit will be many times greater than the former.

Suppose there were a person who, using the entirety of the four continents, established dwellings for the Sangha of the four directions, providing them fully with bedding, seats, and medicines, and enabling hundreds of billions of śrāvaka disciples and bodhisattva-mahāsattvas to practice various immeasurable Dharma gates—practicing dhyāna, reciting sutras, and performing various virtuous acts of transformation—would the merit of such a person be great?
If one practices the perfection of giving for a thousand years, the merit of such offerings is twice that of the former.

Suppose there were someone who, throughout the four continents, established monasteries, halls, and pavilions, fully equipped with bedding, furniture, and medical provisions, for a full hundred trillion śrāvakas and bodhisattva-mahāsattvas; and suppose they cultivated all dharmas and every kind of goodness, including meditative concentration, reciting the sūtras, and teaching others—how much merit would be obtained from such deeds?
He replied: "World-Honored One!
The merit obtained from this is immeasurable, boundless, and incalculable (asaṃkhyeya)."
“Good son! Suppose that throughout a trichiliocosm, for the sake of the śarīra relics, various stūpas and temples were erected until they completely filled the trichiliocosm.

The merit of constructing such a stūpa is immeasurable; its blessings increase constantly day and night. If one constructs monastic quarters in the four directions and provides all necessities, such as bedding and medicine, the merit of erecting the stūpa is twice that of the former.

Suppose that the three-thousandfold great thousandfold world-system were filled with bodhisattvas who have perfected the six pāramitās, as densely packed as rice, hemp, bamboo, or reeds; and suppose further that it were likewise filled with śrāvakas and arhats who possess the eight liberations, as dense as rice, hemp, bamboo, reeds, thickets, and forests, all of whom were imprisoned and bound with firm fetters for as long as one kalpa.

Furthermore, there appears in the world another person who, by virtue of the causes and conditions of merit, completely releases all bodhisattvas and arhats who have been bound, and provides them with baths, as well as clothing, water jars, alms bowls, dwellings, food and drink, medicine, and various kinds of bedding, until they finally enter parinirvāṇa after hundreds of thousands of millions of years.

Furthermore, they took up the *śarīra* relics and made offerings to them; for each individual relic, they erected a stupa made of the seven precious gems. Because they made offerings to these stupas of the seven precious gems, they each presented incense, flowers, various musical performances, silk canopies, banners, and streamers.

Furthermore, if there were someone who, for the sake of the Tathāgata, were to erect various stūpas and temples until they filled the entire trichiliocosm, the merit they would obtain—even by a factor of hundreds of thousands of billions—would not equal the merit of understanding this liberation from bondage.

A truly virtuous kṣatriya, a truly virtuous brāhmaṇa, a truly virtuous householder, and a truly virtuous śramaṇa—in this way, their accumulation of merit increases to an immeasurable and incalculable number.

In the final dharma age, when the dharma is about to perish, you shall be able to skillfully protect yourselves and others; throughout future generations, you shall constantly protect the Buddha-dharma and likewise protect my śrāvaka disciples—whether they are fit vessels for the dharma or not—even those who have shaved their hair and beards and donned the kāṣāya robes; you must not disturb or harm them.
If there are those who associate with and make offerings to followers of the Śrāvaka-yāna, one should neither disturb them nor take pleasure in making offerings to them;
toward those of the Mahāyāna, one should never deceive or disparage them;
and toward those who cultivate the Pratyekabuddha-yāna, one should likewise personally associate with and make offerings to them.

Those who firmly uphold the Mahāyāna Dharma and dwell securely in the Mahāyāna with its attendant merits, who possess skillful eloquence and constantly delight in drawing near to inquire about and discuss its meaning, and who, having questioned, accordingly receive and uphold it—such persons should remain far removed from all bhikṣus of evil conduct; they should not partake of the communal food of the Saṃgha of the four quarters nor share in receiving offerings together with them.

One should not become defiled by or attached to the wheel of the ten unwholesome actions, nor should one teach others to give rise to such attachment; rather, one should cultivate all the implements of the former kings, practice the ten wholesome deeds, and always draw near to spiritual friends who cause the eye of the Dharma to blaze forth.
Such a truly virtuous Kṣatriya attains merit many times greater, immeasurable and boundless; he shall never consume the stipends and emoluments of the people in vain.
Devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, and even pūtanas—all shall love and cherish him, and together protect him.
If there are those who are capable of being fields of merit and vessels of the Dharma, they shall all be cherished and protected together, so that their own country may flourish.

They shall also cause other lands to expand, dry up the evil realms, and benefit devas and humans; they shall protect the life-span so that it may be long, extinguish their own fetters and afflictions while also being able to extinguish all the afflictions of others, and achieve Bodhi by fulfilling the six *pāramitās*.

They shall remain far removed from all evil paths, yet undergo the cycle of birth and death for countless eons; within this cycle of birth and death, they shall be free from reproach, always encounter spiritual friends, and dwell together with all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas.
“By distancing oneself from evil associates, one will before long achieve the Buddha-land and attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.

At that time, all the celestial emperors and their retinues, down to the Vaiśravaṇas and Śakras and their retinues, rose from their seats, joined their palms toward the Buddha, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!”

In future ages, there will be true and virtuous Kṣatriya kings, up to true and virtuous householders, who, if they can distance themselves from these ten wheels of evil, will protect their own bodies and likewise protect others; they will uphold and maintain the True Dharma, continuing the lineage of the Triple Gem, causing it to blaze forth without interruption, bringing the three vehicles to maturity, being able to believe and accept all that the Buddhas have spoken, making offerings in accordance with the Dharma, and never concealing what the Buddhas have taught.
We, along with our retinues, together with true and virtuous kṣatriya kings and even true and virtuous householders, shall protect this person by means of ten dharmas so that they may attain growth.
What are the ten? To protect one's life so as never to die an untimely death;
to eliminate all that is contrary to the Dharma and always remain free from much illness.
Their retinue will be secure and their wealth will increase;
they will possess great riches and their fame will spread far and wide;
by associating with virtuous friends, their wisdom will grow.

In this way, true and virtuous kṣatriyas, up to true and virtuous householders, who have distanced themselves from all ten wheels of unwholesome action, should, as the Buddha has taught, protect and cause to increase these [virtues] by means of the ten kinds of wholesome dharmas.
What are the ten? They are:
enemies, bandits, and external foes cannot inflict harm;
and among forms, sounds, odors, tastes, and tactile objects, there is nothing that is not pleasing.

All illnesses and pains, all evil fetters, all false refuges, all doubts and regrets, all wicked flattery, all evil friends, all unwholesome roots, and all untimely deaths—these shall all be utterly extinguished for a truly virtuous Kṣatriya who is endowed with merit as described above; one should protect such a person by means of the ten wholesome paths of action.
Furthermore, World-Honored One!
If a truly virtuous kṣatriya fulfills and practices all the merits as described above, I shall, by means of these ten dharmas, protect the people of that kṣatriya’s realm.

What are these ten? They are: fear of hostile enemies from neighboring states; fear of non-human beings; fear of drought; fear of excessive rain; fear of unseasonable winds; fear of unseasonable and malevolent stellar portents; fear of famine; fear of untimely death by disease; fear of evil and heterodox views; and fear of a truly virtuous kṣatriya.
"Regarding those who are able to practice as described above, we shall protect the land and its people through ten dharmas.
At that time, the World-Honored One praised Śakra, Lord of Devas, and even Pūrṇa, saying:
"Excellent, excellent!"
“Good sons! All these are what you ought to do.
At that time, the Great Brahmā Devagarbha rose from his seat, adjusted his robes, knelt with his right knee on the ground, joined his palms, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
We only pray that you will listen as we speak.

This is the heart-mantra of the *dhāraṇī* for turning back the non-retrogressive stage, spoken by a truly virtuous Kṣatriya. By the power of this *dhāraṇī* mantra of the non-retrogressive stage, may the enemies and adversaries of bordering nations naturally retreat and disperse in future ages.”
May they achieve the precepts of body, speech, and mind;
attain supreme wisdom and be praised by all those who possess omniscience;
and remain far removed from all evils while constantly practicing what is wholesome.
They are far removed from all wrong views and false refuges;
through firm diligence, they bring immeasurable sentient beings to maturity and thus attain sovereign wisdom;
and they fully increase the precious treasury of the six pāramitās.
They remain far removed from all anger, stinginess, greed, and various forms of malice and envy;
they are constantly protected by devas and humans;
and they attain the non-retrogressive mind of enlightenment (bodhicitta).
Not abandoning any sentient beings;
attaining the four means of integration without doubt or hesitation;
maturing the vessels of the Dharma and being fully endowed with the field of merit;
He draws near to Bodhisattvas and the assembly of Śrāvakas to benefit all beings.
Son of good family!

A truly virtuous Kṣatriya never regresses from the mind of enlightenment; he attains the merit and power of dhāraṇīs, and in future ages, he shall be most excellent, indestructible, and beyond reproach, constantly drawing near to all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas.
At that time, the Great Brahmā Devakūṭa spoke this mantra:

“Tajjha | Munīcche | Munaśarave | Munīcilidye | Madriluśavijaḷe | Munaliñci | Anigame | Kkhalabodhe | Parasa-bodhe | Mila-bodhe | Sārassatī | Dharanilipatekhale | Jujunamile | Abhikkhabho anugili brahma | Munipadave | Svāhā. Having spoken this mantra, the Great Brahmā Devakūṭa addressed the Buddha, saying:
“I pray that the World-Honored One will rejoice in this dhāraṇī.”
The Buddha said: “Excellent, excellent,
Great Brahmā!”
"I have given rise to joy in my heart regarding this mantra.
At that time, the great assembly also exclaimed: "Excellent!"
"Quickly speak this dhāraṇī! At that time, the Buddha addressed Mahāmaudgalyāyana and the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Maitreya:

"You should receive and uphold this *cittadhāraṇī* of the stage of non-retrogression. It can bring peace, happiness, and benefit to truly virtuous Kṣatriyas; for the sake of turning the wheel of Dharma; for the sake of renown and profit; for the sake of majestic power; for the sake of extinguishing all false views; for the sake of establishing right view; for the sake of guarding the eye of the Dharma; for the sake of bringing infinite sentient beings to maturity; for the sake of making them firm in the Great Vehicle so they do not regress; and for the sake of fulfilling the six pāramitās."
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke in verse:
"At that time, the Brahma Tiṣya Questioned the Honored One among Two-Legged Beings:
'Beings of sharp faculties and the like, Who practice dhyāna and engage in recitation and study—'"
With courageous and firm resolve, O wise Kṣatriya,
how does one extinguish the afflictions?
How does one abide in non-retrogression?
The Buddha then replied to him:
"One who has committed a grave offense and fallen [from the precepts], though their mind may be clear and sharp, will swiftly hasten to the Avīci Hell."
These ten kinds of evil wheels are practiced by those lacking wisdom;
they sever the very roots of goodness and swiftly cause one to fall into hell.
Even meditative concentration extinguishes the fetters, not merely the wisdom derived from extensive learning.
If you wish to attain liberation, you should diligently practice dhyāna.
The wise who are ever persevering protect my True Dharma;
by honoring the kāṣāya, they are able to cross the ocean of afflictions.
Delighting in dwelling within empty forests, far removed from the five heinous crimes,
upholding the precepts and practicing meditative concentration, one can cross the ocean of afflictions.
If there are those who have faith in the Three Vehicles and blaze forth with vigor for the Buddha-dharma, [they shall likewise attain liberation].
One who makes offerings to those clad in dyed robes attains a great ocean of merit.
Able to subdue the mind that is difficult to tame, they do not proclaim the faults of bhikṣus;
cultivating the noble lineage of few desires, they attain the state of the Honored One among Two-Legged Beings.
Stay far away from wicked bhikṣus, Reverently associate with the noble and holy, And do not consume the property of the Saṅgha; Thus you shall swiftly reach Bodhi.
May the Three Realms obtain sublime bliss, And may the Triple Gem appear in the world.
If you wish to attain peace and happiness, you should make offerings to the Triple Gem.
Those who treat the Triple Gem like outcasts, who commit transgressions as kṣatriyas,
and who are associates of wicked bhikṣus, will swiftly fall into hell.
These ten offenses of the wheel are equal to one offense of sexual misconduct;
these ten offenses of sexual misconduct are likewise equal to one offense of intoxication;
these ten offenses of intoxication are again equal to one offense of slaughter.
For these ten crimes of a butcher, one is equal to a single king.
A truly virtuous Kṣatriya who makes offerings to the True Dharma shall cause the Three Vehicles to flourish and shall obtain an ocean of merit.
Even if one were to fill Jambudvīpa with the seven treasures and offer them all to the Buddhas, the merit thereof would still have its limit.
Even if one were to construct monasteries throughout the four continents as offerings to the Sangha;
Though one may gain great merit thereby, it is not equal to protecting the True Dharma.
Even if one were to build stūpas and temples filling the worlds of all the Buddhas,
though one may gain great merit thereby, it is not equal to protecting the True Dharma.
Arhats and various Bodhisattvas, having been liberated from bonds, offer worship;
yet to manifest within my Dharma brings merit twice as great as theirs.
Even if one practices dhyāna for billions of kalpas, one will not be protected by the Buddhas.
If one does not conceal the True Dharma, all Buddhas will swiftly protect and mind them.
If there are true and virtuous Kṣatriyas who remain far removed from the wheel of the ten non-virtues,
they are able to guard the Buddha-dharma and uphold those who wear the kāṣāya.
They do not slander or disparage the True Dharma, nor the Three Vehicles taught by me;
having heard it, they are able to make offerings to those who protect and uphold the Dharma-vessel.
Just as when five suns arise, they are able to dry up the great ocean;
If one protects my Dharma, then the fetters of affliction will be exhausted;
just as when the wind-disaster arises, it utterly destroys all mountains,
so too for one who protects the True Dharma, all afflictions are extinguished.
Just as when a flood of water arises, It sweeps away and destroys the great earth;
So too for those who protect the True Dharma, All afflictions are extinguished.
In the world there is a wish-fulfilling jewel, Which can satisfy the aspirations of people.
If one preaches the Dharma of the Three Vehicles, all shall attain it according to their vows.
Just as obtaining a vessel of virtue completely dispels poverty,
so too does the destruction of afflictions lead swiftly to the attainment of Bodhi.
Like the moon on the fifteenth day, its radiance fills the void;
those who attain this wisdom will fully protect the True Dharma.
Just as space has nothing within it, being without substance and without characteristics;
Those who protect the true Dharma possess wisdom free from doubt.
Just as wherever the sun shines, it can dispel all darkness;
so too do those who protect the true Dharma attain illuminating light.

Chapter Seven: The Chapter on the Marks of All Virtues At that time, Vajragarbha Bodhisattva rose from his seat amidst the great assembly.
He bared his right shoulder, placed his right knee upon the ground, knelt upright with palms joined in reverence toward the Buddha, and asked in verse:
"Those who violate the prohibitions and precepts, who have lost the dhūta practices, and who have committed the heinous crimes—it is not for my sake that you pass into extinction."
As the Buddhas of the past have taught: one who has violated the pure precepts does not enter the assembly.
All matters pertaining to a śramaṇa are abandoned by such a person, like a charred wick.
Defiled by the three stains and separated from liberation, they are unworthy of receiving the offerings of the nation.
The livelihood and requisites of the Saṃgha from the four quarters— Not even the slightest portion of these is permitted to be taken;
If one commits any of the four grave root offenses, One shall be cast out by the assembly like a corpse.
How is it that this sutra teaches patience, arousing compassion for wicked bhikṣus,
restraining all forms of punishment, and further commanding that one should make offerings to those wicked bhikṣus?
Furthermore, in another sutra it was said:
"You all should have faith in the Mahāyāna; this is called the supreme enlightenment of straightforwardness. You should abandon the two vehicles."
Furthermore, this sutra expounds the three vehicles, as well as the faculties, powers, and factors of awakening;
the methods of the three vehicles regarding meditative concentration and liberation—listen attentively and with faith, for these are the causes of liberation.
Herein lie the four fruits of the śramaṇa’s noble path; outside of this sutra, there is no śramaṇa.
The Three Vehicles are all identical in the Eightfold Noble Path; those who seek liberation must apply themselves with diligent vigor.
If there are wise ones among humans and devas, or Bodhisattva Mahāsattvas who have come here, this great assembly has already realized such as these Mahāyāna practitioners.
If there is one who can correctly explain and reveal the meaning, and if there is one who is able to listen, what benefit will they obtain?
Among the ten types of discriminating śrāvakas, who would not benefit from such an exposition?
If there is someone who hears the Dharma, how can they hear it so that it increases?
Furthermore, who hears it such that it diminishes? And who, as a listener, exhausts themselves through old age and death?
Feeling weary of and detached from all conditioned phenomena, he practices meditative concentration day and night;
when shall he attain liberation? One who can cross over the four floods is called a Savior of the World.
At that time, the Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva Vajragarbha:
“Excellent, excellent, son of good family!”
For the benefit and happiness of all sentient beings—whether humans or devas—none are able to question the Tathāgata in such a manner.
Son of good family!
Listen attentively, listen attentively!
"Reflect upon this well!
I shall analyze and explain it for you. "So be it!"
“World-Honored One!
I now listen attentively and wish most earnestly to hear it. “Good son!”
Furthermore, there are ten kinds of difficulties regarding obtaining a human body.

What are these ten? Not having planted roots of goodness in previous lives; not having cultivated merit such that the mind is constantly agitated; following evil associates and fearing nothing of future worlds; being addicted to greed, hatred, and delusion; and being deranged or losing one's mind, even to the point of holding wrong views. These are called the ten factors through which it is difficult to obtain a human body.

Furthermore, there are ten factors by which one commits a root offense through the absence of reliance on the causal conditions; due to this violation of the precepts, one falls into the evil realms. What are these ten? There is one who lacks reliance on proper deportment (*īryāpatha*);

there is one who has gone forth within my Dharma but whose inner mind is not corrupted while the path of cultivation is corrupted; there is one whose path of cultivation is not corrupted but whose inner mind is corrupted; there is one whose both inner mind and path of cultivation are corrupted; there is one whose precepts are corrupted but whose view is not corrupted; there is one whose view is corrupted but whose precepts are not corrupted; there is one whose both precepts and view are corrupted; and there is one whose inner mind, path of cultivation, precepts, and view are all uncorrupted.

"If one follows evil associates and lacks the majestic deportment of reliance, even upon encountering virtuous friends, one remains as foolish as a white sheep; having heard the sublime Dharma, one is unable to receive and uphold it, nor does one analyze and explain it for others. Failing to distinguish between the wholesome and the unwholesome, lacking the majestic deportment of reliance, and possessing immeasurable requisites yet remaining insatiable."
Because of these causes and conditions, the mind is constantly distracted; this is called having no reliance on proper deportment.
Afflicted by various illnesses, one practices various incantations for this reason.

"If there are those who, relying on these ten forms of lack of decorum, commit root grave offenses, yet remain fearful and apprehensive, harboring a sense of shame and remorse, and do not repeatedly engage in various evil deeds."
Because the Tathāgata desires to benefit such individuals as these, they are called "defilers of the path.

Why is this? If one commits such evil deeds, they should repent, renounce them, and disclose them without ever concealing them; if they can thus cause their offenses to be extinguished and refrain from committing them again, then even if they are abandoned by the assembly, they shall not be permitted to use the communal property, bedding, or any necessary requisites of the Sangha. Because such persons have become fit vessels for the Dharma, it is within the realm of possibility that the Tathāgata will preach for them the teachings of the Śrāvaka, Pratyekabuddha, and Mahāyāna vehicles.
If, in two or three lifetimes, they encounter virtuous friends (kalyāṇamitra), all their evil karma will be extinguished without remainder.

They will attain the fruit of a śrāvaka or the fruit of a pratyekabuddha, and even enter the profound and correct Dharma of the Mahāyāna; such a person is said to have broken the precepts, but not to have broken their views.

If there are those whose inner conduct is impaired but whose views are not, and whose views are not impaired, for these the Tathāgata teaches the four immeasurable minds; they are also fit vessels for the śrāvaka vehicle or the pratyekabuddha vehicle. However, if there are those whose conduct is impaired and whose very essence is impaired, they are entirely unfit vessels for these two vehicles.
For the sake of such sentient beings, the Tathāgata then teaches the Dharma of giving.

Furthermore, there are those who perceive the destruction of precepts yet do not themselves destroy them; for the sake of such sentient beings, he teaches the Dharma of the twelve links of dependent origination. Having become free from the view of destruction, they may, within a single lifetime, enter the Śrāvaka Dharma, or, upon changing their bodies, attain the Pratyekabuddha Dharma.
"If there is someone whose morality is impaired but whose view is not, they are capable of being a vessel for the noble Dharma.

If there is someone whose inner mind, conduct, views, and morality are all impaired, yet they follow a spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra), then by reason of this cause and condition, the Tathāgata will preach the ten wholesome dharmas for them."

If there are those who are foolish and follow evil associates, being ignorant of what is wholesome and what is unwholesome, the Tathāgata teaches them for their sake to recite and practice [the scriptures].
If there are people deluded by false views who seek liberation, the Tathāgata immediately expounds the Dharma of the Four Noble Truths for them by means of the Śrāvaka-yāna.
"If there are those who give rise to the view of annihilationism, I explain the Dharma of the twelve links of dependent origination for them.
If there are those who give rise to the view of eternalism, I explain for them the cycle of birth and death within the three realms."
Knowing such dharmas as dying here and being born there, he teaches the Dharma of the Śrāvakas.

The Tathāgata observes all things and never speaks falsely; whether there are sentient beings who are matured or those who are not, he employs skillful means to penetrate without obstruction all grave offenses, including the various heinous crimes of immediate retribution.

"If there are sentient beings who cause harm, even to the point of destroying the pure eye of the Dharma, I shall, for the sake of benefiting all sentient beings, accord with the Śrāvaka vehicle, the Pratyekabuddha vehicle, and the Bodhisattva vehicle."
If one slanders the true Dharma, obstructs it, conceals it, or fails to manifest it—even if only a single verse—such persons are said to slander the true Dharma.

They destroy the Eightfold Noble Path and likewise destroy the Dharma-eye of all sentient beings; such people lose great benefit and bring no advantage to sentient beings, for they slander the true Dharma by relying on a deluded saṃgha.
"Furthermore, son of good family!
There are four kinds of Saṃgha. What are the four?
The Sangha of Ultimate Meaning, the Pure Sangha, the Dumb-Sheep Sangha, and the Sangha Without Shame.
What is meant by the Sangha of Ultimate Meaning?
It refers to the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, the Great Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas, and the Pratyekabuddhas, who have attained complete mastery over all dharmas.
The Arhat, the Anāgāmin, the Sakṛdāgāmin, and the Srotāpanna—these seven types of persons are called the Saṃgha of the Ultimate Truth (paramārtha-saṃgha).

Furthermore, there are those who, though living as householders and not wearing the Dharma robes, are unable to fully receive the Prātimokṣa precepts and do not participate in the Poṣadha or Pravāraṇa ceremonies, yet they attain the fruits of the noble ones; having attained these fruits, they too are called the Saṃgha of the Ultimate Truth.
"What is meant by the 'pure Sangha'?
Those who are able to uphold the Pratimokṣa and the full precepts, practicing according to the Vinaya and not transgressing in their deportment—these are called the pure Sangha."

"What is meant by 'dumb sheep monks'? They do not know the root offenses; they do not know what constitutes an offense or what does not; they do not know the gravity of offenses; they do not know the subtle offenses that can be confessed. Being foolish and ignorant, they do not perceive that there are offenses to be feared, nor do they rely upon virtuous spiritual friends (kalyāṇamitra). Because they do not frequently associate with virtuous spiritual friends, they are unable to inquire about the profound meanings within the sūtras, such as: 'What is wholesome and what is unwholesome?'"
What constitutes a grave offense and what a light one?
In the practice of cultivation, what is virtuous and what is evil?
Those who possess such characteristics are called "mute sheep" monks.

"What is meant by the 'monks without shame or remorse'? If there are those who enter the Buddha-dharma merely for the sake of their own livelihood, yet completely violate the *prātimokṣa* precepts they have received; who break the harmony of the Saṃgha without shame or remorse; who do not fear future lives and harbor internal corruption; whose voices are like conch shells and whose speech is harsh and rigid; who constantly harbor jealousy, folly, and arrogance; who abandon the three karmas solely for the sake of profit and gain; who indulge the six sense faculties and are greedily attached to the five desires—form, sound, fragrance, taste, and touch; and who slander the True Dharma—such persons rely upon my Dharma while their hearts lack shame and remorse. For this reason, they are called 'monks without shame or remorse.'"
"What is called the Sangha of the Ultimate Truth?

Although the Noble Path may be hidden and not manifest, one who is able to cross the swift current of the afflictions and the three realms of existence by means of the Eightfold Noble Path—this is called the True Path."
Why is this? The Buddhas, World-Honored Ones, Pratyekabuddhas, and Arhats sever all that has a name; this is called the True Path.

Furthermore, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas examine their own faults and seek all dharmas; having attained unimpeded wisdom, they do not take realization as their goal, yet for the sake of sentient beings, they manifest the path of extinguishing the fetters.

"Furthermore, if there is a person who has not yet perfected the *prātimokṣa* precepts, they are said to rely upon the Sangha of the ultimate meaning (*paramārtha*) up to the pure Sangha (*viśuddha*).

If there are true and good ordinary persons (*pṛthagjana*), up to those with true and good right view and various other ordinary persons, who through supernormal powers and transformations demonstrate the right path to others—all such individuals are called 'those capable of showing the path.'"

The second is the srotāpanna, the third is the sakṛdāgāmin, the fourth is the anāgāmin, and the fifth is the bodhisattva mahāsattva dwelling in the first bhūmi, up to dwelling in the tenth bhūmi as one destined for birth in the next life (ekajātipratibaddha); those such as these are called "those who demonstrate the path."
"If there is another person who accomplishes the *prātimokṣa* precepts, this is called 'living in reliance upon the Path.

When Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas practice the six *pāramitās* in order to gather and mature all sentient beings, such as these are also called 'showing the Path,' 'living in reliance upon the Path,' and 'the path that extinguishes the fetters.'"

Such individuals are called the "field of merit" for the world; apart from these, all others are termed "defilers of the path. They are also called "evil fields of merit" and are monks who rely on shamelessness and lack of remorse. Within the Buddha-dharma, they are also termed "corpses," and are fit only to be discarded.
Within the great ocean of the Saṃgha, such a person is also called one who has not become a vessel for the Dharma; they are not my disciple, nor am I their teacher.

Furthermore, there are those who have not become vessels for the Dharma, yet they declare, "The Buddha is my World-Honored One. After my parinirvāṇa, they will attain faith and inclination toward the Dharma, the Saṃgha, and the noble precepts; they will not themselves give rise to evil views, nor will they disparage the evils of others, but will widely proclaim my Dharma for the sake of others.

By refraining from slander and making right vows, and by repeatedly repenting for the evils one has committed, one can eliminate immeasurable and manifold transgressions. To possess such faith enables even those of the ninety-five kinds of heterodox teachers and non-Buddhist paths to cross over toward Nirvana; this is a merit that cannot be equaled by that of a Cakravartin King.
"For this reason, the Tathāgata, having observed the fundamental karma of all sentient beings, has spoken thus.

For these causes and conditions, those who have gone forth within my Dharma—having shaved off their hair and beards and donned the dyed robes—should not give rise to evil. All Buddhas of the past, future, and present, through their great compassion, protect and sustain such as these who have gone forth and wear the dyed robes."

For this reason, if one gives rise to an evil mind toward anyone who has left the household life, it is no different from having committed evil in the presence of all Buddhas of the past, future, and present.
“Furthermore, if there are those who break the precepts and fail to become vessels for the Dharma, such individuals will give rise to evil views and also revile the evils of others.

For example, they will claim that there are no true and virtuous Kṣatriyas, true and virtuous ministers, true and virtuous high officials, true and virtuous śramaṇas, true and virtuous brāhmaṇas, true and virtuous householders, or true and virtuous Vaiśyas and Śūdras; that there are no men or women; that there is neither father nor mother; that there are no arhats in the world; that there is no right path and no one who proceeds toward right view; that there is no cultivation of good or evil and no retribution for them; and that there are none who attain the fruits [of the path], for all phenomena are without causes and conditions.”
"Some may speak thus: 'The realm of form (rūpadhātu) is permanent and a non-perishing dharma.
Or they may reckon that the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu) is permanent and a non-perishing dharma."
Some speak of the ascetic practices of non-Buddhists—such as binding oneself with rafters and thorns or scorching the body with the five fires—as being supreme;

some speak of the Śrāvaka vehicle alone as being supreme, failing to mention the Pratyekabuddha vehicle and even slandering the Mahāyāna Dharma, concealing and obscuring it so that they cannot reveal, explain, or analyze it;
or there are those who place their faith exclusively in the Mahāyāna while disparaging the Śrāvaka and Pratyekabuddha vehicles.
Some say: "Generosity is supreme; from ethical discipline up to wisdom, none are supreme. Others say:
"Precepts are foremost; from generosity up to wisdom, none are foremost.
Or some may say: "Patience is foremost; generosity, ethical discipline, and even wisdom are not foremost."
Or some may say: "Diligence is the foremost; giving, ethical discipline, patience, and even wisdom are not the foremost."
Or some might say: "Meditative concentration is the foremost; giving, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, and even wisdom are not the foremost."
Some may say: "Wisdom is the foremost;
generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, and meditative concentration are not the foremost."
"Or some may say: 'The ascetic practices of the non-Buddhists are supreme.
Thus it is, son of good family!"

Monks who violate the precepts and engage in evil conduct will give rise to various slanders against those who have become vessels for the Dharma; they will speak such words to those with wrong views, and being possessed of inverted views themselves, they will destroy true and virtuous kṣatriyas.
Faith, precepts, learning, generosity, and wisdom are all utterly destroyed.

True and virtuous ministers, true and virtuous śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas, true and virtuous householders, true and virtuous vaiśyas and śūdras, and true and virtuous men and women—when their faith, precepts, learning, generosity, and wisdom are thus destroyed, they are called kṣatriya-cāṇḍālas, and so on, up to householder-cāṇḍālas.
“A bhikṣu who breaks the precepts severs his own roots of goodness, and can also cause even a truly virtuous kṣatriya to lose his roots of goodness, even to the point of falling into hell.
‘O son of good family!
For example, a corpse that is festering with pus is foul and stinking wherever it is approached; wherever it goes, it is itself putrid and causes others to become putrid as well.

In the same way, when a truly virtuous kṣatriya associates with evil friends—monks who have broken their precepts—every place he frequents will give rise to the foul stench of evil views. This can cause the kṣatriya to sever his roots of goodness and head toward the Avīci Hell.

In this way, from a truly virtuous counselor down to a truly virtuous woman, whoever associates with a bhikṣu who has broken the precepts and engages in evil conduct becomes a caṇḍāla, severing their roots of goodness and heading toward hell.
Son of good family!

Observe how those who associate with bhikṣus of broken precepts and evil conduct fall away from all that is wholesome. Therefore, those who wish to attain the bliss of Great Nirvāṇa should all associate with and make offerings to those who have extinguished the fetters and cultivate the Path; they should associate with and make offerings to those who study under such teachers and fully demonstrate the Way of the Three Vehicles. They should be complete in their inner mind, complete in their cultivation of the Path, and complete in their knowledge and vision.
One should listen to the paths of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, not disparaging the noble ones, nor should one disparage the Mahāyāna.

According to one's aspiration, one should apply diligence; within the three vehicles, one may practice and study whichever single vehicle one has vowed to follow. One must not disparage the Mahāyāna sūtras, even so much as a single sentence or a single verse.

If one slanders [this teaching], they should not dwell with them nor should they associate with them; if one associates with or dwells with such a person, they will immediately fall into the Avīci Hell.
Therefore, son of good family!
Among the three vehicles, one should follow one’s inclination and aspire toward the Single Vehicle (*ekayāna*).

Those who wish to be far removed from all suffering should have faith in the Śrāvaka and Pratyekabuddha vehicles as taught by the Tathāgata; they should rely entirely upon all the dharmas taught in the Mahāyāna, and must not slander, conceal, or hide them. Even a single sentence or a single verse should be heard with careful attention, and one should give rise to a vow of right commitment.
If there are those who slander the True Dharma, one should not dwell with them, nor should one seek instruction or listen to the Dharma from such persons.
If one approaches them to listen to the Dharma, by reason of this cause and condition, one will constantly fall into the Avīci Hell and undergo great suffering and affliction.
Why is this? O son of good family!

When I was originally practicing as a bodhisattva seeking the unsurpassed path, I relied upon the Śrāvaka vehicle to seek even a single verse; for its sake, I even gave up my body, hands, feet, limbs, head, eyes, marrow, and brain. In this same manner, I sought the Pratyekabuddha vehicle and the Buddha vehicle.

When I was originally a bodhisattva, for the sake of the unsurpassed path, I did likewise: for the sake of a single verse, I gave up my body, hands, feet, head, eyes, marrow, brain, flesh, blood, skin, and bones.
Through such ascetic practices, one shall ultimately achieve the Unsurpassed Way.

These teachings of the Three Vehicles have been expounded by all the Buddhas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges throughout the three periods of time; they are protected by their spiritual powers out of compassion for all sentient beings, and also so that the lineage of the Triple Gem may be inherited and never severed.

"Furthermore, in future ages, if there should be Kṣatriya-cāṇḍālas, or even women-cāṇḍālas, who, out of folly, consider themselves wise; who are full of evil and coarseness, fearing nothing of the next world; and who commit acts of killing up to holding wrong views, being jealous, stingy, and greedy, following after evil associates."

Furthermore, they do not become vessels for the Dharma of the Three Vehicles; having acquired only a slight amount of learning in the Śrāvaka Vehicle, they slander all the vehicles from the Pratyekabuddha Vehicle up to the Mahāyāna—all that which is protected and sustained by all Buddhas—and they conceal and obstruct them so that they do not manifest.

If one has heard even a little of the Mahāyāna, yet gives rise to slander and disparagement toward the vehicles of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas—which are sustained by the spiritual power of all Buddhas—[one commits a grave offense].

Regarding those who do not believe in my Mahāyāna nor in those capable of discerning and expounding the Mahāyāna—if they say, "I have heard the Mahāyāna, yet I do not accept the Śrāvaka or Pratyekabuddha vehicles"—it is because of the power of their own meager wisdom and the darkness of ignorance. Nevertheless, by the power of the great compassion of all Buddhas of the past, future, and present, and with the desire to benefit all sentient beings, there are two kinds of protection and sustenance.
First, desiring to perpetuate the lineage of the Triple Gem so that it remains unbroken, one leaves the household life to practice the Way, shaves off hair and beard, and dons the kāṣāya robe.
Second, one explains the Dharma of the Four Noble Truths for the purpose of advancing toward the Three Vehicles.

These two kinds of protection upheld by the Tathāgata cannot be maintained by Śrāvakas or Pratyekabuddhas; nor can they be maintained even by hundreds of thousands of Śakras or Brahmās, nor by hundreds of thousands of nayutas of Cakravartin kings.

Furthermore, there are Kṣatriya-cāṇḍālas who, upon seeing anyone who has gone forth within my Dharma—such as a śrāvaka disciple—imprison them, flog them with whips, penalize them, or even deprive them of life;
they cause total disruption and confusion of this profound Dharma protected by all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, and they slander and conceal the true path of the Three Vehicles.
Such a person does not recognize the Mahāyāna; being a Kṣatriya-cāṇḍāla such as this, he is not even fit to be a vessel for the Śrāvaka vehicle, let alone for the Mahāyāna.

Furthermore, there are women who are outcasts (caṇḍālī) who deceive the world by claiming, "I am one who practices the Mahāyāna. Due to their ignorance and darkness, as well as their stinginess, greed, and jealousy, they destroy my Dharma, saying, "I myself shall swiftly attain Nirvāṇa."

"Furthermore, one incurs offenses against all the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, the World-Honored Ones; one also commits offenses against all Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas and all the Śrāvaka disciples of the Buddhas. This causes one’s lifespan to be shortened, brings about manifold sufferings and afflictions, results in the impairment of the sense faculties and the incompleteness of the limbs and joints, and leads to constant and frequent illness."
"Whether they be *kṣatriya-cāṇḍālas* or even *strī-cāṇḍālas*, those who commit various evil deeds all give rise to inverted views and sever all roots of goodness.

Although they may practice much giving, they receive retributions by taking on various forms among the animals; when their bodies perish and they die in future lives, they will ultimately be unable to give rise to the roots of goodness of the form realm or achieve unimpeded wisdom, nor can they proceed toward omniscience (*sarvākārajñatā*).
Furthermore, they will suffer many illnesses and be unable to speak, heading straight for the Avīci Hell."

Therefore, the Tathāgata, desiring to benefit true and virtuous kṣatriyas so that they may obtain peace and happiness, and likewise wishing to bring benefit to true and virtuous women, for these reasons does not permit the harassment or disturbance of those who have gone forth within my Dharma.
"Furthermore, those who give rise to various slanders against the Dharma taught by me shall obtain the retribution of great sin as previously described. Why is this?
Wearing the *kāṣāya* is the sign of liberation for all Buddhas.

Therefore, all Buddhas uphold the great banner of the True Dharma—the equal flavor of the liberation of the *śrāvakas*—and it is also the supreme banner of the flavor of liberation of the Great Vehicle for the *pratyekabuddhas*.

Therefore, those who seek liberation should first recite and study the Śrāvakayāna and other vehicles, listening attentively to their teachings; they should distance themselves from all evil associates and draw near to all virtuous friends, making offerings to and honoring them. Only thereafter should they recite and study the Vaipulya Mahāyāna and the six pāramitās.

Having fully disclosed and repented according to the Dharma all the evil and unwholesome deeds they have committed, and having made great vows, it is possible that at the end of their lives, when their bodies perish, they will be able to become vessels for the Dharma of the Śrāvakas in future lives; they will also possess the seeds of Pratyekabuddhas, and even the unsurpassed seeds of the Mahāyāna Avaivartika.
Why is this? Good son!

Furthermore, there are ten kinds of wheels of reliance; if one accomplishes these wheels, then true and virtuous kṣatriyas, up to true and virtuous women, will be able to swiftly become vessels for the lineage of śrāvakas, the lineage of pratyekabuddhas, and the lineage of the non-retrogressive Mahāyāna.
What are these ten?

"In this way, a truly virtuous kṣatriya, up to a truly virtuous woman, believes in the retribution of karma and is fully possessed of shame and remorse; they distance themselves from wrong views and evil associates, uphold the precepts by abstaining from killing up to abstaining from intoxicants;

with a mind of loving-kindness toward all, they are free from anger, vexation, and harm; they are fully possessed of compassion, rescuing and aiding sentient beings who are distressed, suffering, weak, and inferior; and they attain a mind of sympathetic joy."

They distance themselves from divisive speech, false speech, and frivolous chatter; they attain a mind free from contention and remain aloof from stinginess, greed, jealousy, and envy. They never rely upon various heterodox paths, and they abandon all nets of doubt as well as all signs of worldly fortune. They exert great diligence, attaining firm stability in all dharmas, swiftly realizing tranquility, and obtaining joy in the Dharma.

“Noble son! These ten wheels of reliance—when true and virtuous kṣatriyas, up to true and virtuous women, accomplish these ten wheels—they will swiftly obtain the vessel for the śrāvaka, the lineage of the pratyekabuddha, and the seed of non-retrogression in the Mahāyāna; these are called the wheels of reliance.”
"Such a wheel as this is shared in common with śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to reiterate this meaning, spoke in verse:
"The foremost among the multitude, With shaven heads and wearing the kāṣāya;
How can an evil bhikṣu, who breaks the precepts yet receives offerings,
who violates the prohibitions and has lost the dhūta practices, who maintains deceitful speech and false views,
who is an unfit vessel and ruins the Path— how can such a person not be subjected to punishment?
If one listens to the Dharma from him, Believes in the quiescence of nirvāṇa,
And attains liberation, It shall be the excellent medicine for them.
In all other sūtras, He speaks only of the path of the One Vehicle.
It is said that there are no two vehicles; this is the foremost liberation.
To benefit all sentient beings, one exhausts karmic retribution and afflictions;
with a heart of constant compassion, one brings peace to the Kṣatriyas and upholds the True Dharma.
Brahmins, Vaiśyas, Śūdras, and others who are defiled by sin;
those who wish to harass a bhikṣu will surely head toward the evil realms.
Thus, all Buddhas protect and uphold those clad in the saffron robe.
The path of liberation of all Buddhas is declared to be the foremost.
Clad in the raiment of liberation, one swiftly abandons evil views;
proceeding toward Nirvana, it is like medicine curing a disease.
Even if one has violated the precepts, yet can extinguish the suffering of others—
I shall never permit such a person to perform the *poṣadha* within the assembly.
If one should preach the Dharma for the sake of others, both parties will obtain merit.
To call me the World-Honored One, to take refuge in the Triple Gem,
and to sever all evil karma— this is far superior to the ways of the outsiders.
It is like a merchant entering a place of terror who encounters the King of Rākṣasas.
By grasping even a single hair of a horse’s mane, one will surely cross the perils of the great ocean;
by breaking the precepts and abandoning evil and heterodoxy, one leaves behind the rākṣasas of affliction.
Therefore, protect your liberation, for this is that which all Buddhas uphold.
One who does not afflict those who break the precepts will surely abandon all evil deeds;
therefore, those possessed of merit who seek liberation can protect both the worthy and the unworthy, and for them, liberation is not difficult to attain.
In this matter they lack power; the Śrāvakas are shrouded in the darkness of ignorance.
It is not those Pratyekabuddhas and the like who can expound the Mahāyāna;
unaware of the Pratyekabuddhas, they instead praise the Mahāyāna.
Having already destroyed their faith, they recite Mahāyāna sūtras;
yet they do not protect themselves from the transgressions of body, speech, and mind regarding other vehicles.
They preach only the view of annihilationism and thus destroy the True Dharma.
Later, when they attain human form, they will fall back into the Avīci Hell.
Therefore, when observing sentient beings, do not harbor thoughts of those who are unfit vessels;
if they violate or destroy the prohibitions and precepts, show them no compassion or pity for their deceit and crookedness.
One should also know that this is the cause: speaking evil words and holding nihilistic views.
Such persons are neither Śrāvakas nor Pratyekabuddhas, nor do they belong to the Mahāyāna;
by slandering the Buddhas of the three periods of time, they will surely fall into the Avīci Hell.
One who maintains precepts with deceit and crookedness, whose mind is distracted and who is stingy with the Dharma,
yet feels aversion toward strife, greed, and envy— such a person is called a śrāvaka.
One who possesses wisdom and delights in practicing giving, who can give rise to the marks of arising and ceasing;
whose mind is focused and who always dwells in solitude—this is called a Pratyekabuddha.
Upholding the precepts without sparing one’s own body, like a fierce lion;
Seeking the path of quiescent extinction—this is called the Mahāyāna.
Guarding the true Dharma, skillfully explaining and revealing it;
attaining the profound forbearance regarding all phenomena—this is called the Mahāyāna.
Whether one is a vessel for the Dharma or not a vessel, their mind always acts with equanimity;
unstained by worldly dharmas—this is called the Mahāyāna.
Therefore, regarding the three vehicles, the wise speak in accordance with the Dharma.
Protect my śrāvakas, so that they may swiftly attain supreme perfect enlightenment.
The Mahāvaipulya Daśacakra Sūtra, Scroll Five.
