Chapter Eight: The Cakravartin Signs upon which the Kṣatriya Relies.
"Furthermore, son of good family! "
The ten kinds of wheels of reliance are equal for all śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and even Tathāgatas.

If there are true and virtuous kṣatriyas, up to true and virtuous women, who accomplish these wheels of reliance, they will swiftly become vessels for the Dharma of the śrāvakas and the lineage of the pratyekabuddhas, and they will also be able to accomplish the vessel for the Dharma of the Tathāgata.
“What are these ten? Noble son! They are:

true and virtuous kṣatriyas, up to true and virtuous women, who purify their actions of body, speech, and mind, practice the Dharma, possess a sense of shame and dread of blame, loathe their own bodies and fear the five aggregates of clinging (*pañca-upādāna-skandha*), do not see the further shore of the great river of birth and death, delight in tranquility and remain aloof from all clamor, harbor no contentious thoughts and do not disparage the faults of others, guard their sense faculties and constantly maintain mindfulness of concentration, skillfully contemplate cause and effect and are able to achieve meditative absorption (*dhyāna*), and always delight in collecting the mind and well understand arising and ceasing. In this way, one can achieve the wheel of the ten reliances.”

These are called true and virtuous kṣatriyas, up to true and virtuous women; they will swiftly accomplish the lineage of the śrāvaka vehicle and the pratyekabuddha vehicle, and shall also attain the state of non-retrogression in the Mahāyāna.
Thus it is, noble son!
One who is able to accomplish the vehicle of the śrāvaka or pratyekabuddha relies upon this wheel to cross the ocean of existence and enter the city of nirvāṇa.
What is meant by "relying upon the wheel of majestic deportment"?
What is meant by "reliance"?
What I call reliance refers to relying upon the five aggregates of clinging; it is called reliance because one regards the five aggregates of clinging as oneself and relies upon them with certainty.
"What is called 'dignified deportment' (īryāpatha)?
There is the deportment of the aggregates (skandha) and the deportment of the elements (dhātu); this is called 'dignified deportment.
What is called 'the wheel' (cakra)?"
The verbal teachings sustained by the supernatural powers of all Buddhas are all termed "wheels" and "sword-wheels.

Thus, those who are Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas rely on these wheels to seek the path to Nirvāṇa; because they are stained by and attached to this reliance, they are not fit vessels for the purity of the Mahāyāna.

"What is the basis? It is the basis of the aggregates and elements, which gives rise to fear; it is the basis of disenchantment, the basis of the body, and the seeking of liberation through one's own aggregate of feeling in order to transcend one's own suffering."
Although they seek the liberation of all sentient beings, because they are attached to their own experience, they are unable to receive the Mahāyāna Dharma!
Merely acting for themselves and not for sentient beings, they lack great compassion; for this reason, they do not abide in the Mahāyāna.

Dwelling long in saṃsāra, they abandon the suffering of others; because they desire only to sever their own afflictions, they are unable to relinquish their hands, feet, head, or eyes. For this reason, they are not fit vessels for the Mahāyāna, nor do they seek the wheel of the Mahāyāna path, nor do they seek the wheel of the Brahma-voice. Thus, being unfit vessels for the Mahāyāna, they enter the city of nirvāṇa alone and without companions.

For this reason, if there are sentient beings who have not heard of the vehicles of the śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas, whose various practices are incomplete, whose roots of goodness are immature, and whose diligence is slight;
if one were to preach the Dharma before such persons, both parties would incur fault, and it would likewise disturb all the Buddhas.

For this reason, if there are sentient beings who have not yet matured their various roots of goodness within the vehicles of the Śrāvakas or Pratyekabuddhas, yet hear these subtle and wondrous Mahāyāna sūtras, those people—being foolish while claiming to be wise—will fall into the view of nihilism. Such individuals will assert that cause and effect do not exist and that there are no wholesome or unwholesome karmas; they will bring disorder to my Dharma, declaring what is not the Dharma to be the Dharma, and claiming to be śramaṇas when they are not, or being bhikṣus when they are not. They will obstruct and cut off all the vehicles of the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas so that they do not circulate.

"If one reviles, robs of robes and bowls, seizes, binds, or imprisons those who have gone forth and received full ordination in the Dharma of the Śrāvakas or Pratyekabuddhas for the sake of accumulating all roots of goodness—whether they be vessels fit for the Dharma or not, those in training or those beyond training, those who have attained the various fruits with skillful speech and unimpeded eloquence, or even ordinary persons who are truly virtuous and fully observant of the precepts—one commits an offense."

Such proponents of annihilationism and eternalism are rākṣasas among human beings. It is difficult to obtain a human body; it would be better to fall into hell and incur immeasurable sins than to receive a human body and give rise to the view of annihilationism.
Therefore, they are born eternally ignorant and mute, unable to speak, and upon the end of their lives, they will head toward the Avīci Hell. A human body is difficult to obtain.

Even if one were to obtain a human body after incalculable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas, one would be born into the five turbidities within the realms of the Buddhas; one’s body would be constantly afflicted by muteness and the inability to speak, with no hearing in the ears, and such diseases as these would press upon the body while the mind and will become deranged.

One would lack food, drink, assets, wealth, and livelihood; being far removed from spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*), one would accomplish all manner of evils and be shrouded and obstructed by wrong views.

Having committed various heinous crimes and espoused the view of nihilism (*ucchedadṛṣṭi*), one would harass and disturb us, the disciples of the Śrāvakas who maintain pure precepts and cultivate merit, becoming defiled by evil.

If a person possesses inferior faculties and inferior diligence, yet does not seek the vehicles of the śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas, but instead gives rise to the view of annihilation regarding the Mahāyāna path, it will be difficult even for them to obtain a human body, let alone seek the vehicles of the śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas.
If even those of the two vehicles cannot practice this, how much less can they comprehend the profound Mahāyāna?
"It is like a clay jar with many holes; if one fills it with oil or water, it all leaks away and the vessel is utterly ruined."
Why is this? It is because of the defect of the vessel.
If there are sentient beings whose faculties are not yet mature, they are likewise identical to that characteristic of the jar.

"Good son! Just as various treasures are shown before a blind person, so too, when the Great Vehicle is extensively revealed to those lacking wisdom—those who are arrogant, heedless, and even hold nihilistic views—they likewise cannot understand it."
"It is, for example, like a person whose body is foul and filthy; even if one were to smear various substances such as sandalwood and aloeswood upon the body, it would still not become fragrant.

In the same way, if one does not diligently seek the vehicle of the Śrāvaka or Pratyekabuddha, and does not sever evil karma up to and including wrong views, then even if one were to smear the fragrance of the Mahāyāna upon oneself, one would still remain without fragrance."
For example, just as a poor field cannot produce a harvest even if excellent seeds are sown therein;

likewise, one who does not diligently seek the vehicles of the Śrāvakas or Pratyekabuddhas, and feels no revulsion toward the five desires—such a person, if taught the Mahāyāna path, will be unable to achieve success.
For example, if a jar of poison contains even a small amount of rock honey, it is unfit for consumption;

likewise, if one cannot cultivate the vehicles of the śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, or even the Mahāyāna, and asserts that there is no cause and effect, then if one wishes to preach the Mahāyāna sūtras to such a person, they will be unable to practice according to what they hear and will fail to believe or accept them—just like a jar of poison containing a small amount of rock honey.

In this way, those who are unfit vessels for the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas yet are placed amidst the flavor of the Mahāyāna—know that for such individuals, both [the Lesser and Greater Vehicles] are useless.
It is like playing the *vīṇā*, *kinnara*, flute, drum, or conch before a madman; though one performs various musical performances, he cannot understand them.

Likewise, those who do not diligently seek the vehicles of the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas, who possess heavy greed, hatred, and delusion, and whose faculties for the Śrāvaka vehicle have not yet matured—even if the path of the Mahāyāna is explained to them, they cannot comprehend it.
"For example, suppose there is a person who enters a battle array without wearing armor or carrying weapons; once he has entered, he will inevitably encounter immeasurable suffering and distress.

In the same way, for one who cannot diligently seek the vehicle of the Śrāvaka or Pratyekabuddha because their faculties are not yet matured, if the Mahāyāna vehicle is revealed to them, it will likewise result in immeasurable suffering and distress."
"Therefore, son of good family!
A person of wisdom first contemplates sentient beings and then preaches the Dharma, employing a mind of loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity; a mind intent on their benefit;

and a mind free from indolence. With a mind of patience, free from arrogance and negligence, free from envy and stinginess, and with a mind cultivated in meditative concentration, they preach the Dharma for others, ensuring that they do not cause others to fall into the evil realms or undesirable states."
Therefore, the Tathāgata is able to know the minds of others and rescue sentient beings; according to their wheel of faith, he preaches the Dharma for them, adorning himself with great adornments.

"If one preaches the Dharma for Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, it is always by means of the causal conditions of great compassion; for the sake of severing all fetters and afflictions of sentient beings, one preaches the Dharma to deliver them from the ocean of existence."

He teaches the Dharma so that, among the three vehicles, one may achieve accomplishment in accordance with whichever vehicle is appropriate; he never teaches the Dharma with the desire to cause others to fall into birth and death.

He teaches the Dharma by discerning the aggregates; he teaches the Dharma by discerning the sense bases; he teaches the Dharma by discerning the elements; he teaches the Dharma by discerning the path of the desire realm; and he teaches the Dharma by discerning the paths of the form realm and the formless realm.

He does not teach the Dharma for the sake of existence in this life, nor for existence in future lives; he does not teach it for the sake of conditioned formations, nor for the sake of mental perceptions, nor for the sake of mental activities, nor for the sake of volitions, nor for the sake of ignorance, and so on, up to: he does not teach it for the sake of birth, old age, sickness, or death. He teaches the Dharma for the sake of beings who are active and those who are inactive; he teaches the Dharma for the sake of the cessation of activity and non-activity; he teaches the Dharma for the sake of the non-arising of all conceptualizations.
"What is meant by 'conduct' (*caryā*)?
Conduct refers to dying here and being born there; if one can conceal this cycle of birth and death, it is called the cessation of conduct and non-conduct.
What is meant by 'wheel' (*cakra*)?"
Just as a wish-fulfilling jewel can sustain all things, pervading the void and traversing all lands;
observing that all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) in the world arise and perish like illusions and transformations, which is not shared with the *śrāvakas* or *pratyekabuddhas*;
for this reason, it is called "the wheel that severs all formations."
"In this way, son of good family!

The Tathāgata, by means of such characteristics, preaches the Dharma in various ways for all sentient beings; yet, like space, he is without discrimination, preaching the Dharma while sporting with mastery in immeasurable samādhis."
"In this way, the bodhisattva adorns himself with great adornments and, for the sake of all sentient beings, teaches that form is not empty, yet apart from form it is not empty;
and so on, up to consciousness, which is not empty, yet apart from consciousness it is also not empty."
The eye is not empty, and that which is apart from the eye is also not empty;
this continues up to the mind, which is not empty, and that which is apart from the mind is also not empty.
Eye-consciousness is not empty, and that which is apart from eye-consciousness is also not empty.
Consciousness is not empty, and that which is apart from consciousness is also not empty.
The sphere of infinite space is not empty, and that which is apart from the sphere of infinite space is also not empty;
the sphere of infinite consciousness is not empty, and that which is apart from the sphere of infinite consciousness is also not empty.
The sphere of nothingness is not empty, and that which is apart from the sphere of nothingness is also not empty;
the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception is not empty, and that which is apart from the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception is also not empty.
The four foundations of mindfulness are not empty, yet apart from the four foundations of mindfulness they are also not empty;
the Path is not empty, yet apart from the Path it is also not empty.

The twelve links of dependent origination, the three ways in which the Buddha needs no protection, the ten powers, the four fearlessnesses, the eighteen unique qualities, great loving-kindness, great compassion, great sympathetic joy, and great equanimity—even up to nirvāṇa—are not empty, yet apart from nirvāṇa they are also not empty.

"Good son! This is called the definitive nature and characteristic of the Tathāgata’s middle way and true meaning. For the sake of other sentient beings, he analytically expounds that all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are non-arising; he upholds the True Dharma, which pervades all of space, including the characteristics of immeasurable meditative concentrations and all dharmas."
All are like the light of the sun, illuminating and revealing the way to lead them into the three vehicles, so that they may attain nirvana and achieve liberation.
When a bodhisattva-mahāsattva teaches the Dharma in this manner, it constitutes the foremost benefit for sentient beings.

Having listened to this profound Dharma, according to their respective inclinations among the three vehicles, they shall, by cultivating various roots of goodness, dwell securely in the One Vehicle; furthermore, they shall not increase any unwholesome dharmas, and their practice being firm, they shall not regress from Nirvana.
“Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas preach the Dharma in order to sever the suffering of immeasurable kalpas of birth and death;
they also do so for the sake of sentient beings of the Śrāvaka and Pratyekabuddha vehicles, to enable them to cross over the four torrents.”
"Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas preach the Dharma for the sake of severing the four floods for all sentient beings;
those of the Śrāvaka and Pratyekabuddha vehicles, however, preach the Dharma only for the sake of severing the four floods for themselves."
"Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas preach the Dharma for the sake of severing the diseases of affliction of sentient beings;
Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas preach the Dharma for the sake of severing their own afflictions."
"Bodhisattvas preach the Dharma for the sake of severing the afflictions, karma, and habitual tendencies of sentient beings so that nothing remains;
whereas Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas, though they have severed the afflictions and habitual tendencies, preach the Dharma because something still remains."
"Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas preach the Dharma for the sake of causing sentient beings to attain the fruit and retribution of great compassion;
Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas, however, preach the Dharma while remaining detached from great compassion."
“Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas preach the Dharma solely out of compassion for all sentient beings;
although Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas also preach the Dharma, they truly lack a mind of compassion and the intent to benefit others.”
"Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas preach the Dharma for the sake of extinguishing the various poisons and sufferings of sentient beings;
Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas, however, preach the Dharma only for the sake of extinguishing their own suffering."
"Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas preach the Dharma for the sake of fulfilling the flavor of all dharmas;
śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas preach the Dharma for the sake of fulfilling their own dharmas."
"Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas preach the Dharma for the sake of all sentient beings so that they may attain the illumination of the Dharma and achieve great clarity;
Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas, however, seek only the illumination of the Dharma for themselves and do not expound the characteristics of the Dharma for the sake of sentient beings."

“Good son! This is called a brief explanation for the purpose of eliminating all the great darkness of ignorance and attaining great illumination, and for the purpose of desiring to accomplish all-knowledge and achieve complete awakening; therefore, one analyzes and explains the Dharma for others.”
Śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, desiring to extinguish the obscuring darkness of their own ignorance, attain internal self-illumination and achieve right awakening.

"Good son! Śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas do not give rise to weariness on account of sentient beings; they do not feel compassion for the sake of rescuing and liberating others; they do not act for the sake of causing others to obtain fame, renown, or praise; they do not delight in being flattered by others; they merely protect themselves and do not protect others, nor do they act for the peace and happiness of all sentient beings."
“Śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, if they see even the slightest fault in another, will inevitably give rise to offenses of body, speech, and mind. ‘Good son!’”

Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who abide in the Great Vehicle all provide rescue and protection out of compassion for others, even to the point of not perceiving any transgressions in the physical, verbal, or mental actions of sentient beings.

“Good son! If there are sentient beings who give rise to coarse, base, foolish, and wicked speech; who consider themselves wise even while not abandoning wrong views; who harbor jealousy in their pursuit of the benefit of others; who crave fame, exalting themselves and disparaging others; who fail to guard their body, speech, and mind; whose minds constantly dwell on evil without compassion; and who delight in disturbing and confusing those they select as fields of merit—[they shall fall into hell].”

If there are those who have gone forth relying upon me, yet they do not see their own faults and instead revile and abuse others with minds constantly distracted; they do not reflect upon themselves but harbor thoughts of disparaging the shortcomings of others; though they may give rise to a desire for the Mahāyāna, they lack a mind of tranquility and harbor grave malice toward others, remaining forever alienated from them; they constantly speak thus of themselves, claiming, "I am a follower of the Mahāyāna," and even teach others to recite its texts, yet they only praise themselves and disparage others;
for these reasons, though they extol the Mahāyāna, they remain undisciplined themselves.
Desiring to instruct others in the Mahāyāna path and cause them to practice the Mahāyāna, one makes such a statement, claiming it to be the Mahāyāna oneself.
This is like a corrupt Vinaya master who teaches others, saying:

Thus, being deceitful and crooked, they find it difficult to obtain a human body; they also lose the vehicles of the śrāvaka and pratyekabuddha, constantly tending toward the evil realms, and yet, unwilling to draw near to those who possess wisdom, they utter these words as a lion’s roar:
"I am of the Mahāyāna."
"Good son! It is like a donkey wearing a lion's skin, which considers itself a lion; someone seeing it from afar would also call it a lion.
As long as the donkey has not yet brayed, no one can distinguish it; but once it lets out its voice, everyone far and near knows it is not a real lion. All those who see it spit upon it and say:"
"This is a wretched, evil donkey; it is not a lion.

What I have now spoken is also like this: if one commits the ten evil deeds, they burn away the human seed and are not vessels for the Śrāvakas or Pratyekabuddhas; they are those who destroy the seeds [of enlightenment] and, out of such folly, deceive others by saying, "I am of the Mahāyāna."

"Good son! It is like a person who, lacking hands and feet, wishes to reach the battlefield but has nothing with which to act; a person who violates the precepts is just the same. If they wish to engage in battle against the fetters and afflictions, I say that such a person will ultimately have no fruit or reward. One who destroys and violates the prohibitive precepts and performs evil deeds does not become a vessel for the Dharma in any place."
If one were to say of oneself,

"I am a follower of the Mahāyāna," yet is unable to break the great array of the afflictions and worldly defilements of all sentient beings, nor lead sentient beings to abide in the Eightfold Noble Path and enter the city of fearlessness, such a thing is impossible.

"Why is this? If there are sentient beings whose deportment is pure, who are endowed with a sense of shame and remorse, who fear future lives, who distance themselves from all unwholesome dharmas, who delight in all virtuous merits, who give rise to great compassion for sentient beings, and who are able to deliver others from all suffering and distress; who rescue and protect those terrified by birth and death; who do not cling to their own pleasure but rejoice in the pleasure of others; who are always diligent and energetic, focused in mindfulness without abandoning their practice; whose hearts delight in tranquil concentration and who abandon flattery, hypocrisy, delusion, and deception; who well understand karma and the retribution of karma; who do not cling to the five desires and cannot be defiled by the eight worldly winds; who observe the aggregates and elements as if their hair or clothes were on fire; and who abide securely in the lineage of the śrāvakas."
Those who possess such characteristics are called followers of the Śrāvaka-yāna; they are incapable of undertaking the Mahāyāna.
Furthermore, what are the characteristics of the Pratyekabuddha-yāna?

If a person is endowed with the aforementioned twenty dharmas, they will be able to constantly contemplate the characteristics of the arising and ceasing of the five aggregates of clinging (pañca-upādānaskandha), clearly observing that all phenomena arise from causes and conditions, and also knowing their characteristic of cessation.
"Such a person is not fit for the Mahāyāna and cannot become a vessel for the Mahāyāna Dharma.
At that time, for this reason, the Tathāgata spoke these verses:
"The Kṣatriya relies on ten; so too do the Brāhmaṇa and the Śūdra."
If one cultivates true and wholesome conduct, one is fit to be a vessel for the Śrāvaka vehicle.
For the superior vehicle of the Pratyekabuddha, the three karmas are entirely pure;
one guards the sense faculties, and one's speech is pleasant and gentle.
Discerningly contemplate the aggregates; the elements and sense-bases are likewise.
Delight in solitary, empty places; with wise intelligence, contemplate causes and conditions.
Constantly restrain all the faculties; rely upon these ten wheels.
Within the indestructible vehicles, they are capable of serving as vessels for the Dharma;
mindful of crossing the ocean of existence, they practice equanimity regarding the three spheres;
not relying on the fetters of affliction, they draw near to the gates of liberation.
Those who are not vessels for the Mahāyāna, those who do not possess the great and supreme wheel;
those who do not diligently seek the Mahāyāna, as well as those of inferior faculties.
If there are foolish people whose minds are constantly filled with indolence;
Therefore, they do not belong to the Mahāyāna, nor are they fit for the great vessel.
Seeking liberation alone, they act with folly, flattery, and a lack of compassion;
constantly practicing the view of annihilationism, they too shall go to the evil realms.
Abandoning the True Dharma, they preach what is not the Dharma;
they obstruct the path of the Three Vehicles and discard the Vinaya while indulging in sensual desire.
They corrupt and destroy the teachings of the noble ones and strike down those who wear the saffron robes.
To disparage and slander others is likewise to destroy one's own body.
To cultivate a human existence, do not die from the ravages of the tongue;
those who constantly encounter the Buddhas shall manifest the teachings of the Three Vehicles.
For those whose desire is ablaze, for those of the three vehicles, and for those who engage in conceptual discrimination—
by joyfully revealing [the truth], they will certainly attain Buddhahood without doubt.
Even those who break the precepts, harbor jealousy, praise themselves, and disparage others;
This is what the wise abandon, yet they attain the status of Buddha, the Honored One of the Three Realms.
Preaching the Dharma with a compassionate heart according to what beings delight in,
and fully discerning the three vehicles, they will certainly become Buddhas without doubt.
Preaching the Dharma like space, with a mind that has no dependence;
the aggregates, elements, and sense-bases are all empty—one will certainly attain Buddhahood, without doubt.
Stubborn and perverse, they delight in breaking the precepts;
yet when they hear the Mahāyāna praised, they falsely claim to be bodhisattvas—like a donkey wearing a lion’s skin.
I now speak for the sake of the multitude: those who desire to attain supreme bodhi, [should beware of such].
Uphold the ten wholesome paths; do not destroy my Dharma.
In other sutras I have taught that one practices the foremost bodhi;
apart from the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, I speak thus for the sake of purifying sentient beings.
I have made offerings to all Buddhas, extinguished evil, and attained liberation of mind;
from them I heard that there is but one vehicle, not two.
Yet this assembly speaks of three vehicles, and among them are those who abide as śrāvakas.
Their minds are troubled by much mental fabrication, for they are not fit vessels for the Path.
There are those who abide as Pratyekabuddhas, ignorant and dark regarding the supreme Dharma;
being unfit vessels for the Great Vehicle, they teach according to their own desires.
If a dhūta practitioner hears [the teaching on] liberation, they will fall into the evil realms;
like one suffering from a cold-natured ailment who consumes milk, their illness can never be cured.
Such is the vessel of the śrāvaka: with a deranged mind, they preach the view of nihilism.
"Therefore, one should first observe [the recipient], and only then should one preach the Dharma.

At that time, when the World-Honored One had spoken this verse, among the immeasurable hundreds of thousands of people in the great assembly, there were many beings with distracted and confused minds who had severed their roots of goodness, denied cause and effect, and were headed for the evil realms. Upon attaining right view, they were able to sincerely repent before the World-Honored One and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Within the True Dharma of the Tathāgata, we have long cultivated the path of the śrāvaka and planted various roots of goodness, yet we were unable to become vessels for the Dharma of the śrāvaka."
We have now further sought the Pratyekabuddha vehicle; yet, deluded and ignorant, we failed to understand and gave rise to the view of annihilationism, thereby incurring immeasurable sin.

We now, before the World-Honored One, sincerely repent with all our hearts. We only pray that you will compassionately accept our repentance, uproot the seeds of our offenses so that we do not suffer their evil retribution, and allow us to once again cultivate roots of goodness and seek the Śrāvaka vehicle.
The Buddha said: "Excellent, excellent!
O son of good family!"
If you are able to confess with a sincere heart, there are two types of people within my Dharma who attain freedom from transgression:
first, those who originally do not commit evil;
second, those who, having committed it, are able to repent. These two kinds of people both obtain purity.

At that time, the World-Honored One, in accordance with the inclinations of immeasurable hundreds of thousands of sentient beings, preached the Dharma of the Four Noble Truths. Some attained the patience of the Dharma (*dharmakṣānti*); some attained the supreme mundane dharma (*laukikāgradharma*); some attained the fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpanna*); some attained the fruit of once-returning (*sakṛdāgāmin*); and some attained the fruit of non-returning (*anāgāmin*). Furthermore, eighty-four thousand bhikṣus, through the exhaustion of all outflows (*āsravakṣaya*), attained liberation of mind and realized arhatship.

At that time, there were also seventy-five thousand nayutas of hundreds of thousands of people in the assembly who had fallen into nihilistic views and severed their roots of goodness, destined for the evil realms; they now regained right view.
Before the Buddha, they all took refuge, confessed their transgressions with sincere hearts, and spoke these words:
"We originally planted the causes and conditions for pratyekabuddhahood but were unable to achieve it; now, hearing of the Mahāyāna, our hearts have conceived love and joy."

We, being ignorant and deluded, gave rise to the view of annihilationism, claiming that there is no cause and effect; by reason of this, we have committed immeasurable physical, verbal, and mental actions, as well as various other evil deeds.
For this reason, throughout many kalpas, they have constantly fallen into evil realms and endured immeasurable suffering.

Now, before the Buddha, they all reveal their transgressions and repent with a sincere heart, not daring to conceal them. Desiring to fulfill the Pratyekabuddha Vehicle, they speak according to its intent and attain the Samādhi of Radiance, reaching the stage of non-retrogression in the Pratyekabuddha Vehicle.

At that time, there were among that assembly eighty nayutas of hundreds of thousands of sentient beings whose tongues were unable to speak; they had all, in the past, slandered the true Dharma spoken by immeasurable Buddhas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, even slandering a single phrase or a single verse. Because of these karmic offenses, they were unable to repent, yet through the Buddha’s spiritual power, they were all enabled to speak today.
At that time, the World-Honored One, knowing [the answer] yet asking on purpose, said:
"What evil karma did you commit in previous lives such that you are unable to speak within this assembly? They then replied:
"In the past, under the Dharma of Vipaśyin Buddha, I slandered the Mahāyāna.
Some say that he slandered the Śrāvaka-yāna, while others say that he slandered the Pratyekabuddha-yāna.

"Due to the causes and conditions of this karmic obstruction and its retributive fruit, for ninety-one kalpas he fell into the cycle of birth and death, constantly dwelling in the hells and undergoing the state of a hungry ghost; his tongue was unable to speak, and he suffered great anguish."
Having today begun to regain a human body, and having received the Buddha’s spiritual power, I have now been able to speak.
By the Buddha’s spiritual power, I have attained the knowledge of past lives (*pūrvanivāsajñāna*), whereby I am able to know the causes and conditions of all evil karmas committed in the past.

Some say that at the places of the Buddhas Śikhin, Viśvabhū, Krakucchanda, Kanakamuni, and Kāśyapa, they slandered the True Dharma even to the extent of a single sentence or a single verse; yet by the spiritual power of the Buddha, all their past misdeeds were fully known, and all their karmic obstructions were clearly understood.

At that time, immeasurable hundreds of thousands of śrāvakas and immeasurable hundreds of thousands of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas rose from their seats, took refuge in the Buddha, and confessed their transgressions:

"In the teachings of immeasurable Buddhas of the past, whether we were fit vessels for the Dharma or not, we śrāvakas frequently gave rise to derision and reproach; we exalted ourselves and disparaged others, slandering, reviling, and proclaiming our faults while suppressing the good. Due to these karmic obstacles, we fell into the three evil realms and experienced various sufferings."

Although they may have made offerings to the Buddhas of the past and the assembly of great Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas, and even though they have repented, received and upheld the prohibitive precepts, heard the Buddha-dharma, and both studied it themselves and taught others, yet because of the karmic obstacles resulting from slandering [the Dharma], they are unable to attain the nirvana of quiescence or the bliss of meditative concentration.
“With these conditions of transgression, we now take refuge before the World-Honored One, confessing them openly and repenting with a sincere heart.
Others further said:

“Regarding the Śrāvaka disciples of the Tathāgatas, we seized their wealth and property, as well as their food and drink, or imprisoned them; because of this karma, we have fallen into the three evil realms and are undergoing great and heavy suffering.”

Although we have confessed our transgressions before the Buddhas, World-Honored Ones, and the great Bodhisattvas of the past, and have received, upheld, and recited various prohibitive precepts, yet due to the causes and conditions of residual karmic obstacles, we are unable to attain the bliss of meditative concentration or the nirvana of quiescence.

Now, before the Buddha, we all repent of all remaining karmic actions and immeasurable obstacles of sin; we only pray that the World-Honored One will accept our repentance and uproot all suffering in the three evil realms.

"From this day forward, I pray that by the Buddha’s spiritual power, my aspirations shall be fulfilled according to my will without hindrance, and that I may attain the bliss of nirvana and meditative concentration.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the śrāvakas and the great bodhisattvas:

"This is the remaining karmic obstruction of the five heinous crimes; it exists only as a name and has no substantial reality. It all arises from having disturbed and troubled the śrāvaka disciples, thereby giving rise to great sin."

Why is this? Even bhikṣus who have violated and destroyed the precepts can still serve as a great treasury of precious jewels for immeasurable hundreds of thousands of millions of nayutas of people; how much more so for one who maintains pure precepts and causes disturbance to those who cause the Three Jewels to flourish? This is called severing the seeds of the Three Jewels and accomplishing evil karma; it is also called destroying the Dharma-eye of all sentient beings and ruining the Buddha’s True Dharma.
"If there are those who, having gone forth under my guidance, cause disturbance, such karmic obstructions surpass even the weight of the heinous crimes of immediate retribution.
Out of compassion and pity for you all, I now permit you to repent of these karmic obstructions so that they shall be entirely extinguished without remainder."
During the Bhadrakalpa, when one thousand Buddhas appear in the world, you shall likewise repent before each of them, never again giving rise to slander against the True Dharma.
At the time of the final Buddha, named Loushi Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, you shall confess all before that Buddha, and all karmic obstructions will be forever extinguished.
Then all the bodhisattvas and great śrāvakas together addressed the Buddha, saying:
"So be it, World-Honored One!
We shall practice according to your instructions."

Within this Bhadrakalpa, we might fall into the three evil realms or the Avīci Hell and endure all manner of sufferings; yet we would still be able to bear them. How much more so when, under that Tathāgata Ruci, he causes us to repent, enables us to attain right view, and completely eliminates all our various karmic obstructions and transgressions born of false views?
At that time, the Tathāgata praised the śrāvakas and the great bodhisattvas:
"Excellent, excellent!

By means of such courageous diligence, you have caused your original evil karma to be entirely extinguished; you have been able to give rise to faith and understanding, supreme reverence, and the meeting with all Buddhas to attain various samādhis; and having abandoned the fetters and outflows, you have attained arhatship."
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Vajragarbha:

“Good son! With my Buddha-eye, I behold all those immeasurable, asaṃkhyeya hundreds of thousands of nayutas of sentient beings—from the outcaste Kṣatriyas down to the outcaste men and women—who, having planted but a small root of goodness, obtain a human body in future ages, yet are destroyed by evil associates; who do not give rise to faith or joy toward the profound Dharma but frequently engage in slander and defamation; who, regarding the blazing Dharma, either possess the vehicles of the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas or obstruct the Mahāyāna; and who, among my śrāvaka disciples—whether they have become fit vessels or not as previously described—out of folly and delusion, claim for themselves to be wise.”
After passing away from this life, they will undergo immeasurable suffering within the hells for countless hundreds of thousands of kalpas, as previously described.
Although these people have obtained human bodies, it would be better for them to endure the great and heavy sins of the Avīci Hell than to ever receive a human body for slandering the Dharma.

Why is this? Because those who follow evil associates, being arrogant and self-indulgent, constantly perform such various evil deeds, will ultimately fail to cross to the other shore of birth and death; drifting upon the four currents, they undergo great suffering and affliction.
At that time, there was one of great wisdom who shed tears and spoke thus:

"Behold all sentient beings who have obtained this human body with such difficulty, yet are far removed from faith and great vows; they are devoid of the characteristics of the mind, devoid of right view, devoid of virtuous friends, devoid of the proper timing, devoid of place, and devoid of ethical discipline, meditative concentration, and wisdom."
"World-Honored One, because these sentient beings are deluded, they act with arrogance and self-indulgence; they harbor such conceptions as to destroy the Buddha-dharma, all as described above."

From this day forward, I too shall make a vow before the Buddha: although we remain within the cycle of birth and death, we shall not allow the True Dharma to perish; may we ensure that the Three Jewels are never interrupted throughout the teachings of all future Buddhas.
At that time, there was again a great being (mahāsattva) of keen intelligence and wisdom who rose from his seat, joined his palms, and made this vow:

"Though we remain within the cycle of birth and death, until we have attained the patience of the Dharma (*dharmakṣānti*), during that interval we pray never to receive a physical body [in such states]. We shall not become ministers or high officials, nor even village elders or lords of towns, hamlets, and settlements; we shall not occupy the positions of royal preceptors, military commanders, or senior generals; we shall not become masters of sacrifices, merchants, or lay householders; we shall not become coarse persons, nor those who adjudicate legal cases. If we do not attain the patience of the Dharma, we shall not dwell in positions of sovereignty over sentient beings. Should we perform such acts, it would constitute a grave causal condition for the Buddha-Dharma, and we would surely fall into the Avīci Hell."
The entire assembly—devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, humans, non-humans, and so forth—all wept and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

Whatever evil karma we have previously committed while dwelling in the cycle of birth and death—whether through bodily action, verbal action, or mental action—and whatever we have extensively created or even rejoiced in, we now disclose all of it before the Buddha. We repent and eliminate it, vowing never to commit it again.

In this manner, the second and third times were likewise; he did not follow evil associates within the cycle of birth and death, and further vowed that his own body would not commit unwholesome karma, all as described above.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the great assembly:
"Excellent, excellent! O sons of good family!"

Since you have thus feared future lives, desiring to cross over the suffering of the various flows of birth and death, and wishing to enter the city of great, fearless nirvana, you have made this vow.
“Good son! By being endowed with ten dharmas, one attains the accomplishment of the dharma-patience of non-attachment. Good son!”
The Bodhisattva Mahāsattva does not cling to the internal body, does not cling to the external body, and does not cling to the internal and external body;
he does not cling to the past, future, or present body.
This is called the Bodhisattva’s initial attainment of the perfection of the patience of the dharma without remainder.
Furthermore, one does not cling to internal bodily sensations, nor to external bodily sensations, nor to internal and external bodily sensations;
one does not cling to past, future, or present bodily sensations;
and so on, up to not clinging to perceptions or mental formations, nor to internal consciousness, nor to external consciousness, nor to internal and external consciousness.
They do not cling to past, future, or present consciousness;
they do not cling to past lives, they do not cling to the present life, and they do not cling to future lives;
they do not cling to the realm of form, nor do they cling to the formless realm.
This is called the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s accomplishment of ten dharmas to attain unattached patience (*asaṅga-kṣānti*).
"If one can thus [practice] regarding the Dharma taught by the Tathāgata," at that time,
seventy-two billion nayutas of hundreds of thousands of bodhisattvas attained the patience of non-arising (*anutpatti-dharma-kṣānti*).
Eighty-four thousand nayutas of bodhisattvas all attained the stage of compliance;
immeasurable hundreds of thousands of nayutas of śrāvakas severed all fetters and outflows and attained arhatship;
and immeasurable hundreds of thousands of nayutas of sentient beings who had not yet resolved upon bodhicitta now all gave rise to that resolve.
Furthermore, immeasurable sentient beings also attained the aspiration for the mind of a pratyekabuddha.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Vajragarbha Bodhisattva:

"If there are sentient beings who have accomplished the patience of the Dharma (dharmakṣānti), they shall obtain the food, drink, and immeasurable wealth and enterprises of a consecrated universal monarch (cakravartin); other sentient beings who have not attained the patience of the Dharma cannot likewise obtain the rank of a consecrated universal monarch."
The Bodhisattva Vajragarbha addressed the Buddha,
saying: “World-Honored One,
for a consecrated Kṣatriya king who has not yet attained patience, how can he obtain food, drink, wealth, and his royal domain?”
The Buddha said:

"Even though an anointed king has not yet attained the patience of the Dharma (*dharmakṣānti*), if he is able to accomplish the ten wholesome paths of action, I likewise permit him to serve as a sovereign; he may enjoy food, drink, wealth, and property according to his own will and ease."
“Good son! If an anointed Kṣatriya king does not attain the patience of the Dharma (dharmakṣānti) and furthermore fails to fully practice the ten wholesome actions, he is called a Kṣatriya Caṇḍāla.”

Thus, being deluded, they shall destroy the profound and blazing Buddha-dharma and sever the lineage of the Triple Gem; they shall further disturb the śrāvaka disciples and inflict immeasurable and various punishments upon them, seizing their wealth, property, and livelihoods, slandering the wholesome Dharma, and concealing it within their hearts so that it does not manifest.
"Or those who seize the property of a stūpa or the communal property of the Saṃgha—all such persons shall proceed directly to the Avīci Hell.
Vajragarbha Bodhisattva addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"

"If an anointed Kṣatriya king does not attain the patience of the Dharma (*dharmakṣānti*), and furthermore does not fully practice the ten wholesome paths of action, will he inevitably fail to escape this evil retribution?

The Buddha said, "Even if an anointed Kṣatriya king does not attain the patience of the Dharma and does not cultivate the path of the ten wholesome actions, if he can accomplish the power of faith and take refuge in the Triple Gem; if he does not slander the True Dharma, even so much as a single sentence or a single verse; if he does not disturb or harass the Śrāvaka disciples who are pure in their observance of the precepts and possess virtue; and if he does not seize the property of the Buddha or the communal property of the Saṃgha—[he shall not fall into such evil]."

"If anyone sees such disturbances among these bhikṣus, and furthermore seizes the property of the Buddha or the Saṃgha, they shall be able to restrain them so that no further injury or destruction occurs."

Frequently hearing and receiving the Dharma that accords with reality, they should always make offerings to and draw near those pure bhikṣus who abide within the Triple Gem and have attained firm vows; they should harbor no doubt in their minds regarding the Mahāyāna, and they shall also be able to bring to fulfillment those sentient beings of the Mahāyāna and establish those who believe in the Mahāyāna in the True Dharma.

“Thus, a Kṣatriya king who has received this consecration has, in previous lives, obtained cities, dwellings, and material wealth from various Tathāgatas; I also know that he shall not fall into the evil realms.”
If one wishes to eternally extinguish all evils, one should practice this True Dharma; thereby, all evil karma committed in past lives will be completely eliminated.

Chapter Nine: Avoiding Censure and Suspicion.
At that time, Vajragarbha Bodhisattva again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!”
How does a bodhisattva mahāsattva not give rise to disparagement toward the vehicle of the śrāvakas or the vehicle of the pratyekabuddhas,
nor harbor disparagement toward other bodhisattvas?
How can one, among the assembly of the Tathāgata’s śrāvakas, be neither a fit vessel nor an unfit vessel without incurring reproach, and constantly practice well in the Mahāyāna path?
How can one attain sharp wisdom, all samādhis, various dhāraṇīs, and the patiences of the various stages?
How does one attain the dharma of advancement and non-retrogression?
How does one always encounter virtuous friends?
And how does one never be separated from the Buddha-dharma, while making offerings to the Saṃgha and all bodhisattvas?
"How does one never become weary or satisfied with roots of goodness?
How does one attain insatiability regarding the practices and vows of a bodhisattva?
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the Bodhisattva Vajragarbha, saying:

“Good son! Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas have ten kinds of wheels. If one accomplishes such wheels, then one will not disparage or find fault with the vehicles of the śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas, nor even with the vehicle of the bodhisattvas.

Among the assembly of the Tathāgata’s śrāvakas, whether they are worthy vessels or not, one will be free from all censure or disparagement; one will always attain advancement and never retreat from the wheel of Dharma.

Furthermore, within the Mahāyāna, one’s practice will increase without deficiency, and one will constantly attain meditative concentrations (*dhyāna*), various dhāraṇīs, and the patiences (*kṣānti*) of the stages.
Without departing from the Buddha-dharma, they make offerings to the Sangha and all Bodhisattvas, seeking roots of goodness without ever becoming weary or satisfied.
They attain firm and steadfast diligence, and give rise to immeasurable vows of practice.
All evil karma committed in the past is entirely extinguished and brought to ultimate completion through the wisdom of the noble vajra-ground.
All present evil karma is rendered without remainder, ensuring it shall never be committed again.

They are able to swiftly accomplish the unsurpassed Wheel of Dharma; they never tire of the seven treasures of the factors of enlightenment; they can eliminate the fetters and afflictions of all sentient beings, and are those upon whom people rely.

“Good son! For example, when a Wheel-Turning Sage King wishes to travel, the precious wheel is always at the very forefront, while all the other treasures follow behind it. It can extinguish the defilements and evils of all sentient beings throughout the four continents, and also causes all the people within those four continents to experience joy in both body and mind.”

The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva is also like this: if they accomplish the ten wheels, they do not disparage or find fault with the Śrāvaka vehicle, and even all sentient beings rely upon them for their existence.

"Good son! It is like a great chariot equipped with four wheels, upon which many people rely to travel along the correct path. Should there be clods of earth, stones, various grasses, or even roots, stalks, flowers, and fruits by the roadside, they are all completely crushed and destroyed when run over by the wheels."

In this way, for the sake of all sentient beings, the bodhisattva-mahāsattva crushes, severs, and eliminates all obstructive dharmas and karmic offenses, ensuring that they do not undergo their retribution.
Good son! It is like a sword-wheel that can completely sever the heads of enemies and others; once their limbs, hands, and feet are cut off, they can no longer be used.

If a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva can achieve these ten wheels, all the evils of the six realms of existence within the desire realm will be completely severed and eliminated until none remain, so that they shall no longer undergo retribution.
“Good son! For example, when five suns appear, all the waters throughout the great earth of the four continents will dry up without exception.

In the same way, when a bodhisattva accomplishes the ten wheels, they can eliminate for sentient beings all karmic obstructions, as well as the offenses that obstruct the Dharma; the roots of all sufferings are entirely extinguished.”
“Suppose, for example, when the calamity of wind arises, great winds from the four directions simultaneously blow forth, able to reduce all great stones and mountains to fine dust.”

In this way, the bodhisattva-mahāsattva is able to accomplish the ten wheels and serves as a common refuge for all sentient beings, causing the mountains of the four inversions, the fetters, the various karmic obstructions, and the heavy offenses of obstructive dharmas to be extinguished, uprooting suffering so that nothing remains.
"Good son! For example, when the lion king roars, all animals and sentient beings are utterly terrified.
In the same way, it is with the bodhisattva-mahāsattva: even non-Buddhists, various heterodox teachers, and evil associates are made to tremble with fear and lose their eloquence."
“Good son! For example, just as Śakra-devānām-indra, surrounded by his army and wielding the vajra-pestle in his hand, destroys the asuras;
so too, the bodhisattva-mahāsattva who has accomplished the ten wheels utterly destroys all those belonging to the heterodox paths of inverted views, as well as evil associates and the like.”
“Good son! It is like a wish-fulfilling jewel placed atop a high banner that rains down various treasures.

In the same way, a bodhisattva mahāsattva who has accomplished the ten wheels can uphold the banner of ethical discipline and rain down the rain of all dharmas, bestowing them upon all immeasurable sentient beings.”
“Good son! It is like the appearance of the bright moon in the darkness of night, which extinguishes all obscurity and enables those who have lost their way to find the correct path.”

In this way, a bodhisattva mahāsattva who has accomplished these ten wheels, for those sentient beings who are shrouded in the darkness of ignorance and have lost the Eightfold Noble Path, also preaches various dharmas to them, causing them to illuminate the end of all suffering and showing them the Eightfold Noble Path.

"Good son! It is like when the sun first rises: all grains and crops increase; various flowers bloom, and all medicinal herbs and cereals reach full maturity; the snow mountains melt and flow, causing the rivers to overflow, which gradually and in succession fill the great ocean."

"When a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva accomplishes these ten wheels, because they are tempered by the precepts and warmed by compassion, they preach immeasurable Dharmas for the sake of all sentient beings. They are able to produce the various flowers and fruits of roots of goodness; all fetters, karmic retributions, evil deeds, and the mountains of false views are completely extinguished. Ultimately, they realize Nirvāṇa, and there is no sublime fruit that they do not fully attain. Faith, precepts, generosity, learning, wisdom, and immeasurable samādhis proceed in this sequence, like a great river gradually becoming full. Because it gradually fills, it enables sentient beings to enter the city of fearless Nirvāṇa."
“Good son! What are the ten wheels of the bodhisattva-mahāsattva?
They are the so-called ten wholesome actions.”
Because Bodhisattvas accomplish these ten wheels, they are able to bring all sentient beings to maturity.

By virtue of abstaining from killing, Bodhisattvas enable all sentient beings to be without alarm or fear, free from all sorrow, grief, and affliction, so that their roots of goodness reach maturity and their karmic rewards are fully realized.

If, throughout the past limit of cyclic existence, one has wandered through the six realms and sunk into the river of birth and death, then by means of such causes and conditions as abstaining from killing, one can [purify] all the karmic offenses of body, speech, and mind, as well as all afflictions committed in previous lives—whether performed personally, taught to others to perform, or even witnessed and rejoiced in—which obstruct sentient beings from the True Dharma.
By upholding such a wheel of non-killing, one completely grinds away all evil karma, obstacles, and retributive sins until nothing remains.
Furthermore, by virtue of the causes and conditions of non-killing, one can cause all devas and humans to give rise to love and joy, free from doubt or regret, and attain long life.
At the time of their impending death, they will be surrounded by their beloved wives, children, and all their kinsmen;
their bodies will not suffer pain, and even when their spirits depart for the place where they go, they will never see King Yama or the various hell-wardens.
If, at the time of death, one encounters a spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*), maintains pure precepts,

and delights the mind in the field of merit (*puṇyakṣetra*), then after casting off this body, one will be reborn among human beings with keen and sharp faculties, and shall again encounter a spiritual friend who maintains pure precepts.
Always delighting in the field of merit and severing all evils, they seek all the practices of the great bodhisattvas; entering the deep ocean of wisdom, they eventually attain bodhi.

In whatever place they are born, they are always far removed from lands of evil where weapons and staves prevail; their lifespans are long and vast, and they dwell in sovereign, pure lands free from all terrors.

Just as that Buddha’s lifespan was immeasurable and boundless, you too shall be able to attain such a lifespan, preaching the Dharma and teaching sentient beings, and even after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, ensuring that the Dharma remains for a long time.
"Good son! This is called the first wheel of the bodhisattva-mahāsattva.

If a bodhisattva accomplishes this wheel, he will have no deficiency in the vehicle of the śrāvakas or the vehicle of the pratyekabuddhas, nor will he have any deficiency among all the śrāvaka disciples of the Tathāgatas."

They do not regress from all Mahāyāna samādhis, dhāraṇīs, and various patiences; they reach the stage of universal mastery; they constantly follow spiritual friends—Buddhas and bodhisattvas—to hear the true Dharma; they make offerings to the Saṃgha and plant various roots of goodness without ever becoming weary or satisfied; and they cultivate all the practices and vows of a bodhisattva without ever becoming weary or satisfied.
Why is this? All Buddhas of the past have completely distanced themselves from these ten unwholesome actions, and they likewise did not praise any single instance of such evil or unwholesome karma.
For this reason, son of good family!
If one can maintain even a single virtuous deed among these ten virtues, the fruit and retribution obtained through such characteristics will also be as previously described.
"Furthermore, noble son!
When Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas practice non-stealing, they are able to bestow upon all sentient beings freedom from alarm, fearlessness, lack of dread, and the absence of sorrow and affliction."

Regarding one’s own possessions, one uses food, drink, and material resources for the sustenance of the body in accordance with the Dharma, constantly seeking all that is beneficial and lawful, and harboring no unlawful desires.

By the fruit of these roots of goodness and karmic actions, even if one has previously wandered through the six realms of existence and been submerged in the river of birth and death, by the power of non-stealing, all the various sins committed through the actions of body, speech, and mind that obstruct the True Dharma—including obstructions regarding wealth and livelihood—whether committed by oneself, incited in others, or rejoiced in when seen being committed, are all ground away and eliminated without remainder by the wheel of non-stealing. Furthermore, it causes all humans and devas to love and rejoice without doubt or regret; and even at the time of death, though surrounded by wife, children, and kinsmen, the body shall suffer no pain.
After life has ended and the spirit has departed, one will not encounter King Yama or the various hell-wardens, but will constantly meet beloved spiritual friends (kalyāṇamitra).
With pure observance of the precepts and a mind that delights in the field of merit, one will eventually be able to abandon all unwholesome dharmas and accomplish all immeasurable wholesome dharmas.

In whatever place they are born, they shall obtain great wealth and resources; having such wealth and resources, they will be able to remain free from fear, never sharing their fortune with water, fire, or thieves.

This continues until they reach Bodhi, at which time they will fully attain the adornment of Buddha-lands with various jewels and jewel-trees, free from the notions of "I" and "mine," without grasping or attachment, thereby accomplishing the karmic activities of all sentient beings.
Being without the notion of "mine" and without anything to be grasped, and being without a life-principle or a sentient being, they bring all beings to full subdual within that Buddha-field.
Good son! This is called the second wheel of the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva.

"If a bodhisattva accomplishes this wheel, they will have no deficiencies whatsoever regarding the vehicles of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas; even the śrāvaka disciples of the Tathāgata will have no cause for reproach. Furthermore, they themselves will never grow weary of the Mahāyāna vehicle, fully attaining all gates of samādhi, dhāraṇīs, and the stages of patience (kṣānti-bhūmi), while never abandoning any of their vows."
"Furthermore, good son!

A bodhisattva-mahāsattva forever distances himself from sexual misconduct throughout his life. While all sentient beings are submerged by the flood of desire, he is able to bestow fearlessness upon them, remaining free from jealousy and the harm of feverish affliction; regarding his own wife, he constantly maintains contentment and never harbors unlawful desire."

By the power of the fruit and retribution of these roots of goodness, if there are any fruits of past-life sexual misconduct—whether committed by oneself, incited in others, or rejoiced in seeing others commit them—as one transmigrates through the various realms of existence within the cycle of birth and death across the six destinies, may they cause all such wheels of sexual misconduct to be entirely abandoned, crushing and severing those evil karmas so that none remain.

Until they attain the path to Bodhi and are born in a Pure Land—a place of supreme purity where there are no women—all those sentient beings are born through transformation; they do not receive bodies through the union of parents.
"Good son! This is called the third wheel of the bodhisattva-mahāsattva.
When a bodhisattva-mahāsattva accomplishes this wheel, they do not abandon any of their vows or practices, even unto the end."
"Furthermore, good son!
A Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva, for as long as his life lasts, abandons all false speech and always speaks in accordance with truth.
By this cause and condition, humans and devas rejoice; and until he attains Bodhi, beings who are free from flattery will be born in his land."
That which is spoken is true and free from falsehood; this is called the fourth wheel of the bodhisattva-mahāsattva.
"If a bodhisattva accomplishes this wheel, they shall constantly seek all the vows and practices of a bodhisattva, never becoming weary or satisfied, and never abandoning them for even a moment."
"Furthermore, good son!

Throughout their entire lives, Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas always refrain from divisive speech. By means of these roots of goodness, until they attain Bodhi, they tame sentient beings and cultivate the six points of harmonious respect so that they may be reborn in his land. There, all shall dwell with a single mind, mutually honoring one another without conflict or transgression, practicing the dharma of uprightness."
"Good son! This is called the fifth wheel of the bodhisattva-mahāsattva.

When a bodhisattva-mahāsattva accomplishes this wheel, they constantly seek the practices and vows of a bodhisattva without ever becoming weary or satisfied, never relinquishing them for even a moment."
"Furthermore, son of good family!

From the time a bodhisattva-mahāsattva distances himself from harsh speech until he achieves enlightenment, his ears shall never hear anything unpleasant. He will always be born in Buddha-lands where he constantly hears various gentle human voices and the sounds of music, and he will hear the sounds of all dharmas pervading the Buddha-lands."
With their aspirations and mindfulness perfected, they possess pure and resonant Brahma-voices; such beings come to be born in that land.
Good son, this is called the sixth wheel of the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva.

"If there is a bodhisattva who accomplishes this wheel, from the first production of the thought of enlightenment until the attainment of Buddhahood, they will constantly seek all the practices and vows of a bodhisattva, never becoming weary or satisfied, and never abandoning them."
"Furthermore, good son!
From their final lifetime until they reach bodhi, Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas remain far removed from frivolous speech.
Constantly in Buddha-lands, they hear the hundreds of thousands of Dharma-sounds of Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas pervading those lands, yet they always remain far removed from all frivolous speech."
Sentient beings who have accomplished virtuous speech and speech in accordance with the Dharma are born in that land. Good son,
this is called the seventh wheel of the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva.

"If a bodhisattva accomplishes this wheel, until they reach enlightenment, they will constantly seek all the practices and vows of a bodhisattva, never becoming weary or satisfied, and never relinquishing them for even a moment."
"Furthermore, good son!

From the end of their lives until they attain bodhi, Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas remain far removed from desire; they are always born in pure lands that are level as the palm of a hand and filled with various jewels, which are further adorned with jeweled trees."

Furthermore, there were various kinds of priceless precious robes, necklaces, banners, streamers, golden cords, and pearl garlands; and that world was adorned with various kinds of jeweled nets and precious trees.

The sentient beings therein are far removed from arrogance, conceit, and haughtiness; they possess dignified countenances, their faculties are complete, and their minds are impartial—such beings come to be born in that land.
“Good son! This is called the eighth wheel of the bodhisattva-mahāsattva.

If a bodhisattva can accomplish this wheel, until they reach bodhi, they will constantly seek all the practices and vows of a bodhisattva, never becoming weary or satisfied, and never relinquishing them for even a moment.”
"Furthermore, good son!

From the end of his life until he attains bodhi, the bodhisattva-mahāsattva remains far removed from anger, completely eliminating all stains, afflictions, turbidity, clouds of dust, and violent winds."

In that Pure Land, there are no turbid evils; pride and arrogance have been severed. Having been born in that land, beings possess upright forms and features, their physical marks are supreme, and their faculties are unimpaired. Adorned with meditative concentration and compassion, such sentient beings come to be born in that country.
"Good son! This is called the ninth wheel of the bodhisattva-mahāsattva.

If a bodhisattva accomplishes this wheel, until they reach enlightenment, they will constantly seek the vows and practices performed by bodhisattvas, never becoming weary or satisfied, and never abandoning them for even a moment."
"Furthermore, son of good family!

A bodhisattva mahāsattva, throughout his entire life, remains far removed from wrong views; moreover, by means of this wheel of being free from wrong views, he causes all gods and humans to feel love and joy."

If there are sentient beings wandering through the six realms of existence, submerged in the river of birth and death—such persons as these give rise to all karmic obstructions and afflictive obstructions of body, speech, and mind that hinder the True Dharma; whether they act themselves, instruct others, or rejoice in seeing others act, by means of this wheel of the elimination of wrong views, one shall crush and sever their karmic fetters so that they are extinguished without remainder.

Surrounded on all sides by his wife, children, and kinsmen, he shall experience no physical suffering at the time of death; as his spirit departs for its destination, he will never see King Yama or the various hell-wardens. Following virtuous friends, maintaining pure precepts, delighting in the field of merit, and constantly generating right faith.

After the end of their lives, they will be reborn among human beings; there, they will encounter virtuous friends and those who are fields of merit through their observance of the precepts, and by relying upon them, they will attain right view.

Instructed by spiritual friends, they cultivate wholesome dharmas, constantly remaining free from all unwholesome and evil states, fully accomplishing all roots of goodness, and practicing every path traversed by bodhisattvas without exception.
By these causes and conditions, they are able to deliver all sentient beings into the great ocean of the Mahāyāna True Dharma, until they attain the path of Bodhi.

All nets of doubt, various auspicious signs, the views of eternalism and nihilism, and the attachment to "self" and "what belongs to self"—sentient beings who have abandoned such things come to be born in that land with immeasurable lifespans. They all share the same flavor of the Dharma and are exclusively of the Mahāyāna; having cast aside the paths of Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas, as well as all celestial Māras, externalists, and the retinues of Māra, they have entirely distanced themselves from such evils and thus come to be born in that land.
The lifespan of that Buddha is immeasurable and boundless; he constantly performs buddha-work therein.
After his parinirvāṇa, he causes the Dharma to abide for a long time, remaining undiminished and even more blazing, all of a single flavor.
"Good son! This is called the tenth wheel of the bodhisattva.

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva accomplishes this wheel, he does not give rise to disparagement toward the Śrāvaka Vehicle or the Pratyekabuddha Vehicle, nor does he disparage those of the two vehicles, and it is likewise for the Mahāyāna."

Regarding those who can cause the Three Jewels to increase, expand, and blaze within the Mahāyāna, they harbor no disparagement toward the Tathāgatas’ śrāvaka disciples, whether they be worthy vessels or unworthy vessels, and are thus able to adorn the path of the Mahāyāna.

They constantly and skillfully cultivate and study all samādhis, dhāraṇīs, and even the stages of patience; they realize the dharmas of supreme progress and never depart from the Buddhas, great bodhisattvas, and spiritual friends, listening to the Dharma with faith and acceptance.

They delight in making offerings to the assembly with a mind that knows no satiety; they seek all roots of goodness and never abandon them for even a moment; likewise, they never grow weary of the six pāramitās practiced by bodhisattvas.
“Good son! If one can accomplish these ten wheels, a bodhisattva-mahāsattva will swiftly attain unsurpassed, perfect, true enlightenment. Why is this?

The Buddhas of the past practiced the ten wholesome paths and distanced themselves from all evils; they were able to manifest such infinite marks of various causes and conditions for karmic retribution, perfected the path to enlightenment, completely severed all fetters and latent afflictions, and utterly exhausted the three evil realms so that none remained.

Therefore, they are able to perpetuate the lineage of the Three Jewels, causing it to abide long in the world and remain ever-flaming; they ensure that one no longer undergoes the body of the three realms of existence, but turns toward Nirvana, severing the aggregates (skandhas), bases (āyatanas), and elements (dhātus) to enter the city of fearlessness.
By thus distancing oneself from the causes and conditions of the ten unwholesome actions, one fulfills the retributive fruits as described above. For this reason, son of good family!
If one does not cultivate even a single one of these ten wholesome paths, yet seeks the Buddha-way and further declares:
"I am of the Mahāyāna; I shall surely attain unsurpassed bodhi"—

"Such a person commits a great falsehood, practicing much flattery and crookedness through various forms of deception; among all Buddhas, they are capable of severing the roots of goodness in all sentient beings and heading toward the three evil realms."

Therefore, good son! Those of the great Kṣatriya clans, the great Brāhmaṇa families, the gods of the Four Great Kings, up to the gods of the Heaven of Neither Perception nor Non-perception, as well as those of the Śrāvaka vehicle and the Pratyekabuddha vehicle, by practicing the merit of these ten wholesome deeds, are all able to fully realize Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.

"Good son! Those who adorn themselves with these ten wholesome deeds, seeking the unsurpassed fruit and training in the Mahāyāna to swiftly attain the Buddha-way, thereby establish themselves in the locus of all meritorious roots and virtues."
"If one can guard the ten wholesome paths of action, then through these roots of goodness and vows, one shall fulfill the unsurpassed path.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to reiterate this meaning, spoke in verse:
"Awakened by the ten wheels, Desiring to leave behind all suffering;
One should not revile the śrāvakas, nor disturb those who wear the kāṣāya.
Following the vehicle of the pratyekabuddhas, with faith and diligent vigor,
one brings peace and happiness to all sentient beings while practicing the Mahāyāna.
All those Pratyekabuddhas, having awakened to the most supreme Dharma,
have purely cultivated the Buddha-way and swiftly realized Bodhi.
By staying far removed from taking life, they are loved and remembered by both humans and devas.
In every birth may they obtain long life, And skillfully cultivate karma free from harm.
In all places where they are born, May they always delight in the Buddha-dharma;
By drawing near to the World-Honored One, May they swiftly realize Bodhi.
If one abstains from stealing, they will be revered by those of all-knowledge;
having utterly extinguished all stinginess and greed, they guard the precept against theft.
In every place of birth, they shall always be of great wealth and act as a benefactor for others.
One thereby attains a majestic and pure land, adorned with myriad jewels;
having eliminated the defilement of afflictions and dried up craving and desire,
one who can distance themselves from sexual misconduct will swiftly attain a pure land.
Forever free from the mire of desire, they liberate and purify sentient beings;
they cause them to enter the Mahāyāna by virtue of abstaining from sexual misconduct.
Those who wish to attain noble wisdom should praise truthful speech.
Abandoning all false speech, one completely extinguishes suffering and affliction.
Ultimately attaining truthful speech, one constantly encounters the Buddhas and swiftly achieves Bodhi.
By staying far removed from false speech, one becomes a fit vessel for the good;
constantly meeting with all Buddhas, one forever abandons the view of nihilism.
Attaining the noble state free from defilement, one reaches the dhāraṇīs and eloquence.
Able to know the deep ocean of Dharma, one will attain Bodhi before long.
Always speaking gentle words and remaining far removed from harsh speech,
one is beloved by sentient beings and is able to extinguish the karma of past lives.
Causing the multitude to attain joy, these Bodhisattvas, leaders of the Dharma,
fully know the conduct of all Buddhas and have attained entry into the tenth stage.
Loved and revered by the wise, they remain far removed from frivolous speech.
Endowed with five virtues, one fully awakens to all that is taught.
Those who wish to hear the instruction of the Honored Sage, as well as those who seek the noble path,
shall offer worship to the ocean of Buddhas and swiftly attain omniscience.
With single-minded resolve, eliminate greed and lust, and do not destroy the True Dharma;
by making offerings to those clad in dyed robes, you cause the path of the Three Vehicles to blaze forth.
You shall always be born in pure lands, the abodes of the Dharma Generals.
Therein one attains wondrous wisdom, the foremost and unsurpassed vehicle;
always practicing a mind of loving-kindness, one remains far removed from all ill-will;
swiftly one attains meditative concentration, with a mind that delights in the conduct of the noble ones.
Born in a pure land, far removed from all faults;
dwelling wherever the Buddha resides, forever free from all anger.
Single-mindedly cultivating pure faith, they remain far removed from all false views.
To manifest the paths of the three vehicles—this is called the offering of Dharma.
It brings liberation from the evil realms and deliverance through meeting with the worthy and noble;
it fulfills the bodhisattva practices and leads to the attainment of supreme wisdom.
Abiding securely to preach the Dharma, one is able to accomplish Bodhi;
the samādhis, dhāraṇīs, and patiences all arise from the ten wholesome deeds.
Possessing the majestic power of the wheels, one completely grinds away and eliminates the evil realms.
Exhausting and extinguishing the obstructions of karmic fetters, One swiftly becomes a General of the True Dharma.
Chapter Ten: On Giving The Mahāvaipulya Daśacakra Sūtra, Chapter Ten: On Giving "Furthermore, son of good family!

If a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva accomplishes the Ten Wheels, from the first moment of generating the mind of enlightenment, they completely renounce all five desires and surpass all Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas; furthermore, they are able to serve as a field of merit for those of the two vehicles.
What are these ten?

They are to constantly practice giving, namely: food and drink, clothing, elephants, horses, and carriages; even one’s own body, hands, feet, head, eyes, marrow, brain, ears, nose, skin, bones, blood, and flesh—each and every thing being relinquished.

When practicing generosity, one should not be attached to body or life, nor seek worldly dharmas or supramundane happiness for oneself; rather, one should constantly keep in mind the liberation of all sentient beings, cultivating great compassion and the wisdom of skillful means.

Thus, one gives with such a mind to all sentient beings: giving for the sake of causing all to attain peace and happiness; giving for the sake of extinguishing the fetters and afflictions of all sentient beings; giving so as not to undergo future existence; giving without a coarse mind; giving without envy; giving even to the lowliest beggar in this same manner; giving not for the sake of receiving a reward; giving not seeking the state of a Śrāvaka or Pratyekabuddha, but giving seeking the knowledge of all modes (sarvākārajñatā); and practicing the cultivation of giving in this way even toward a single person.
This is called the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva’s mental giving, which accomplishes the first wheel of the adornment of the gift of Dharma.

"In this way, from the first moment of generating the mind of enlightenment, a bodhisattva is able to serve as a great field of merit for all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas; they should be protected, revered, and made offerings to."
