Why is this? Because all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, in order to sever their own rebirths in the three evil destinies and poverty, cultivate the practice of giving solely for their own benefit and not for the sake of others.

Because Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice giving with a heart of great compassion and pity in order to sever the suffering and affliction of all sentient beings, they are able to serve as fields of merit for śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.

One practices giving not for one's own sake nor to seek karmic retribution, but solely for the sake of the supreme and foremost bliss; one practices giving because one is ultimately untainted by the pleasures of the five desires within the cycle of birth and death among humans and devas; one practices giving for the benefit of all sentient beings without regard for the good or evil experienced by oneself; and one practices giving in order to sever the retribution of suffering for all sentient beings.
Because a bodhisattva is able to practice the dānapāramitā in this manner, they are capable of serving as a field of merit for śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.

If one is not stained by or attached to the five worldly desires, and is able to give such gifts while being fully endowed with great loving-kindness and great compassion, they are called a bodhisattva-mahāsattva, and are also called a field of merit for śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.

Suppose one practices immeasurable giving; if one does not sever the five worldly desires, it cannot be called giving, nor can one be called a bodhisattva. Such a person cannot serve as a great field of merit for śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas, nor will they receive the seal of approval from the noble ones. Therefore, one should sever the five desires and practice giving free from attachment.
If one is stained by the five desires, one is not called a bodhisattva, nor is one a field of merit.
A donor such as this cannot extinguish even a fraction of their afflictions, let alone be able to eliminate all fetters and habitual tendencies.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
"Accomplishing the wheel of giving, The wise one with a pure mind,
Completely detached from the five desires, Causes all beings to attain wondrous bliss."
Even giving but a small portion, it is all for the sake of eliminating manifold sufferings;
do not let [the recipient] receive but a meager fruit, for they should obtain the supreme field of merit.
Although one may practice various kinds of giving, if one does not depart from the five desires, [it is not true giving].
This giving is not the seal of the noble ones; it does not fall within the group of those destined for certainty.
One who abandons desire and practices giving—though the gift be small, the retribution is weighty—and both śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas serve as fields of merit for such a person.
Therefore, one should abandon desire and always practice pure giving to bring peace and happiness to all sentient beings; this is called the true field of merit.
"Furthermore, good son!

Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas have ten wheels of the Dharma-gift (*dharma-dāna-cakra*). If they can accomplish these ten wheels of the Dharma-gift, they will swiftly attain the Sunlight Samādhi (*sūryaprabha-samādhi*) and become a great field of merit for all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.
What are the ten? They are: relying on the Buddha-dharma;

relying on the Śrāvaka-dharma; relying on the Pratyekabuddha-dharma; relying on the Mahāyāna-dharma; relying on mundane and supramundane dharmas; relying on contaminated and uncontaminated dharmas; receiving and listening to them all with respect and reverence; accepting and upholding them in accordance with them; and explaining them extensively for others.

"If it is for the sake of śrāvakas, one should preach the Dharma of the Four Noble Truths leading to ultimate nirvāṇa; yet one must be free from envy and arrogance, not seeking profit, offerings, or any fame.

One should neither exalt oneself nor disparage others, but always give rise to great compassion for all beings and explain the teachings with discernment, without preaching the Dharma of the pratyekabuddhas or the Mahāyāna."

"If it is for a person of the pratyekabuddha vehicle, one should teach them the dharma of the twelve links of dependent origination, so that they may leave behind old age, sickness, and death and reach the end of suffering; one should not at all teach them the dharmas of the śrāvaka, the Hīnayāna, or the bodhisattva."

"If one is a person of the Mahāyāna, one should preach the six pāramitās, so that they may fulfill all practices and realize the unsurpassed path; nor should one preach the Dharma of the śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas for them."

They shall preach in accordance with the specific practices that each sentient being ought to cultivate; regarding the verbal teachings expounded by all Tathāgatas, even down to a single phrase or a single verse, they shall always revere and honor them, never slandering them, nor concealing or obstructing them.

One should regard the teacher of the Dharma as the World-Honored One, regard those who listen to the Dharma as patients, and regard the True Dharma as a sublime medicine; having renounced the five desires, one should always maintain an equanimous mind when wishing to preach the Dharma, without grasping at signs.
"Good son! These are called the ten wheels of the Dharma-gift of the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva.

If a Bodhisattva accomplishes these ten wheels of the Dharma-gift, they will swiftly attain the Sunlight Samādhi (Sūryaprabha-samādhi), become a great field of merit for all Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas, and be constantly protected and honored by all."
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
"The wise practice the gift of Dharma, expounding the Three Vehicles;
yet they never cause those who are unfit vessels for the Dharma to slander it."
Many śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas practice [the path];
those pratyekabuddhas of sharp wisdom are taught to enter the Mahāyāna.
This is done solely to make them fit vessels for the Dharma; one does not speak recklessly to those who are not such vessels.
According to the sharpness or dullness of their faculties, they are gradually taught to advance.
They always revere the Dharma, accepting it with faith and never slandering it;
toward those capable of preaching the Dharma, they make offerings as if to the World-Honored One.
May all sentient beings who hear the Dharma be caused to extinguish their afflictions;
may they not preach the Dharma out of greed for fame, reputation, profit, or sustenance.
Chapter Eleven: The Characteristics of the Precepts The Mahāvaipulya Daśacakra Sūtra, Chapter Eleven: The Characteristics of the Precepts "Furthermore, good son!..."

When a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva resolves upon the Great Armor and fulfills the wheel of precepts, if they achieve this wheel, from the first moment of generating the mind of enlightenment they remain far removed from the five desires. Among Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas, they are the foremost and most supreme, serving as a great field of merit; all should make offerings to them and protect them.
"What is the bodhisattva-mahāsattva’s wheel of adorned precepts? Good son,
it is when a bodhisattva-mahāsattva is able to leave the household life and receive full ordination, accomplishing the *prātimokṣa* that is not shared with śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas."

If a bodhisattva cannot, by means of this precept, eliminate the afflictions and all false views of sentient beings, then they are not called a Mahāsattva, nor are they called a great field of merit for śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas.

"Good son! If a bodhisattva-mahāsattva maintains a mind that is always equal toward all sentient beings, upholds the pure precepts with firm resolve and does not regress, and keeps the mind constantly single-minded without giving rise to divergent thoughts."

If one perceives beings of various kinds and immeasurable numbers—whether observing precepts or breaking them, being stingy or practicing generosity, or being of superior, middling, or inferior capacities—and whether they are acting with anger or malice, walking, standing, sitting, or lying down, as well as those within the intermediate state (*antarābhava*), the sense bases (*āyatana*), and the elements (*dhātu*) of the three realms of existence, one remains free from discrimination.

Thus one upholds the precepts: not clinging to the precepts of the desire realm, not clinging to the precepts of the form or formless realms, not conceptually analyzing or observing the precepts of those with perception, and not upholding the precepts for the sake of reaching or not reaching [a destination].

“Good son! By means of such characteristics, a bodhisattva mahāsattva gives rise to the great adornment of the pure wheel of precepts. From the first production of the thought of enlightenment, they are always detached from the five desires. Such a bodhisattva mahāsattva is then able to serve as a great field of merit for all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, and is likewise protected and honored by sentient beings.”
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
"The discipline of the upāsaka dwells in the precepts of liberation;
though shared with those of the Two Vehicles, it is not called the Mahāsattva."
If one cultivates the dharma of emptiness, One does not rely on the world;
Nor does one rely on any state of existence— The wise person guards the pure precepts.
Without grasping at the characteristics of the precepts, They are pure and free from all outflows.
One who thus guards the precepts is the most supreme field of merit.
Chapter Twelve: On Forbearance. The Mahāvaipulya Daśacakra Sūtra, Chapter Twelve: On Forbearance. "Furthermore, son of good family!
What is called the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva’s Great Armor, the Wheel of Perfect Patience?

If a Bodhisattva accomplishes this wheel, from the first moment of generating the aspiration, they are able to eliminate the five desires and become a great field of merit for Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas; furthermore, they are respected, honored, provided with offerings, and protected by sentient beings.
“Good son! The patience of a bodhisattva mahāsattva is of two kinds:
first, worldly; second, supramundane.”

Furthermore, when a bodhisattva possesses impure patience (*sāsrava-kṣānti*), they undergo the various states of existence (*bhava*). They are likewise unable to be without the notion of sentient beings (*sattva-saṃjñā*); relying on karmic retribution and relying on merit, this is also called "dwelling in patience regarding form, sound, smell, taste, and touch," and it is also called "inferior patience. It is a lack of true endurance, wherein one practices patience out of a compassionate concern for sentient beings.

However, if one endures out of a desire to please others through flattery and crookedness, rather than for the sake of bringing peace and happiness to sentient beings, such endurance is identical to that of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas; it is not a great adornment, nor is it truly that of a bodhisattva—it is merely a nominal designation.
Such a bodhisattva is ultimately incapable of serving as a great field of merit for śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas;
this is called the bodhisattva’s wheel of worldly patience.
"What is called the Bodhisattva’s supramundane patience of great adornment?

For the sake of all sentient beings, one practices patience without becoming stained or attached. Whether in all activities, speech, physical appearance, sounds, names, or the abodes of the noble ones, one accords with them all yet does not abandon the three fetters, the three feelings, the three marks, the three times, the three realms of existence, or the three karmas. One does not rely upon any such things, but practices patience with a mind that is constantly quiescent;
this is called the Bodhisattva’s wheel of supramundane patience."

“Good son! When Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas achieve such a wheel of patience for great adornment, from the first production of the thought of enlightenment they are constantly free from the five desires. These Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas are able to serve as a great field of merit for Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas, and they are protected and honored by all sentient beings.”
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
"This patience is said to be of two kinds: With signs and without signs.
The practice of patience with signs Is not esteemed by the wise."
To speak of the three karmas as having signs is based upon the aggregate of patience;
this is called tainted patience and is not the mark of a Great Being.
Within the four inversions, one cultivates unattached patience.
To bring the three karmas to stillness— this patience is supreme.
To extinguish all conditioned formations, neither relying on signs nor signlessness,
with a mind like space— this patience is supreme.
All sentient beings share one and the same mark; all phenomena are empty and quiescent.
When the mind has nothing to which it clings, this patience is the greatest benefit.
*The Vaipulya Daśacakra Sūtra*, Fascicle Seven.
The Vaipulya Sūtra of the Ten Wheels, Scroll Eight.
Translator’s name lost; now appended to the Northern Liang Record.
Chapter Thirteen: The Characteristics of Diligence. Chapter Thirteen: The Characteristics of Diligence.
"Furthermore, good son!

A bodhisattva-mahāsattva who accomplishes the wheel of great adornment and diligence, having departed from the five desires from the first moment of generating the mind of enlightenment, can serve as a field of merit for śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, and is likewise protected and venerated by all."
“Good son! The diligence of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas is of two kinds:
first, worldly; second, supramundane.”
There are three further kinds of worldly diligence:

first, the diligence of cultivating merit; second, the courageous diligence of practicing giving, precepts, and meditative concentration; and third, that which takes conditioned existence and sentient beings as its objects, abiding in the sphere of meritorious actions and their karmic retributions.
These are called worldly diligence and do not belong to a Mahāsattva.

"Furthermore, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva maintains a mind that is always equal toward all sentient beings. He exerts diligent effort solely for the purpose of eliminating the fetters of afflictions and karma; yet he remains in the noble, untainted state, neither grasping nor rejecting, and has no point of dependence. His mind is free from defilement and free from distracted thoughts. Whether it be those who uphold the precepts or break them, those who are diligent or indolent, those who practice giving or are stingy and greedy, or those with turbid minds or compassionate minds—he practices diligence with equanimity toward all such as these, and does not give rise to various conceptualizations regarding the three realms."

Regarding all sentient beings, whether hearing their speech or observing the places where they create karma, one practices diligence without forming any notion of grasping toward the aggregates, elements, or sense bases.
One does not rely on the desire realm, nor does one cling to the form realm or the formless realm; one practices diligence without giving rise to the notion of reaching or not reaching.
They do not cling to any conditioned activities, nor do they rely on the three kinds of merit as they exert diligent effort.

When Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas achieve such a wheel of great adornment, from their initial resolve they remain free from the five desires and are thus called Mahāsattvas; furthermore, they are capable of serving as a great field of merit for Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas, acting as protectors and objects of veneration for all sentient beings.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
"Attached to the six sense faculties, They are ignorant and dark regarding the four currents;
Though their diligence is ever courageous, Such people are censured by the wise."
Exerting effort within the spheres of sensory objects and skillfully grasping at that which is tainted is not called a field of merit, nor is such a person a mahāsattva.
The wise exert diligent effort to eradicate all attachments.
With a mind that has no point of reliance, one is called a field of merit.
Unattached to name and form, one acts as a refuge for the multitude;
courageous and detached from all aggregates, one is called a field of merit.
Illuminating the darkness of ignorance, One transcends and reaches the other shore;
Such is the wheel of diligence, Which severs the bonds of all afflictions.
Chapter 14: Characteristics of Dhyāna The Mahāvaipulya Daśacakra Sūtra, Chapter Fourteen: Characteristics of Dhyāna "Furthermore, son of good family!

Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas possess the great wheel of meditative concentration of grand adornment. If a bodhisattva accomplishes this wheel, from the first moment of generating the aspiration for enlightenment they sever the five desires; such a one is then fit to be a field of merit for śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, and shall be protected and venerated by all sentient beings.
“Good son! There are two kinds of dhyāna practiced by Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas:
first, the mundane; second, the supramundane.”
What is called mundane dhyāna?

If a bodhisattva, relying on the characteristics of the aggregates (*skandha*), practices dhyāna while being stained by attachment to the desire realm, the form realm, and the formless realm; or relies upon and becomes attached to the three gates of liberation, the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right efforts, the four bases of power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, the eightfold noble path, and even to earth, water, fire, wind, space, and consciousness—if they practice dhyāna in such a manner, this is called a bodhisattva practicing mundane dhyāna. It is shared with all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, and cannot be termed the practice of a Mahāsattva.
What is called supramundane dhyāna?

"Good son, it refers to when a bodhisattva is able to transcend the world and radiate great light, yet does not cling to the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right efforts, the four bases of power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, or the eightfold noble path. He practices dhyāna without depending on any such dharmas, including the precepts of body, speech, and mind, the three gates of liberation, the aggregates, elements, and sense-bases, the three feelings, the four great elements, the sphere of infinite space, the sphere of infinite consciousness, the sphere of nothingness, and the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception; he is entirely detached from emptiness and stillness regarding this life and future lives, and does not rely upon emptiness or great emptiness. This is called the supramundane dhyāna of a bodhisattva mahāsattva."

“Good son! By means of such characteristics, a bodhisattva mahāsattva is able to accomplish the great adornment wheel of dhyāna. From the first production of the thought of enlightenment, they remain detached from the five desires, becoming a field of merit for śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, and are likewise protected and honored by all.”
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke in verse:
"To cast off the heavy burden, One practices dhyāna with signs;
Yet merely severing one's own fetters Is not what is called being wise."
If one practices dhyāna with defiled attachment, relying upon liberation and clinging to the further shore, one cannot benefit sentient beings. If, however,
one seeks to cast off the heavy burden and desires to benefit all sentient beings;
One who extinguishes the fetters and cultivates the various dhyānas is called a true wise person.
One who severs craving for existence and, for the benefit of all sentient beings,
cultivates signless dhyāna is called a Mahāsattva.
Severing the bonds of sentient beings, Causing the world to be without fear;
Practicing dhyāna in tranquil extinction— This is called a Mahāsattva.
Chapter Fifteen: Characteristics of Wisdom The Mahāvaipulya Daśacakra Sūtra, Chapter Fifteen: Characteristics of Wisdom "Furthermore, son of good family!..."

Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas possess the Greatly Adorned Wheel of Wisdom; if they can accomplish such a Greatly Adorned Wheel of Wisdom, then from their first resolve they remain free from the five desires and are thus able to serve as a field of merit for śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, and are likewise protected and venerated by all.
“Good son! Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas have two kinds of knowledge:
first, worldly; second, supramundane.”
What is called worldly knowledge?

It refers to a bodhisattva who, relying on recitation and study, desires to extinguish the ignorance and darkness of all sentient beings and provide great illumination. They listen to and receive all the various and immeasurable teachings spoken by the Tathāgata within the Śrāvaka vehicle.

Whether writing it oneself or having others write it, reading and reciting it oneself or teaching others to read and recite it, or explaining the Dharma of the Pratyekabuddhas and the Mahāyāna, all shall be followed and accepted with faith by everyone.

Whether reciting it oneself or teaching others to recite it, whether writing it oneself or teaching others to write it, one is able to extensively explain, analyze, and reveal its meaning for the sake of sentient beings.

To recite and study the sutras and dharmas while seeking the various outflows-free states (*anāsrava*) and the flavor of liberation through the factors of the Eightfold Noble Path, yet not seeking the wisdom of cessation (*nirvāṇa*), and to constantly maintain a mind that clings to and grasps at signs—this is called the Bodhisattva’s worldly wheel of wisdom; it is no different from that of the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas!
One cannot be called a bodhisattva-mahāsattva [merely by this]. What is meant by the "Wheel of Supramundane Wisdom"?

When a bodhisattva-mahāsattva cultivates the path, whether walking, standing, reciting, or practicing, they do not grasp at, cling to, dwell upon, or conceptualize those signs. Such a mode of practice is not inferior; their mind is like space and identical to quiescence. They contemplate the equality of all phenomena, remaining entirely without attachment or bondage. Being without arising or ceasing, their minds never regress as they constantly practice the equality of the *bhūtakoṭi* (the limit of reality) of all dharmas. Deeply entering into quiescence, they attain the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
Not grasping at any marks, the mind neither increases nor decreases; not relying on the various stages (bhūmi), one likewise does not dwell in wisdom.
If a bodhisattva attains such fully perfected wisdom, this is called the bodhisattva’s supramundane wisdom.

Possessing this category of practice, one is able to accomplish the wheel of wisdom of great adornment; from the first generation of the mind of enlightenment, one remains unstained by the five desires and is also capable of serving as a field of merit for śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and all sentient beings, who shall protect and make offerings to them.
"Furthermore, good son!

A bodhisattva-mahāsattva possesses the Great Adornment Wheel. If a bodhisattva accomplishes such a Great Adornment Wheel, from the first moment of generating the mind of enlightenment, they sever the five desires and become a great field of merit for śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, as well as one who is protected and venerated by all."
“Good son! The skillful means of a bodhisattva are further of two kinds:
first, worldly; second, supramundane.”
What is called the bodhisattva’s worldly skillful means?
Constantly maintaining concern for both oneself and others, one brings sentient beings to maturity through various arts and crafts.

One can manifest such diverse forms of bodies—sometimes manifesting as a Buddha-body, sometimes as a pratyekabuddha-body, sometimes as a śrāvaka-body, or sometimes as the body of a parent—manifesting these appearances according to what is appropriate for those who see them.

If there are sick people or those who tend to the sick, who are emaciated and weak with no one to rescue them—whether they face all manner of terrors or even the point of death—he shall, by every means possible, rescue them and bring them to liberation.
They constantly practice the four means of integration (*saṃgrahavastu*) to bring sentient beings to maturity and establish them in the Mahāyāna.

If there are those among the śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas who are incapable of the Mahāyāna because their faculties are not yet mature, they cause them to cultivate such profound and subtle teachings within the vehicle of the two [vehicles].
They reveal and manifest the ultimate truth (paramārthasatya), which transcends the inverted realms of ordinary beings.

Relying upon the four reliances and endowed with the four analytical knowledges (pratisaṃvid), they abide in the path of right apprehension and enter the path of skillful wisdom to bring sentient beings to maturity—namely, through the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right efforts, the four bases of power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, and the eightfold noble path.

If there are sentient beings who cultivate fame for its sake, who are stained by attachment to gain and offerings, and whose faculties are restless such that they do not accomplish the roots of goodness for *nirvāṇa*,

[the Bodhisattva] instructs such persons to practice and recite the Śrāvaka and Pratyekabuddha vehicles taught by the Tathāgata, and instructs them to encourage and assist in accomplishing the merit of renunciation.

If there are sentient beings who frequently give rise to anger, whose minds are extremely malicious and devoid of compassion, he teaches them to practice the four immeasurable minds so that they may reach maturity. If he sees such sentient beings who are indolent, he teaches them to practice diligence; to those with much anger, he teaches the practice of patience; to those with distracted minds, he teaches meditative concentration; and to those who are ignorant, he expounds the True Dharma, causing them to cultivate wisdom so that they may be transformed and brought to fulfillment.
If there are sentient beings who have no place of reliance and lack a mind of reverence, one should instruct them to reveal and take refuge in the Triple Gem.
For those such as these, one should teach them to practice the Upāsaka precepts and also instruct them in the method of the Eightfold Precept Fast.
There are sentient beings who engage in various crafts and occupations; [the Bodhisattva] teaches and brings such people to maturity.

There are Bodhisattvas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges who possess worldly skillful means and wisdom. When a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva achieves such a wheel of skillful means and wisdom, he uses various sūtras, śāstras, crafts, and occupations to crush and subdue all the wheels of knowledge of external paths, heterodox teachings, and ascetic practices. This is called the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva’s achievement of worldly skillful means and wisdom, which is shared with all Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas.
“Good son! If there is a bodhisattva who does not rely on a wise teacher, nor take refuge in a virtuous friend (kalyāṇamitra),
then by such conduct and characteristics, they become defiled and attached to the world, thereby deluding themselves.”
Such a bodhisattva is unable to abide in the wheel of supramundane skillful wisdom; they are not called a field of merit, nor can they skillfully know the various conducts of sentient beings.

If one sees sentient beings who have not become vessels for the Dharma, as well as those whose faculties for the vehicles of the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas are not yet matured, and yet displays the Mahāyāna to such persons, this is called folly.

To teach those who follow the Mahāyāna without skillful means, causing them to abandon the bodhisattva path and instead cultivate the dharmas of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, is an error arising from failing to recognize the faculties of individuals.

If one sees a person who is a pratyekabuddha and instructs them to abandon that path to cultivate the vehicle of the śrāvaka, or if one preaches the Dharma erroneously without discerning the faculties of others, such faults constitute a transgression and a downfall.

If one sees a śrāvaka who is weary of birth and death, yet for such a person preaches that there is delight in the worldly fruits and retributions of the three realms and attachment to birth and death—thus preaching erroneously without discerning the individual's faculties—one commits such a fault and falls into transgression.

If there are sentient beings who do not cease killing and stealing, up to and including not ceasing wrong views, and who fully practice the ten non-virtuous actions and the roots of unwholesomeness—should one see such individuals and yet display to them only the profound Dharma of the Bodhisattva Mahāyāna, while failing to speak of the retributions of the evil realms, the suffering of saṃsāra, and the wandering through the various destinies; and if, failing to discern their faculties, one recklessly expounds the various Dharmas, thereby falling into fault and error, this is also called being foolish and lacking the wisdom of skillful means.

If one sees those who delight in upholding the precepts and speaks to them of generosity; sees those who delight in diligence and speaks to them of upholding the precepts; sees those who delight in patience and speaks to them of diligence; sees those who delight in meditative concentration and speaks to them of patience; or sees those who delight in wisdom and speaks to them of meditative concentration—this is called the folly of a bodhisattva. Such a person lacks the wheel of skillful means and wisdom, and possesses only worldly knowledge. They share this with all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, and thus cannot be called a mahāsattva.
"What is called the bodhisattva-mahāsattva’s wheel of supramundane skillful means and wisdom?

It is when whatever deeds a bodhisattva performs are all for the sake of others and not for their own body; they practice various kinds of arts and crafts, even desiring to share them entirely with others, as previously described."
If one has personal benefit, they dedicate it to others; seeing those who are capable vessels, they preach the Dharma for them, gradually teaching the vehicles of the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas.

Seeing those who are Pratyekabuddhas, they teach them to gradually cultivate the Mahāyāna vehicle. Furthermore, they do not preach the dharma that delights in saṃsāra to those Śrāvakas whose faculties are not yet mature.
For those who commit acts of killing up to and including wrong views, he teaches the Śrāvaka Dharma regarding the destinies within saṃsāra.
For those who delight in practicing generosity, he teaches the unsurpassed art; and for those who delight in wisdom, he teaches the noble, untainted path of knowledge.

By means of this wisdom, they bring sentient beings to maturity, yet they do not grasp at the notion of "sentient beings" nor the notion of "wisdom. This is called the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva’s wheel of skillful means and wisdom, which is the greatest adornment for transcending the world.

If a bodhisattva-mahāsattva accomplishes this wheel, from the first production of the thought of enlightenment they sever the five desires; such a one is called a bodhisattva-mahāsattva, capable of serving as a great field of merit for śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, and is constantly protected and honored by all.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke in verse:
"One should speak of the path of the Single Vehicle, yet one preaches the Two Vehicles;
this is to deceive oneself, and cannot be called saving sentient beings."
Those who are destined for the assembly of the heterodox and manifest inferior vehicles are indeed deluded; they are not called Mahāsattvas.
Those who aspire toward the Single Vehicle do so because they desire to hear the Dharma.
To delight in dwelling within birth and death is what the wise have taught.
With a resolute and single-minded focus, they transform others according to their inclinations;
this is called skillful means, praised by the wise.
For those who are solely Śrāvakas, he teaches so as to engender revulsion;
for those who are capable of being vessels, he teaches the Mahāyāna.
"Furthermore, son of good family!
The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva adorns the wheel with the compassion that takes hold of phenomena (*dharma*), yet does not take hold of the marks of sentient beings. Why is this?
To adorn [the wheel] by taking hold of the compassion for sentient beings is the practice of the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas; it cannot adorn the path of the Mahāyāna.

Although śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas cultivate loving-kindness, they do so only for their own sake and not for the benefit of others; they practice it to discipline themselves and extinguish their own karmic fetters, seeking nirvana once all afflictions are exhausted. They cultivate loving-kindness for the sake of the self, the person, and sentient beings, yet they constantly abandon other sentient beings in their hearts. Therefore, this is not called the Great Wheel of Adornment.
While one who has merely severed their own fetters cannot eliminate the afflictions of others, it is not so for the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva;
they constantly cultivate a mind of loving-kindness for all sentient beings, adorning themselves with great compassion.
This is called the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva’s "non-reliant compassion," because it does not rely upon the aggregates (skandhas), elements (dhātus), or sense bases (āyatanas).

One practices loving-kindness without relying on the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right efforts, the four bases of power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, or the eightfold noble path;
one practices loving-kindness without relying on the realm of desire, the realm of form, or the formless realm; one does not rely on this.
One practices loving-kindness for the sake of this world and the world beyond;

one practices loving-kindness without relying on this shore, one practices loving-kindness without relying on the other shore, and one practices loving-kindness not for the sake of reaching some destination.

Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice loving-kindness by taking only dharmas as their object; this is not something that śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas are capable of practicing. Only bodhisattva-mahāsattvas can accomplish such a great wheel of the armor of loving-kindness that takes dharmas as its object.

If a bodhisattva, from the first production of the thought of enlightenment, remains detached from the five desires, such a bodhisattva-mahāsattva is capable of serving as a great field of merit for śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, and is likewise protected and venerated by all sentient beings.
"Furthermore, good son!

When a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva cultivates the wheel of great compassion, from the first moment he generates the resolve, he cuts off the five desires and is thus called a Mahāsattva; he is capable of serving as a great field of merit for Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas, and is constantly protected and venerated by all sentient beings."
Why is this? Because all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas cultivate compassion solely for their own sake.

The bodhisattva-mahāsattva is not like this; rather, he disregards his own self and cultivates compassion for the sake of all sentient beings. Therefore, he is capable of serving as a great field of merit for all sentient beings.

In this way, a bodhisattva mahāsattva is able to practice the four means of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*) for the sake of others as well; for the purpose of maturing sentient beings, they may even sacrifice their own limbs, body, life, and wealth. Because of this great compassion, which seeks to bring peace and happiness to all sentient beings, they do not apprehend the mark of a sentient being, nor the mark of a giver, nor the mark of a recipient, nor even the mark of the karmic fruit of the act of giving.
When practicing the perfection of giving (*dānapāramitā*), one does not grasp at the characteristics of giving, nor the characteristics of kind speech, beneficial action, or cooperation.

Although practicing the four means of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*), one does not grasp at their signs. Always with the most excellent mind, the foremost mind, the mind of quiescence (*śānticitta*), and even with immeasurable *asaṃkhyeya* minds, one possesses a mind that is free from the aggregates, elements, and sense bases (*skandhadhātvāyatana*). Being without fluctuation, one always dwells in stability, adorning the mind of quiescence with great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*) to bring sentient beings to maturity.
“Good son! By means of such characteristics, one is able to achieve great adornment, which is not shared with any śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas.

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva fully accomplishes this wheel of great compassion, from the first moment of generating the resolve for enlightenment, they sever the five desires and become a great field of merit for śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, constantly being protected and honored by all sentient beings.”
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
“This Dharma is inconceivable, Profound as empty space;
Without form and without abode, It is accomplished through great compassion.”
Constantly and diligently practicing the dhūtas, the Bodhisattva’s supreme wisdom,
and the power of great compassion and heroic progress, he surpasses all people.
Sentient beings have no refuge, bound as they are by the suffering of birth and death.
Wishing to bring universal liberation, they wash away [defilements] with the waters of great compassion.
To dry up the ocean of birth and death is not the stage of the śrāvaka, nor that of the pratyekabuddhayāna; it is what the bodhisattvas take pity upon.
Craving, hatred, and delusion cause sentient beings to sink into the evil realms;
with this water of great compassion, I bathe those suffering beings.
"Furthermore, son of good family!

There is also the Great Adornment Wheel of Samādhis, Dhāraṇīs, and Forbearances, which consists of all kinds of distinct voices and eloquence that pervade space extensively, being boundless and immeasurable in number.

If a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva accomplishes this wheel, having severed the five desires from the first moment of generating the resolve for enlightenment, he is then able to serve as a great field of merit for Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas; all should offer him support and protection.

"What is called the Great Adornment Wheel of the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva—the various distinctions of eloquence in speech and all samādhis, dhāraṇīs, and patiences that pervade space, being boundless and immeasurable?"

What is called the Bodhisattva’s illumination of all phenomena is like the moonlight that shines universally upon the world: it is signless and without dependence, the mind is unstained, and within all samādhis, both body and mind are unmoving. The eye, visual contact, and visual consciousness are all unmoving; if visual contact conditions the arising of the three internal feelings—painful feeling, pleasant feeling, and neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling—the Bodhisattva gives rise to a mind of cessation and a mind of non-arising.
It is the same for the ear, nose, tongue, body, and even the mind, mental faculty, and mental consciousness—all are non-arising in this way.

One is able to give rise to a mind of the cessation of the three feelings and a mind of non-arising; all aggregates, elements, and sense bases of the three periods of time are likewise non-arising and without movement. The three realms, the three types of action, the three precepts, the three vehicles, the three liberations, the three faculties, and the three contacts are also a mind of cessation and a mind of non-arising.

Abiding nowhere in any place, they practice the dāna-pāramitā of signlessness, and likewise the śīla-, kṣānti-, vīrya-, dhyāna-, and prajñā-pāramitās, all while abiding in a mind of quiescence free from agitation or distraction.

The four foundations of mindfulness, the four right efforts, the four bases of power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, and the eightfold noble path all abide immovably; the nine successive meditative attainments are likewise immovable, and even the three modes of conduct—whether they conform to reality or not—are entirely immovable.

Knowing that all phenomena are entirely without obstruction, one abides in the Eightfold Noble Path; regarding dwellings and non-dwellings, grasping and non-grasping, outflows and the absence of outflows, this shore and the other shore, the absence of this shore and the other shore, the great and the small, the conditioned and the unconditioned, the wholesome and the unwholesome, the determinate and the indeterminate—one’s mind remains unmoved in all such places, and it is thus that one can give rise to great kindness, great compassion, and great skillful means.

To bring sentient beings to maturity, they protect the three vehicles and the four fearlessnesses; they distinguish the ten stages up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha. In all places, they abide in the unconditioned and the non-arising; their minds are ever-stable, and the three types of sensation born of grasping at signs are entirely extinguished.
The Bodhisattva Mahāsattva, having detached from all marks, attains the Great Adornment Wheel of the King of All Samādhis, which is the Samādhi of the Illumination of the Fire-Light of the Space-Eye.
If a bodhisattva abides in this samādhi, they can eliminate all past karma, and the sufferings of the three evil realms will be entirely extinguished until nothing remains.
“Good son! For example, when five suns arise, all springs, streams, ponds, and rivers, as well as the four great oceans, will completely dry up.”

In this way, the bodhisattva-mahāsattva, by means of the great wheel of adornment consisting of all samādhis, dhāraṇīs, and patiences—skillfully explained through eloquence and speech using analogies as vast, pervasive, boundless, and immeasurable as the void of space—[turns the wheel].

If a bodhisattva can accomplish this wheel, they will exhaust the three realms of existence, eliminate all evil destinies, and ensure that all karmic obstructions from past lives are forever extinguished without remainder.

“Good son! For example, when the kalpa of this world is about to end, these four continents, the eighty-four thousand rivers and islands, and all the mountains of the Four Heavenly Kings are all utterly destroyed, extinguished, and completely exhausted until nothing remains.

“Good son! It is the same for the bodhisattva-mahāsattva: one who has accomplished all samādhis, dhāraṇīs, and the wheel of patience can extinguish the evil karma created in previous lives, such that all evil destinies within the three realms of existence are forever exhausted without remainder.”
“Good son! It is like when thick darkness fills the void and the solar disc emerges, whereby all that darkness is entirely dispelled.

So it is with the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva: if they can accomplish this Great Wheel of Adornment, up to and including the wheels of all samādhis, dhāraṇīs, and patiences, the various darknesses of inversion within themselves and others will all be extinguished.”

In this way, the sun of wisdom, which is as boundless as space, is able to utterly extinguish all evil, unwholesome, and habitual karmas from previous lives until they are forever exhausted without remainder.

Such a bodhisattva does not follow evil associates, never departs from the Buddhas to hear the True Dharma, and likewise never departs from the practices of the bodhisattvas; even in their dreams, their mind constantly recollects the Buddha.

“What is the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva’s great adornment that pervades space, vast, boundless, immeasurable, and incalculable—the wheel of various expressions, sounds, eloquence, all samādhis, dhāraṇīs, and forbearances?”

“The bodhisattva-mahāsattva enters the first dhyāna up to the fourth dhyāna; enters the sphere of infinite space up to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception; enters the fulfillment of the meditative absorption of cessation, up to the fulfillment of the mind that has ceased the three types of conditioned activity.”

With the mind free from movement, perception, contact, and mental formations are stilled and unmoving; for one day and night, or even for seven days and seven nights, he dwells in the flavor of dhyāna and likewise abides in the emptiness of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-śūnyatā*).

Warmth issues from all the pores of his body, incinerating the fuel of all fetters and karmic actions; thus, in successive stages, he attains profound right mindfulness, and his entire body is filled with joy and satisfaction.

“It is, for example, like the son of a sovereign deva entering the samādhi called ‘Manifesting All Pleasures. Having entered this samādhi, every pore of his body experiences pleasure. In the same way, when such pleasurable sensations touch the body of the bodhisattva, he immediately recollects the Buddha; having recollected the Buddha, he then sees the Buddha and no other phenomena.”

"If one contemplates a single Buddha, one sees a single Buddha; if one contemplates immeasurable Buddhas, one sees immeasurable Buddhas; if one contemplates a partial portion of the Buddha’s body, one sees that partial portion; if one contemplates the boundless body of the Buddha, one sees the boundless body.
If one contemplates one's own body as having the marks of a Buddha, one sees one's own body likewise endowed with the complete adornment of the Buddha’s marks and signs.
If one contemplates another's body desiring to become a Buddha, one sees that other's body likewise endowed with the same adorned marks and signs as that Buddha."

If one wishes to observe all sentient beings as having the marks of a Buddha, then according to that observation, they will appear identical to the physical marks of a Buddha's body, with nothing else seen.

Whatever thoughts arise in the mind are all real and not false; one knows that all phenomena are like illusions and like reflections in water, and observes that the three types of sensation and the three types of mental formations are forever exhausted and extinguished.

Having observed thus, he re-enters the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*) and partakes of the food of the flavor of dhyāna-joy; for one week, two weeks, three weeks, or even seven weeks, or ten days, fifty days, and so on, up to hundreds, thousands, tens of thousands, millions, and billions of kalpas. He then re-enters the contemplation of the emptiness of true reality (*bhūtārtha-śūnyatā-darśana*) and, as before, practices mindfulness of the Buddha; having accomplished this contemplation, he completes it.

“Good son! By such characteristics, there is the wheel of various verbal expressions, sounds, and eloquence, as well as all samādhis, dhāraṇīs, and forbearances, which is vast, pervasive, fills empty space, and is immeasurable, boundless, and incalculable (asaṃkhyeya).”
"Because Bodhisattvas accomplish such wheels as these, they sever the five desires and extinguish all past evil karma.

They cause the three realms of existence and the six destinies to be entirely eliminated without remainder, becoming great fields of merit for Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas, and likewise being protected and venerated by all."

Having departed from the great darkness of ignorance regarding the four inversions, they shall no longer follow evil associates; they will never be separated from the Buddha and will hear the True Dharma.

Even in their dreams, they will see the Buddha, listen to the Dharma, and make offerings to the Sangha. Regarding all the paths practiced by Bodhisattvas, they will swiftly attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi and acquire a pure Buddha-field.
"In that buddha-field, all sentient beings are born by transformation, their marks and signs are like those of a Buddha, they abide in the Mahāyāna, and their fetters are thin and slight.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke in verse:
"Those who are capable vessels of the Dharma Shatter all fetters and afflictions."
Able to abide in the well-abiding, they are entirely free from doubt or difficulty.
Wishing to sever the bonds of existence, one should don the great armor;
practicing and learning all meditative concentrations, their wisdom is inconceivable.
Cultivating and training in the various dhyānas, one contemplates the supreme quiescence;
by means of this wisdom of mindfulness of the Buddha, one can exhaust all evils.
Characteristics and the absence of characteristics are equalized, for through emptiness they are all extinguished.
Forever severing the evil realms, never being parted from seeing the Buddhas;
skillfully training in all dharmas and making offerings to all Buddhas;
swiftly attaining perfect enlightenment, because of cultivating the mark of emptiness.
Acting as a kinsman and friend to the multitude, They abandon and eliminate all fetters and afflictions;
These are called the pure field of merit, Swiftly approaching Bodhi.
The marks of a Buddha appear among sentient beings, Pervading all worlds.
"For the sake of seeking the Buddha-way, one remains far removed from the two vehicles.

When this Dharma was spoken, immeasurable bodhisattvas, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, who had previously heard the true Dharma of mindfulness of the Buddha but had neglected or forgotten it, now all recovered it once again.

Immeasurable sentient beings, having heard of these hundreds of thousands of samādhis of mindfulness of the Buddha, all entered the skillful means of every samādhi and attained the flower-garland of the dhāraṇī of recollection.
Immeasurable sentient beings all relied upon the Śūraṅgama Samādhi, even attaining the Vidyutprabha Samādhi.

They obtained illumination regarding all dharmas, reached the stage of non-arising forbearance (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti), and, being far removed from dust and free from defilement, attained the purity of the Dharma-eye.
Immeasurable sentient beings attained the fruit of srotāpanna, sakṛdāgāmin, anāgāmin, and arhat.

Immeasurable sentient beings all sought to leave the household life and enter the Buddha-dharma; immeasurable sentient beings abided in the ten wholesome paths of action; some gave rise to the mind of a śrāvaka, some gave rise to the mind of a pratyekabuddha, and some gave rise to the mind of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, attaining the stage of non-retrogression.

Immeasurable sentient beings attained mundane right view; by reason of this right view, they severed the fetters of the evil realms and were all reborn among the devas or in the human world. Taking refuge in the Triple Gem and renouncing the five desires, they left the household life within the Buddha-dharma, abandoning all false views and attaining pure faith.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Vajragarbha:
"Good son! You should now confer this Dharma-wheel of non-retrogression upon the Bodhisattva Kṣitigarbha and bestow his prophecy."
If there are sentient beings who read and recite this sutra, explain it to others, and abide in this Dharma, they should be protected by ten dharmas. What are these ten?

They shall protect all wealth and property, and cause one to be free from all evils, all wrong views, all false refuges, the ten non-virtuous actions, all faults of body, all faults of speech, all slander, all violations of the precepts, all untimely illnesses, and all untimely deaths; thus, when such sentient beings approach the end of their lives, they shall all behold the Buddha and be immediately reborn in the heavens.
"If there are sentient beings who read and recite this sutra, they should protect these ten dharmas; these are called the hidden treasures of all Buddhas.

When the Buddha had finished speaking this sutra, the fourfold assembly, as well as the devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, humans and non-humans, and the Bodhisattva Kṣitigarbha and others, having heard this sutra, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
The Vaipulya Sūtra of the Ten Wheels, Scroll Eight.
